en: The *Vādanyāya* of Ācārya Dharmakīrti,
accompanied by the commentary titled *Vipañcitārthā* composed by Ācārya Śāntarakṣita.
Homage to the Subduer of Obstacles!

To that noble Mañjuśrī, who has forever dispelled the darkness by the radiance of a mass of various jewels of excellent qualities, and who is ever most diligent for the sake of attaining the fruits desired by beings of manifold kinds, because he is intent upon the arising of the welfare of the entire world; [to him I bow].
This pure and concise *Vādanyāya-vibhāga* is now commenced.
(1) That which is devoid of purpose is not undertaken by those who act with foresight,
such as, for example, the determination of the nature of a *balī* [or the investigation of its skin].

Fearing that this treatise might be considered purposeless, and desiring to dispel that suspicion, he has introduced the statement beginning with "the proponent of logic" (*nyāyavādin*) in order to demonstrate its purpose.
As for how the purpose is demonstrated by this sentence—let that be set aside for now;
rather, the meaning shall be explained.
The term *nyāya* refers to the reasoning characterized by the three-fold mark (*trirūpaliṅga*).

It is so called because by means of it, the establishment of the intended object is led to or attained; for this very reason, he will immediately state that the mark is indeed three-fold, beginning with the words "the mark is of three kinds.
Others, however, maintain that it refers to the speech that expresses that [mark].
One whose nature is to speak thus is so described.
They "restrain" him as well, meaning they defeat him.
Indeed, let them restrain one who speaks unrighteously, precisely because he is the subject of defeat.

It is not conceivable that those who offer instruction would defeat one who does not deserve defeat; however, for those whose minds are intent on attributing excellence to others, it is even possible that they might defeat such a person. In this regard, the word "api" (even) serves either as a conjunction or to highlight an extraordinary degree. To whom do they defeat? He says: [to those] in whom... [they defeat].
"In debates" (*vādeṣu*) means in investigations designated as proof and refutation; that is to say, in deliberations. In some places, the reading is "in disputes" (*vivādeṣu*).
In that case, it should be explained as: "disputes" (*vivādāḥ*) are contradictory arguments (*viruddhā vādāḥ*), and [the term refers] to those.
And how could they be contradictory? For the investigations designated as "proofs" and "refutations" function by establishing meanings that are contrary to those [positions].
Furthermore, how can they defeat a proponent of logic (*nyāyavādin*) on account of fallacies of the reason (*hetudoṣa*), such as being unestablished (*asiddha*)?
To this he replied:
"By means of the presentation of the systems of the non-existent and the wicked;
that is, the systems of those who are non-existent and unrighteous."
Alternatively, the "unreal" (*asatya*) are the formal positions (*vyavasthā*), because they are censured by the wise.

And those [positions] are characterized by the non-existence of the type of result and the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); their "propositions" (*upanyāsa*) are the applications (*prayoga*) by means of them—such is the analysis of the compound.
Who, then, are those shameless ones of such a kind? To this he says:
"Deceitful" means rogues, those who are full of guile and envious of the prosperity of others;

that is to say, because they suppress [the truth] in such a manner, this treatise is commenced for the purpose of refuting them—namely, for the purpose of the negation, the removal, of these three: the deceitful persons themselves, their presentation of false doctrines, or that suppression itself.
This is how the compound *tadartham* should be analyzed: "that which has this as its object."
The intention is that once that [superimposition] has been negated, correct inquiry proceeds, and all human goals (puruṣārtha) are preceded by such inquiry.
However, for one whose object is immediate, this internal discourse— which revolves within [the mind]— is grasped by means of this [word] "this" (idam),
because it is fully established as having the nature of an internal thread.
Otherwise, because it would lack existence due to its non-established nature, this employment of the word "this" would not occur.
The statement "it is being commenced" is a reference to the present time.
If one asks how so:

If it is argued that—on the basis of the grammatical rule *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavat* ("that which is near the present is treated as the present")—the relation must also be explicitly stated, otherwise this [work] would be as unacceptable to discerning people as the prattle of a child or a madman—the answer is:
this is true;
however, because it is subsumed under another purpose, it has not been stated separately.
For it is in this way that [the objection] is refuted, as this [work] is commenced for that purpose;
thus, it is indicated that the relationship between the purpose and the treatise is characterized by that of the goal and the means (*sādhyasādhanalakṣaṇa*).

As for other types of relationships—such as that characterized by immediate succession in action (*kriyānantarya*) and so forth—they need not even be mentioned, because they do not constitute constituent parts of the activity of the treatise.
For indeed, even when those [other conditions] are present, a treatise is not commenced in the absence of a purpose;
and even when they are absent, it is certainly commenced when a purpose exists.
Therefore, since the commencement of a treatise follows the presence and absence of a purpose, a discerning person must state that very purpose.
And when that [purpose] has been stated, it is considered that the relationship is also thereby expressed.

If it is argued: "Discerning persons do not engage in an undertaking whose body (the subject matter) has not been determined; therefore, since it is a necessary factor for engagement with a purposeful work, the body of the treatise must also be stated," [we reply:
this is true, but because it is already expressed by the statement of the purpose, it does not deserve to be mentioned separately, just like the relationship.
Since it was stated that this [treatise] is commenced for the purpose of refuting that [position], it follows that its body is the refutation thereof.
And when this is commenced for the purpose of refuting that, then the previous reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, by this [statement], two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are indicated: "This treatise must be commenced by a discerning person, provided they possess the capacity [to do so]."

Alternatively, it [the treatise] is to be accepted because it possesses a purpose and because it possesses a connection, like other treatises; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Having thus stated the purpose, he recites a verse that summarizes the entire meaning of the treatise, beginning with "The statement of what is not a member of the proof," and so forth.

The statement of what is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) and the failure to point out a fault (*adoṣodbhāvana*) are, respectively, the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), that is, the grounds for loss, for the two parties—the proponent and the opponent. As for the phrase "but other [points]," this refers to the points of defeat such as the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*) and so forth, which were devised by Akṣapāda and will be discussed later; these are not accepted as points of defeat because they are considered improper.
The term "point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*) carries over [from the previous context].

This, first of all, is the meaning of the verse in brief. With the words "of the desired" (*iṣṭasya*) and so forth, he begins the detailed analysis: the "desired object" (*iṣṭo 'rthaḥ*), such as "sound is impermanent," is that which is intended as the probandum (*sādhyatvena īpsitaḥ*).
Its accomplishment (*siddhi*) is its realization (*pratipatti*), which is the means of proof (*sādhana*).
By this, he shows that in this explanation the word *sādhana* is intended as the accomplishment of the state (*bhāva-sādhana*), and not as the instrument of action (*karaṇa-sādhana*).
Regarding that means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), what is its member (*aṅga*) characterized by the attainment of the desired object?
To this he says: it is the "accomplisher" (*nirvarttaka*), which is to say, the "producer" (*janaka*). By this, he explains the word "member."
The meaning is that the word *aṅga* here is a synonym for "cause" (*kāraṇa*), not a synonym for "component part" (*avayava*).
Furthermore, that which is called a "member of the proof" (*sādhanāṅga*) here is the logical mark (*liṅga*) whose nature has been ascertained.
The statement of this member of the proof is the communication of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*).
The non-statement, non-utterance, or non-expression of that member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) is what constitutes the "statement of a non-member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacana*).

By this, he conveys that in this interpretation one should not understand "statement of a non-member of the proof" to mean the statement of things such as the application (*upanaya*) which are not members of the proof;
rather, it means precisely the non-statement of a member of the proof itself.
Therefore, the statement of that which is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*) is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent.
By this, he explains the first half of the verse. He asks: "But how can the non-utterance of a member of the proof constitute a point of defeat? To this, he says:

"Accepting that" means: by means of a "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*)—functioning as the instrument of the proposition (*pratijñā*) "I shall prove this, having accepted this desired probandum"—one remains silent.
Here, "lack of ingenuity" is understood as the forgetting of a previously understood matter and a state of being paralyzed.

By this, he states that there is a total failure to utter a member of the proof; for even if it were uttered, if it is not established, then although spoken, it is as if unspoken because it does not perform its own function.
Intending this, he said:
"Or because of the failure to establish a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*). The phrase "having admitted that" (*tadabhyupagamya*) carries over [from the previous context].
The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative in relation to what precedes it.
The non-justification of a member of the proof consists in the failure to demonstrate certainty regarding all three aspects [of the reason].
Therefore, due to silence and due to the lack of justification, there is the non-utterance of a member of the proof.
And thus, the connection with the subject at hand is that "the ground for the defeat of the proponent (*vādī*) is due to not providing the form of the matter promised.
In some places, however, the reading is *vādinaḥ* (genitive);
in that case, the word *tat* refers back to the aforementioned non-utterance (*anuccāraṇa*).

How, then, does the lack of support for the members of the proof (sādhanāṅga) occur? For one might occasionally say that because of the lack of support through the opposite of those [members], and because it fails to establish the meaning of the thesis (pratijñātārtha), the proponent (vādin) is subject to defeat (nigrahādhikaraṇatva). Desiring to refute this, he sets forth the initial argument beginning with "only threefold," etc., stating that the sign (liṅga)—which is the means of making [the proof] a member—is indeed of only three types; [it is the means] for the comprehension of what? Of non-establishment (asiddhi), which consists in the form of cognition.
To whose success [does it belong]? He says:
"Of that which is not perceived"—that is to say, of an object that is not directly manifest but is to be inferred.
The restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) expresses the exclusion of four [senses] and so forth.
"It is indeed threefold.
If it is asked how this restriction [is established],
it is because the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is established as being twofold, by way of affirmation and negation.
And that [logical reason] must be either positive in form, consisting of existence, or consisting of a cause; it cannot be otherwise,
because in those other cases there can be no necessary connection (pratibandha) with the probandum.

For it is not logical that the existence of one thing should entail the existence of another thing that is neither its cause nor its effect— just as the existence of a camel does not entail the existence of a mat.
Nor is it reasonable that the cessation of one thing should entail the cessation of another thing that is neither its cause nor its effect.
It would be like [using] a camel as a sign for the exclusion of a cloth;
nor is it logical that something devoid of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) should possess the capacity to indicate,
because it would follow that a cloth could also indicate a camel.

However, when there is the existence of a phenomenon that constitutes its own nature (*svabhāva*), the existence of another thing that also constitutes its own nature is logical; for a nature does not exist while abandoning its possibility [of being present], because it would follow that it lacks the state of being that very nature. And when that [nature] ceases, there is cessation.
It is logical that when the effect exists, the cause also exists;

and upon the cessation of that [cause], there is cessation [of the effect]. Otherwise, if it could exist even without that [cause], then it would not be the effect of that [cause] at all, just like anything else.
Therefore, there is a distinction between the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the cause (*kāraṇa*), and the probandum (*sādhya*).
The probandum (*sādhya*) is indeed twofold in its positive form, because the logical reason (*hetu*) is necessarily connected to it:

a probandum that is of the nature of an essential identity (*svabhāva*) is established by an essential-reason (*svabhāvahetu*), and a probandum that is of the nature of an effect (*kārya*) is established by an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). This must be accepted; furthermore, even regarding negation, it is only non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta-anupalabdhi*) that establishes it.
He will explain this further in detail later;
for now, the essential point here is summarized as follows: the determination of the mark (*liṅga*) as the cognizer depends upon its object (*viṣaya*).
And that object must be either an affirmation (*vidhi*) or a negation (*pratiṣedha*).

In an affirmative [inference], either another object is affirmed or not another object is affirmed; even when another object is affirmed, either the effect or both the cause and the effect are established.

Even in the presentation of an effect, either the generality of the cause—such as a mere entity distinguished from non-clouds—is stated as the logical mark (*liṅga*), or it is a specific cause, such as clouds, whose capacity is unimpeded.
A negation, moreover, must be established either through the non-perception or the perception of that which is intended to be negated.
Even in the case of non-perception, there are the following alternatives: it may consist merely in the cessation of perception;
or it may be of a state where the conditions for perception are equally present, consisting in the perception of another object alone.

In this regard, even a mere cause such as a cloud, though possessed of deep rumbling and other signs, does not necessarily bring about its effect, such as rain; for there is the possibility of an intervening obstacle, which constitutes a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Therefore, a mere cause is not a reliable indicator (*gamaka*).

Furthermore, even from a specific cause whose power is unimpeded, the effect itself arises prior to the cognition of the inferable object—which is mediated by the recollection of the relationship—such that it becomes perceptible to sensory cognition (*akṣajñāna*); thus, that [specific cause] is also not [the indicator].
The state of being a mark (liṅgatva) is as follows: it is logical that the effect is a mark of the cause,
because of its invariable concomitance with it.

Alternatively, if one were to overstep that [definition], one would violate its logical necessity (*hetumattā*). Furthermore, neither of these two [alternatives] is tenable: [the first] because it lacks a connection and a consistent application, and [the second] because it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It is therefore logical that even when there is no distinct object (*anarthāntara*), [the probans] is understood through non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*).
Even a negation is not tenable through apprehension, because of the contradiction;
for how indeed can it be logically consistent that something is both apprehended and does not exist?
Furthermore, even the mere cessation of the cognition of that [object] is inconclusive.

However, the conventional designation of non-existence for that which is associated with a single cognition is logical because of its perceived isolation; for if it were actually present, it would necessarily be perceived.
Furthermore, it is not logical for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is impossible to have that as its object, just as, for example, a horse's horn.

Furthermore, according to the manner already described, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth would be a logical mark (*liṅga*) imagined by others as being connected with something else; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the cognition of blue and so forth is [the probandum], or that very same [cognition] is the logical mark, such as an effect (*kārya*) and so on.

The impossibility of the meaning of the word *naimittika* (indicative) serves as a subverting argument. What, then, is established in this way? That other [terms] are non-indicative. For instance, "being the object," "being indicative," and "being illuminating" are synonyms.

Therefore, since the probandum (*sādhya*) is of three kinds, it is established that the logical reason (*hetu*) which establishes it is likewise of only three kinds. To explain how it is of three kinds, he says:
"essential nature" (*svabhāva*), and so forth.
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a conjunction with respect to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*).

This demonstration of the intended reasons is threefold—due to the divisions of intrinsic nature, effect, and non-perception (*anupalambha*)—and constitutes a member for the establishment of that which is not perceived.

It is not, however, [threefold] due to the divisions of cause (*kāraṇa*), co-inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*), contradictory (*virodhin*), and so forth; this is for the purpose of showing [that].
But should it not rather be stated as "non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension"?
For it is only that [non-apprehension] which is established as a valid member [of the proof] by the logic to be stated later, and not mere non-apprehension.
If it is asked: "In that case, why was it stated in general terms?"

Thus, because this section concerns the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) as they have been established, even though this word "non-perception" (*anupalambha*) is a general term, it refers specifically to non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
For indeed, even general words, through the proximity of other words and the force of the context, come to rest upon specific meanings.
As it has been said:
For it is not only the proximity of words with specific meanings that is the cause for the establishment of a specific sense; rather, context, capacity, and so forth are also factors.
Furthermore, he will demonstrate later on how it is impossible for mere non-perception (*anupalambha*) alone to constitute a valid member of a proof.

Alternatively, this objection is simply not to be raised, because the present section deals specifically with inferential marks (*liṅga*) that serve as causes for establishing what is not perceived through direct perception.
Furthermore, what is the justification for these three types of means of proof (*sādhana*), such that their lack of justification would arise from their opposite? To this he says:
"Of that," and so forth.

In this context, the word *sādhya* denotes the property (*dharma*) alone, such as impermanence and so forth, by means of a metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) applied to the collection of its parts; it does not denote the collection of both the property and the subject (*dharmin*), because that would entail the impossibility of pervasion (*vyāpti*). This is because impermanence and other such properties, when qualified by a specific subject like sound, do not exist in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*).

Having established pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance has been stated. The proof of existence (*bhāva-sādhana*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*)— such as sound (*śabda*)— whose specific nature is sought to be known,
means the statement of its presence (*sattva*) by means of the valid cognition that establishes the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
By this as well, the ascertainment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) has been stated.

But how is it that, having established pervasion (*vyāpti*) through a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), the presence [of the reason] in the subject (*dharmin*) is then stated? To this, he provides an example, beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*).
By the phrase "all that," he explains the demonstration of pervasion through a comprehensive summary.
For what purpose?
To eliminate misconceptions.

For instance, some opponents maintain that internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) and external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) are demonstrated respectively with respect to the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
That is not correct, because pervasion follows from the nature of things (*vastubalāyātatvāt*).
He asks: does such a restriction of sequence exist here—that one must first establish pervasion with the probandum (*sādhya*) and only afterwards state its presence in the locus (*dharmin*)?

Regarding the passage beginning with "atrāpi" and so forth: here, in my own system (*manmate*), which establishes the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), the word "api" (even/also) is to be connected with either "restriction" (*avadhāraṇa*) or "negation" (*pratiṣedha*).
That is to say, there is no such fixed rule of sequence (*kramaniyama*)—meaning, no fixed rule of order—at all.
He asks: "What is the reason?
and replies: "Because there is no difference between the two cases regarding the establishment of the desired object.

This refers to whether one first states the proof of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and then states the proof of the existence of the locus (*dharmin*), or whether one first states the proof of the existence of the locus and then states the proof of pervasion.
The meaning is that there is no distinction in the accomplishment of the goal to be proven (*sādhyārtha*).
Such is the underlying intention: for what purpose is a fixed order (*kramaniyama*) resorted to?
It is for the sake of accomplishing the goal to be proven.
Just as in the case of the similar instance (*sādharmyavat*):
in the formulation of an example, the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of the reason with the probandum alone is demonstrated,
not that of the probandum by means of the reason.

Likewise, in the case of the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyavat*), it is stated that the absence of the reason (*hetu*) occurs only where there is the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*); however, it is not stated that the probandum is absent where the reason is absent.
For what purpose?

Let it not be that, due to the failure to demonstrate the reason’s inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*), there results both the non-establishment of the intended object and the establishment of its opposite. As it has been said:
"For in this way, the reason exists only in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)."
And it is possible to demonstrate non-existence precisely in the absence of the probandum,
not by the reverse;
for example, here [in the case of sound], there is no permanence because of being unproduced, or no perishability because of being an effect.
It might be argued that the application (*samanvaya*) is unspoken, performed, and culminates in pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*).
In that case, it would be appropriate here to rely upon a sequential order.
However, since the intended meaning is established even without this [sequence], it is well said that there is no fixed rule regarding sequence.
If it is asked why this is so— namely, that there is no difference between the two cases regarding the accomplishment of the desired object— he says:
"Because [it occurs] in the locus (dharmin)," and so forth.

It was stated previously that pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be established by means of the probandum (*sādhya*). [The author] asks: "What, then, is the proof of that pervasion? and answers with the words beginning "In this regard" (*atretyādi*).
"Herein" refers to this reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*).
As for the reasons based on effect (*kārya*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*), the proof of pervasion will be stated later.
"Of the opposite" means of that which exists as the probans (*hetu*) while the probandum (*sādhya*) is present; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

The meaning is that the statement of the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)—by which the reason (*hetu*), when occurring in the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaye*), is subverted—is the means of establishing pervasion (*vyāptisādhana*). What, then, is this demonstration of the subverting proof? He says: "If not all things are existent and produced," whereby he refers back to the two previously mentioned reasons.
The connection [of the argument] is as follows: if it were to perish at every moment, then it would be non-existent.
Why? Because for a non-momentary entity, purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is impossible through either succession or simultaneity.
As it has been said: "First of all, purposeful action by way of succession is not possible for an entity that is considered to be momentary."
Because the nature capable of accomplishing the effect exists at all times;
otherwise, it would not produce it even later,
since it has not fallen away from its former nature and remains as it was before.
If it is argued that [the cause] acts by depending upon auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), we say no;
for since it cannot have any excellence added to its nature and does not relinquish its prior nature, dependence upon auxiliaries is illogical.
If it is argued that the auxiliaries indeed impart an excellence to its nature, [we reply:]...
This is because an excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by auxiliary causes cannot be established as being either identical to or different from that [entity].
To explain: first of all, this excellence of the self is not identical with its nature (*ātmabhūta*).
For if it were not distinct from it, then—just like the excellence of the self—it would follow that it must arise through the power of the auxiliaries.

And if this is accepted, its non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*) is lost. If it is argued that "it is indeed distinct from that," let it be so; however, since the production of the effect arises from that very excellence of the self (*ātmaniśaya*), its incapacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsvasāmarthya*) remains as it was.
Thus, an unavoidable logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) ensues.
Furthermore, the question "How does this [cause] have a relation [to the effect]? inevitably enters the domain of inquiry.
Even regarding the claim that it acts by means of an excellence (*atiśaya*), the same fault raised against the position that requires auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) applies here as well.
If it is argued that, because its nature is inherently capable, it produces an effect by depending on something else— just like a weaver and so forth— even though no excellence can be imparted to it,
this is not sound.
For the auxiliary conditions are not able to impart any excellence whatsoever to it.
Furthermore, dependence upon an entity that provides no assistance is not logical, as it would lead to an infinite regress.
And in this case, there would be the undesirable consequence that this [entity] would never produce its effect at any time.
This is because even weavers and others would either be producing something of that same nature [as the permanent cause], or else they would be non-producers.
The argument beginning with "because it has that as its intrinsic nature" (*tatsvabhāvatvāt*) and so forth is stated in the *Hetubindu*, and thus is not discussed here.

In this way, first of all, the performance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by this [entity] is not tenable either successively or simultaneously. To explain: if its form were permeated by an intrinsic nature capable of producing causal efficiency, then it would have to produce the effect both simultaneously and subsequently; otherwise, because of its lack of connection with that nature, its destruction would occur immediately after its arising.
It might be argued that even for that which is accepted as non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), no effect is ever observed to be produced all at once, since we observe that effects occur sequentially.

Thus, this non-momentary entity is incapable of accomplishing even the slightest portion of any causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), whether successively or simultaneously; therefore, its very non-existence is established.
If it is argued that since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not possible for that [entity], why should it be non-existent? To this he says: "Causal efficiency," and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: that which has causal efficiency as its capacity is precisely the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of existence (*sattva*).
Therefore, it is excluded— that is, differentiated— from existence characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*).
This is [the meaning] of the word "iti" when used as a reason (*hetu*),
or [it refers to] that object.
How, then, is this determined—that the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is the defining characteristic of existence (*sattva*)? To this, he says:
"All," and so forth.

The term *anupākhyatvam* (the state of being indefinable) refers to that which lacks the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of being "indefinable" (*nirupākhyasya*). It is so designated because its definition consists precisely in the absence (*abhāva*) of that which is called *upākhyā*. This *upākhyā* is the verbal testimony (*śruti*) that describes all capacities;

it is so called because by means of it something is described (*upākhyāyate*). Thus, the absence of that [testimony] constitutes its definition. That which possesses such a definition is known as "indefinable."
The phrase "here too" (*atrāpi*) refers to the reason [stated] in the scripture.

The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of excluding the non-existence of even things such as jars, which—though intended to be momentary—are thought to lack causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) due to the difference in their objects.
If it is argued that causal efficiency is not the definition of existence, but rather the connection with "being-ness" (*sattā*), [the response follows].
It is not [the case that existence is established] because of the absence of existence (*sattā*).
And since that absence has been demonstrated elsewhere, it is not stated here.
Furthermore, existence itself does not attain the state of being existent, because of the absence of its connection with existence.
This is because of the convention that universals are themselves devoid of commonality.
Furthermore, the natures of entities, which are not themselves of that [universal] form, do not acquire that very form even when they come into contact with another nature;
it is as futile as claiming that crystals, clouds, and the like take on the color of hibiscus flowers and so forth. Thus, this [objection] is trivial.

If it is argued that only this much should be stated—that "the indefinable" (*nirupākhyam*) is characterized by the loss of all causal capacity—and therefore what is the purpose of including the term "designation" (*upākhyā*) here? This is well said; however, [the term is included] to demonstrate that that which is devoid of all causal capacity cannot be the object of any linguistic expression based on such capacity, and thus it is the domain of the conventional usage of the term "non-existent" (*asat*).
It is understood that this was stated for the purpose of establishing that the meaning of the term "notion" (saṃjñā) follows its etymological derivation.
If one asks, "What would happen if no subverting proof were presented against the reason when it is the opposite of the probandum? he says:
"In this way, when no subverting proof is presented against the reason when it is the opposite of the probandum, there is simply no cessation of doubt"—this is the connection [of the sentence].

What, then, is that doubt? It is this: "Has it been produced, or is it eternal?"—such is the nature [of the doubt]. One might object: "Since the presence of the reason in the counter-example (vipakṣa) is not perceived, how can there be non-exclusion [of the reason from the counter-example]? To this he says:

Even when there is no observation of this activity, there is indeed an embellishment (*upaskāra*) of the probandum (*sādhya*) upon the reversal of the sense-faculties (*akṣa*) of this means of proof (*sādhana*).
To the question, "Why is there still no cessation [of the doubt] even in this case? he says:
"Because of the absence of contradiction (*virodhābhāvāt*)."
The phrase "of the means of proof (sādhana) and the counter-example of the probandum (sādhyavipakṣa)" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

His intention is this: if the mutual contradiction between the means of proof and the opposite of the probandum were established, then non-observation alone would suffice; otherwise, if the subverting proof (bādhaka) were not established, doubt would be unavoidable. Anticipating this objection, he says:

And it is not the case that the non-apprehension of all [things] is logically a subverter or a negator; this is the supplementary statement. Of what? Of a "being" (*bhāva*), that is, of an existent (*sattva*); the remainder is "of the reason when its opposite to the probandum [is established].
This is indeed understood from the context.
This is what is meant by "unreleased":
it is precisely the non-perception of the pervader that subverts the coexistence of the reason with the absence of the probandum,
as was demonstrated previously.
Nor can exclusion be established by mere non-perception, because for one who perceives all things at a distance, non-perception does not prove non-existence, and so forth.
Therefore, it is well said that otherwise, in the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), doubt would be difficult to avoid.
By this, he recalls what was stated previously.
And thus, this [definition] is meaningful.
It has been stated that "non-perception which establishes non-existence" is not being negated.

In this regard, someone might have the suspicion: "What is the purpose of this qualification 'which establishes non-existence,' since every non-perception whatsoever is an establisher of non-existence? Therefore, he says the following in order to dispel that suspicion.
"And not," and so forth.
Here, the word "ca" (and) is to be understood in the sense of "hi" (for/indeed).
Or rather, it is used as an emphatic particle (*avadhāraṇa*) meaning "not at all"; the explanation is as before.

But surely, the pervasion of the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)—namely, the impossibility of [causal efficiency] occurring either successively or simultaneously—is not established by its own power; how then can it, being itself one whose pervasion is unestablished, suffice to establish the pervasion of another reason such as existence? If it is argued that the pervasion there is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [we reply:]...
Anticipating that the opponent might say, "In that case, this very same fault of infinite regress (anavasthā) follows," he states all of this,
beginning with the word "tatra" (therein).
Therein, the word "tatra" serves the purpose of introducing the statement.
The capacity that constitutes the definition of a real entity is established as being pervaded by the occurrence of either succession or simultaneity.
If it is asked why this is so—namely, that wherever there is capacity, there must be causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through either succession or simultaneity—the answer is:
because no other alternative is possible.
Since there is no other alternative mode apart from succession and simultaneity,

therefore, wherever this characteristic of existence— namely, the capacity for causal efficiency— is found, there it must necessarily be characterized by causal efficiency occurring either successively or simultaneously.
But surely, is there not a third category distinct from succession and simultaneity?
How is it established that "it does not exist"?
We say: because succession and non-succession are characterized by mutual exclusion, they exclude a third possibility, just like existence and non-existence.

If it is asked, "Let it be so; but how is it that [the causal capacity] consists only of the forms of succession and simultaneity?"—then what else could it possibly be? If you say, "It might be something else," [we reply: what could that be?
Why, then, have you fallen into such a great calamity, such that you are even unable to name it as it truly is?
If it is argued that capacity (*sāmarthya*) is established as being pervaded by the application of succession and simultaneity (*kramākrama-yoga*), even so, what is established? To this he says:

because capacity is pervaded by the application of succession and simultaneity, there is the non-perception of its pervader, namely, the property (*dharma*) consisting of the application of succession and simultaneity.
The meaning is that when a non-momentary entity is accepted, [the argument] subverts—that is, refutes—its causal capacity.
For this application of succession and simultaneity is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of that capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Therefore, upon the cessation of the former, there must necessarily be the cessation of the capacity as well; otherwise, this [application] would not truly be its pervader.

Since it sublates that [capacity], the pervasion is established between the absence of the pervader—the non-application of succession and simultaneity—which functions as the object (*karman*), and the absence of the pervaded—the absence of capacity—which functions as the agent (*kartṛ*).
Having thus stated the justification for the probative member of the essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), he now concludes with the words beginning "In this way" (*evam*).
He applies what was previously established: that if such a justification is not provided, it brings about the defeat of the proponent.
[The author] states "the non-establishment of that" and so forth. Why? Because of the failure to establish the intended meaning once it has been commenced.
For a proof that has not been established is not capable of establishing the intended meaning that was commenced.

Because it would follow that there is no possibility of dispute. For instance, when establishing the knowledge of an omniscient being, it is possible through the distinction of the excellence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); thus, qualities such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth, which function at the limit of their highest degree, reside in a stable substratum. Without this, there could be no cause for producing a specific quality within the self, even if it were somehow established once.
If, then, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason is established by demonstrating a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*),

[the opponent] says "In this case too," and so forth, setting forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) to dispel the suspicion that, if that were so, you would fall into an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Regarding the phrase "here [in this] subverting proof":

for you, who do not accept non-perception as a valid means of knowledge, there is no certainty regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on the reason of mere non-perception. By this formulation, the word "also" (*api*) indicates that it is not only the case with the original (*mūla*) reason; rather, it implies that even the previous original reason suffers from the fault of being under-distributed (*avyāpti*). This is the meaning of the verb "is made" (*kriyate*).
What is the reason?
Because the pervasion is not established by the mere absence of [the reason] in the case of the impossibility of succession and simultaneity through the force of [the argument].

For if the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) were not based on mere non-perception, then it could be that there is the impossibility of succession and simultaneity, yet there still exists the characteristic of existence and causal capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Regarding the question "What is the contradiction between these two?", the pervasion (vyāpti) is not established in that very subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa).
If it is argued, "Even if it is not established here, the pervasion will be established in the original reason (maula-hetu) by the force of this [subverting proof]," he replies:
"The original reason itself would also result in being non-pervasive"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

For instance, a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) that is itself not established by a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*) is not capable of establishing another as a means of valid cognition, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [all things] being means of valid cognition.
If this is so, then in this case as well, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the pervading proof is determined by another pervading proof; thus he says:
"In this case too"—by the word "too" (*api*), he indicates that it is not only in the case of the fundamental reason (*maulahetu*).
Furthermore, if one were to begin a further proof, there would be an infinite regress.
For instance, regarding that subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) which is stated for the sake of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*),
the pervasion therein must also be established by another subverting means of valid cognition.
For it can also be said of that [inference] that it is not itself a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) capable of establishing the validity of another.

If you argue that its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by yet another [inference], then if this were the case, the same argument would apply there as well; thus, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result for you.
Thus, having presented the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the mind’s being composed [of atoms], he now states the rebuttal (*pratividhāna*) here:
"Not [the case] for that which establishes non-existence," and so forth.
The phrase "by way of establishing exclusion" (*vyatirekasādhanattvena*) is to be supplied as a supplement.
This is what is meant: not every non-perception here is rejected,
because the non-perception known as the "non-apprehension of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), which establishes negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), is not denied.
"But it is merely non-perception," as he said: "That which is non-perception establishes the opposite, namely non-existence."
For what reason, and in regard to what, is the non-perception of this reason in the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) called the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)? [The answer is:
"Because it establishes the contrary," which refers back to "of this" (the reason).
For instance, that which lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through either succession or simultaneity lacks existence characterized by capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Just as in the case of the son of a barren woman and so forth, so too for momentary things, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible through either succession or simultaneity.

This "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalambha*), namely "because causal efficiency is impossible through succession or non-succession," is called the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) which establishes the opposite of the probandum—namely, non-existence—in opposition to the reason "because of existence.
And in this same manner, it should be stated accordingly for [the reasons] such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*).
Why is this called a "subverting means of valid cognition" (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) because it establishes the opposite? He says:

For in this way, that reason characterized by existence and so forth would be established as being absent when the probandum is absent, provided that it is subverted—that is, refuted—there in the absence of the probandum.
By what? By its own opposite; that is to say, by that which is contrary to its own nature, such as non-existence and so forth.

By what kind of [reason]? By one that possesses valid cognition (*pramāṇavat*), that is, one endowed with proof (*pramāṇayukta*). Why is it that this [reason] establishes what is non-existent there? He says: otherwise, if there is no establishment of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against this reason when the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) occurs, then doubt remains.
The ellipsis is that [the position] "it would be both existent and eternal," and so forth, would be difficult to avoid.
"Difficult to avoid" (durnivāra) means that which is hard to ward off; the sense is that it is difficult to refute.
Here, by the term "sublating cognition" (bādhaka-grahaṇa), one understands the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that presents a contradictory [proposition].
Or [the reason] may be contradictory to the reason because of the presence of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*).
But surely, since the exclusion of the reason from the opposite of the probandum is ascertained through mere non-perception alone, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) will be free from doubt;
so why do you speak of the removal of suspicion?
But if a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) is not demonstrated, that very [invariable concomitance] is not established; how then could this [doubt] be removed?
If indeed this suspicion does not cease, what follows from that? He says:
Therefore, because doubt has not been dispelled, the fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) would be inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Why? Because there is doubt regarding the absence of the reason where the probandum is absent—which is the defining characteristic of a valid reason—and for that reason, the fallacious reason would be one whose exclusion from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) is doubtful; such is the meaning.
How much more so, then, is there no cessation of doubt even upon non-perception, since that non-perception establishes absence? To this he says:

"Nor is the exclusion of the reason from the absence of the probandum established by mere non-perception"—this is the completion of the sentence. The word *api* (also/even) has the sense of "because."
The inclusion of the term "only" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding non-perception that meets the conditions for perceptibility. Why is this so?
Because the non-perception of objects that are remote due to distance of place, time, or nature—such as China, Rāma Dāśarathi, or piśācas—does not establish their non-existence.
If it is asked, "Of what does he establish the non-existence? the answer is understood to be: "of remote objects," because they are by nature distant.

Now, one might object: since he knows that which pervades all objects he has attained, and thus establishes the non-existence of even remote things through their non-perception, why was this [specific] statement made? To this, he says:
Regarding the term *asarvadarśinaḥ*: it is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) meaning one whose nature is not to see everything.
Why does its non-perception not establish its non-existence?
Because a person of limited vision does not perceive certain objects that exist even though they are remote,
this [objection] has been raised:
"The vision of the All-Seeing One here does not encompass the existence of all things."
By means of that [non-existence], the exclusion of the object’s existence would exclude the *śiṃśapā* tree like the word "tree" does, because of their difference;
nor is it the cause of that [existence], such that its own exclusion would exclude it like fire excludes smoke,
because [the effect] exists even in the absence of that [cause].
"Furthermore, the subverting means of valid cognition," and so forth.

On this point, some raise the following prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*): "What, then, is the subverting means of valid cognition, by the demonstration of which the understanding of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the original reason (*maula-hetu*) occurs? To this he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore, the subverting [proof]," etc.:

one should consider how the demonstration of the subverting valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite case serves as the proof of pervasion (*vyāpti*) for them, such as "if everything that exists or is produced were not subject to momentary destruction," and so forth. It should be considered whether the fault of tautology does not arise here because the meaning has already been stated previously; however, enough of this recital of others' faults.

Therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated otherwise. To the question, "How can this not be a fault even for one who possesses a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)," he says: "Furthermore, a subverting means of valid cognition, when it operates, brings about an incapacity"—this is the verbal action (*kriyāpada*).
What is the definition of a "thing" (malla)?
What is its measure? It is that entity for which there is an impossibility of successive or simultaneous [action].
The term "of causal efficiency" (arthakriyāyāḥ) is to be supplied [as the object of the impossibility].
It has no capacity for any causal function whatsoever, just as [the example] "like a lotus in the sky" should be supplied.

And since that [capacity] is absent in a non-momentary entity due to the impossibility of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) occurring either successively or simultaneously— this being how [the argument] proceeds— if one asks, "What follows from this?", he says:

For that reason, by means of that [reason], it draws forth the fact that what is currently occurring lacks the characteristic of existence and is devoid of causal capacity; thus, it is established that whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent. Even so, he asks: "What is established? and says:
And by that much—namely, by the mere presentation of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)—the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the probans-property alone is established; this is the sense.
By what means? He says: this genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is to be understood as denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) of the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*).

The meaning of the sentence is established as follows: by means of that property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the mere property that serves as the proof (*sādhanadharmamātra*)—which does not require the operation of any other cause—is established.
However, one should not formulate it thus: "the positive concomitance [of the probandum] with the mere property that serves as the proof.

For if it were so, the property to be proven itself would become inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) with the reason, rather than the reason [being connected to the probandum]; consequently, the reason would fail to be a prover (*agamakatva*).
He then states what benefit is obtained [from this]:

"And by that much, the definition of the essential-nature reason (svabhāvahetu) is established. This is how the sentence continues. Furthermore, the definition of the essential-nature reason is that even when the subject (dharmin) lacks that nature, [the property] does not depend on further effort once the conditions for its non-existence have ceased.

Arguments such as "like the purification of the impurities of gold" possess a preeminent capacity that has indeed been attained; and if these were to make known what is to be known even when they themselves remain unestablished, then there would be no dispute at all with Jaimini and others.
But surely this very thing is not possible.
In response to the doubt that one might be subject to defeat even when stating a reason (*hetu*) that is ultimately capable, he reveals his own intention:
"Even if a reason that is substantially capable is employed, its capacity has not been demonstrated.

His point is this: although he may have indeed employed a reason that is ultimately capable, nevertheless, because he has failed to support the members of the proof (*sādhana*), his capacity has not been demonstrated by him; thus, it is equivalent to being incapable.
It is thus: for it is not the object that is subject to the presence of merits or defects in an inference for the sake of another;
rather, it is the speaker who is censured because of his statement being non-conformable to reality.

For this very reason, even in cases where the merits and defects of an object are being evaluated, they are done so solely by means of the verbal expression. This must be accepted; otherwise, after merely stating the proposition "sound is momentary," one would have to stop, since the intended meaning would be established simply from that statement itself. || 0 ||

Having thus demonstrated the justification of the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) regarding the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*), he now states it regarding the effect as a reason (*kāryahetu*) with the words "In the case of the effect as a reason also," and so forth. He asks: "What, then, is that? and replies:
The meaning is as follows: when an effect, such as smoke and so forth—known by the technical term *liṅga* (the sign)—is employed for the purpose of establishing a cause, such as fire and so forth;

then, the very establishment of the relationship of cause and effect (*hetuphalabhāva*) between that smoke and the like and that fire and the like—which is the proof of the relationship of probans and probandum (*liṅgi-liṅgabhāva*)—is precisely what constitutes the "supporting of the member of proof" (*sādhanāṅgasamarthana*) in the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
To the question, "By what means, then, is the relationship of cause and effect between those two established? he says:
Regarding the phrase "by the two means of valid cognition that establish existence and non-existence":

the analysis of the compound is as follows: *bhāva* and *abhāva* refer to the existence and non-existence of cause and effect; *sādhana* refers to the means of establishing those two; and the term *pramāṇa* refers to the instruments of knowledge. Furthermore, the word *sādhana* here functions as a *karaṇa-sādhana* (an instrument). Thus, the means of valid cognition that establish existence and non-existence are, respectively, perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).
How, then, is the causal relationship established through perception and non-perception? To this he says:
"Just as," and so forth.
This effect, designated as smoke and the like, occurs when this fire exists.
The ellipsis of the sentence must be supplied as: "having met the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), it was previously unperceived.

Otherwise, the causal operation of the fire with respect to that smoke would not have been stated at all, because the suspicion could arise that "this [smoke] existed even before the presence of the fire. However, when the non-perception is understood as specified above, this suspicion does not occur.
For this very reason, it has been stated in exactly the same way in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya* and other works;
by this, the operation of direct perception as a means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇavyāpāra*) is described.
For it is thus: "When this exists, that comes to be"—this is understood through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Desiring to point out the function of non-perception (*anupalambha*) at present, he says:
"Even when [the causes] exist," and so forth.
Therefore, even when other things exist besides that fire—

namely, when its causes such as fuel, wind, and so forth, are likewise present and capable— the word "even" (*api*) from the previous context is understood here; and the particle "ca" (and) should be understood as being elided and supplied as "and [when they are] capable."
In the absence of that fuel, this [fire] does not exist;
"this" refers to what is under discussion.
The word "iti" (thus) functions in the sense of "in this way" or as a delimiter.
Thus, by this [argument], the causality of cows, horses, and so forth— even those present at that place and time— with respect to the production of smoke is refuted.
For if those cows, horses, and so forth were its cause, then even after the fire has passed away, smoke would necessarily arise because they remain present.

If it is argued that those [causes], such as fuel and so forth, become the producers of that [smoke] by depending on other causes, and therefore this undesirable consequence does not follow; [we reply:

if that were the case, they too would be present right there, and thus the undesirable consequence would not be averted. If it is further argued that even fire produces that [smoke] by depending on auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), and therefore this is not logical;
[we reply: in that case, it follows that fire possesses causality with respect to the production of smoke.
Therefore, why is this said—that oxen, horses, and so forth, which are contradictory in their prior and subsequent [statements], are its cause and not fire?
If it is argued, "Let it be that fire is also its cause, as well as oxen, horses, and so forth," we reply:
this is not tenable.
In this regard, it is difficult to establish the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
For even when cows and other such things have been removed, as long as fire exists along with the collection of fuel and so forth, the production of the fire-cause certainly occurs.

This is because the relationship of cause and effect among entities is considered by relying upon the continuity of causes and the continuity of effects; that is, the continuity of effects is preceded by the continuity of causes.
That [cognition], however, does not distinguish between moments;
for those who have attained the excellence of knowledge, no cognition arises that apprehends a distinction such as "this is the preceding moment" or "this is the succeeding moment.
Furthermore, it was by taking ordinary perceivers as the subject that the compassionate ones formulated the definition of valid cognition.
As it has been said, this nature of conventional valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*) has been explained here; yet even regarding this, others, being deluded, mislead the world.
If it is argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because smoke exists in places such as bedchambers even in the absence of fire, [we reply:
even in such cases, the state of being preceded by a continuous series of fires certainly exists.
The distinction, however, is made by whether [the perception] is direct or mediated.

Those whose intellects have become refined through the power of practicing the discernment of the diverse natures of things clearly perceive the difference between two series of smoke—one arising from a continuous stream of perception and one arising from a broken stream—whether occurring in a dwelling house or in a region containing a kitchen.

Therefore, inference based on a distinction is not contradictory; for this very reason, it has been stated that inference depends upon place, time, and other factors, both in the case of an effect as a logical reason (*kāryahetu*) and in the perception of a contradictory effect.
"Even in the case of an effect that is contrary to what is desired, there is a dependence on place, time, and so forth;
otherwise, the means of proof would be fallacious, like [the argument] 'he sits because he goes. (2)

Furthermore, suppose someone—whose eye of wisdom has been opened by the superior skill of discerning the distinctions between various phenomena—distinguishes that "this smoke is produced from fire" and "this smoke is produced from smoke.
Even so, there is no greater deviation [from the rule].
For instance, smoke produced from fire does not arise from smoke, because that would entail the absurd consequence of it being causeless (*nirhetukatva*).
And likewise, as it has been said:
"Therefore, if smoke could arise from what is not fire,
then it would likewise [arise] from the head of Śakra."
"By what could its arising be prevented?
(3)—since such [arguments] are devoid of substance, they too are disregarded.
Therefore, let the certainty be established that those things, such as cows and horses, do not possess causality in that regard.
Therefore, it is established that fire alone is its cause, and not horses or other such things.

Thus, the causality of fire has been established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the manner already described; in this same way, the causality of the entire collection of conditions (*sāmagrī*), such as fuel and so forth, should be established.
Or, it may be explained as a single coherent statement.
Therefore, even though other capable causes such as fuel exist, [the effect] does not occur in the absence of this [specific cause].

However, the fact that cows, horses, and so forth are not causes should be understood through the aforementioned method by way of the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). If it is asked: "Is it not more appropriate to say simply that 'it occurs through the absence of that' (i.e., the specific cause)? Why then is it stated that 'even when other capable causes of that [effect] exist'? he replies:
"Thus, indeed," and so forth.

Because, by means of the statement beginning with "even when these [other causes] exist," the fact that this smoke is an effect of fire—that is, its being produced from fire—is established and becomes certain and free from doubt.
Otherwise, if it were not demonstrated in this manner, [the conclusion would remain uncertain].

The overall meaning is as follows: it is merely demonstrated that [the effect] arises in the absence of that [cause]. When such a demonstration—that it arises in the absence of that—is being made, since other things such as cows, horses, and fuel are also absent in that location on the ground devoid of fire, the capacity of this [specific] fire remains doubtful; therefore, how can there be certainty regarding the presence of the cause?
For this very reason, he says:
For when those causes capable [of producing the effect] are present, the non-arising of the effect indicates the deficiency of some other cause.
The fact that its capacity is suspected to be otherwise is indicated by the phrase "that very thing is other than that," and so forth.
In that context, regarding the effects of smoke and a horse, [the respective causes] are indeed other things, such as fire and a horse.

The meaning is: since that which is capable [of producing an effect], such as fuel and so forth, is absent, it has not arisen in a place devoid of fire; how, then, can there be this certainty that "it has not arisen from its own nature"? If one objects: "If something else were capable there, then because of its absence it would not have arisen; but if that [other thing] is excluded, how is the exclusion of this [fire] established? he says: [The response follows: ... [as provided in the source text].
"In the cessation of this," and so forth.
Upon the cessation of this fire, the cessation of smoke that occurs is a coincidental concurrence (*yadṛcchā-saṃvāda*).
The meaning is that it is according to the maxim of "the crow and the palm fruit" (*kākatālīya-nyāya*).

But when [the phrase] "even though [others] exist" (*satsvapi*) is employed, then because all [causes] are present there, one reaches the certainty that "when this very [cause] ceases, this [effect] ceases"; thus, the intention is that this is not a coincidence (*yadṛcchā-saṃvāda*).
To the question, "How is it that the cessation [of the effect] upon the cessation [of the cause] is not a coincidence?", he says:
"In the case of a mother's marriage," and so forth.
The marriage of a mother is that which is customary and practiced in a particular region;
thus, it forms a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) with the word "region" (*deśa*). In that context, the term [for marriage] is applied metaphorically because it depends upon birth.

For that which has its birth or origin in the land of the Persians, as long as it does not exist in another country such as Mālava and so forth—just as there is an absence [of the custom] due to the absence of mother-marrying and a coincidence of chance (yadṛcchā-samvāda)—so it is here as well.

For instance, in another country, its absence is due to the absence of a particular type of soil, and not due to the absence of mother-marrying; thus, its presence when that [soil] is absent is a mere coincidence (kākatālīya).
And this is so;
or rather, it is explained otherwise:
just as this effect, such as smoke, occurs when this collection of causes, such as fire and fuel, is present.
The ellipsis of the sentence, however, is to be supplied as before;
its purpose is to be understood as that very same thing.
This is a mention of the operation of direct perception.

By the phrase "even when [the other causes] exist," etc., [it is shown that] non-perception occurs; furthermore, among other things—such as cows or horses—even when their respective causes are capable, this [effect] does not arise in the absence of that specific causal complex consisting of fire and so forth.
And this has been stated from the perspective of the opponent's view.
But they do not possess the status of being its cause.
If, on the other hand, they were its causes, then it would follow that smoke would be produced even before the proximity of that collection [of causes], just as it is produced afterwards.
If it is argued that they are "produced by that" (tatkṛtakatva) because of their dependence upon it;
If it is argued: "In that case, let that bundle (kalāpa) possess causality; since this applies to both [theories], there is no loss for us," we reply: No.
For it has been stated that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in that regard is difficult to establish.

If it is argued that even when all those [causes] have departed, as long as that bundle (kalāpa) exists, its production certainly occurs, and thus it should be said that it does not occur in its absence—then for what purpose was it stated, "even while they exist," and so forth? To this, he says:
"For in this way," and so on.

Otherwise, if it were shown that [the effect] does not arise in the absence of that complex (*kalāpa*), yet there were another [cause] such as a cow or a horse present there, the capacity of this complex would remain doubtful. For, since another thing like a cow or a horse is capable there, and the effect did not arise due to its absence, the cessation [of the effect] upon the cessation of this complex would be a mere accidental coincidence (*yadṛcchā-saṃvāda*). The rest is as before. Having thus explained the method for determining the relationship between cause and effect, he concludes the subject at hand.
By the words "in this way" and so forth:
in this manner, according to the stated procedure, that smoke and so forth—the effect of that fire and so forth—is established, meaning it is determined and proven.
That which is thus established becomes free from doubt and is definitively ascertained.
Alternatively, in this way, its being an effect is established through perception and non-perception. Even if it is indeed established, he asks: "What of it? (i.e., what follows from that?).

Because the causal relationship is ascertained, it is established that the characteristic of "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*) applies to each individual thing. Wherever such [an effect] is perceived, there, by its mere existence, it leads one to understand its own cause—taking into account factors such as place and time. Why is this so? He says:
Because the effect does not deviate from its cause;
for otherwise, it would not be the effect of that [cause] at all,
due to such deviation.
The intention is that it is not logical for something to be the effect of another unless it arises in dependence upon that other,
just as a bracelet is [the effect] of a bangle.
Now, one might object: "Granted that smoke does not deviate from being an effect of fire;
however, since other things such as sprouts do not deviate from their own causes, namely seeds and so forth, on what basis is this [rule] established?
To this he says: "And in the case of non-deviation," and so forth.
This is what is meant:

when the non-deviation of smoke from its own cause is established by virtue of its arising therefrom, then the same principle of non-deviation applies equally to all effects, such as sprouts and the like, with respect to their own respective causes, such as seeds and so forth.
For these too, being established as effects of those [causes] through the aforementioned methods of perception and non-perception, are proven to be non-deviant from them.

This demonstration of the adequacy of the members of the proof pertains to the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). Its opposite, namely inadequacy, constitutes the ground for the defeat of the proponent; showing this, he says:
"Thus," and so forth.

"Thus" means by means of perception and non-perception in the manner already described; it indicates that not only in the case of the previously mentioned mode [of proof], but also in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the proponent's failure to establish it constitutes a point of defeat (*parājayasthāna*).
This is the meaning of the word "also" (*api*).
He asks, "Why is this so? and replies with the words beginning "asamarthita" (unestablished).
If that relationship of cause and effect between the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) is unestablished...
Alternatively, regarding the statement "because the object already commenced would not be established if the mark were its effect," this is a verbal expression [of a reason].
The "object already commenced" refers to the proof of the existence of the cause;
because that is not established, it constitutes a point of defeat for him—this is the connection with the subject at hand.
He asks, "Why is this so? and replies:
because there is no rule of necessity regarding the existence of one thing (such as fire) when another thing (such as smoke) exists;
the inclusion of the term "rule" (*niyama*) is for the purpose of excluding accidental coincidence.
Since the necessity of that [other] thing’s existence is indeed established when there is the existence of something whose nature is connected to it, even if it is a different object, he says:
“of that which has a nature not connected to its existence.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: that whose nature (*svabhāva*) is not connected—that is, not dependent—upon its existence, namely the existence of fire and so forth.
And this should be understood as the reason for the statement that "there is no necessity of its existence when another thing exists," because [the latter] is a different entity.
Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is a different entity and whose nature is not tied to [another], there is no necessity of its existence when that other exists;
just as, for example, there is no necessity of the existence of a crown when an anklet exists.
Furthermore, this smoke and so forth is a different entity from that fire and so forth, and its nature is unconnected to it; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Or, by means of the positive formulation of the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), he explains why the nature of the reason is not connected to the existence of that [fire], stating:
"because its being an effect is unestablished."
Furthermore, this should be understood as occurring when that [reason] has not been established.

And since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), you have employed only an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), even if that effect is not established by him, how then is he defeated? To this, he says:
In reality, because the material cause is also presented as the effect, the distinction lies in its being that specific effect. || 0 ||
Having thus stated the support for the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) regarding the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), he speaks regarding non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).
The connection is: "there is also support in the case of non-perception.
The term "this member of the proof" (*sādhanāṅga*) is to be supplied [to the sentence].
What, then, is that? He says:
it is the means of proof consisting in non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). Is it the means for proving anything whatsoever? No; he says: [it is not].
"Of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension" means:
of that which has a visible nature, and not of anything else;
"apprehension" (upalabdhi) refers to cognition (jñāna).

Since the word *upalabdhi* (apprehension) functions as either an abstract noun (*bhāva*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*), it is a synonym for "cognition" (*jñāna*); therefore, its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is its cause.
Because the word *lakṣaṇa* functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*), it denotes that which is produced [by that cause].
And that [cause] consists of the completeness of other conditions and a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*), as well as the non-apprehension of that which is pervaded by them.
The etymological derivation is that its *sādhana* means its demonstration (*pratipādana*).

If it is asked, "How can there be non-perception of such a thing?", we reply: it is not asserted that there is no perception of it in that very place, but rather that there is no perception of something of that same class elsewhere.
To whom, then, is such non-perception established? He says:
to the cognizer, that is, the opponent.
And if even piśācas and the like have reached the conditions for perception, or if there are others of their kind who possess supernatural power;

Therefore, does this also constitute a means of proof through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) and a justification of the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) for them? No, he says: [it is so] for the cognizer (*pratipattṛ*).
This is what is meant:
the non-apprehension that serves as a means of proof applies only to that very object which is intended to be established and which meets the conditions for apprehension, and not to anything else.
But what is the reason that the means of proof consisting of non-apprehension applies only to such a kind of object?
He says it does not belong to anything else:
"Because the conventional usage of non-existence is established from such a non-apprehension alone.
The intended meaning is that a non-apprehension that has met the conditions for being perceived (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) cannot be a means of knowledge, as it serves as a cause for doubt.

The statement "because the conventional usage of 'non-existent' is established" is intended to demonstrate that by means of this [non-perception], it is precisely the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvyavahāra*) that is proven, and not non-existence itself; for the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is itself of the nature of non-existence.
Furthermore, the mention of "the conventional usage of non-existent" is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, the cognition of non-existence and the word for non-existence are also to be understood.
If it is asked, "But from what is this inferred? he says:

The perception of an object by a cognizer that has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is itself its apprehension; since the non-existence [of such an object] is not established even when that perception does not occur, the mention of "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is intended as an indication of the linguistic convention of non-existence and the cognition thereof.
Furthermore, the phrase "conditions for apprehension" includes the factor of cognition in order to exclude those things that are known through other means of valid cognition.
What, then, is this "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*), by virtue of which something is said to have "attained the conditions for perception"?
To this he says: "In that regard," and so forth.
Therein, [the word] "therein" (*tatra*) serves the purpose of introducing the scriptural statement.
The distinction of intrinsic nature. Is it only this much? No, he says:
And there is the completeness of other causes.
Therefore, "other causes" refers to those other causes such as the sense faculties, mental attention, and so forth, distinct from the specific nature [of the object];
"completeness" means their totality.
The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to the specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*).
To the question, "What, then, is this specific nature?
he says: "Nature," and so forth.
If this specific nature is said not to be remote— unlike the forms of Mount Meru, Rāma, or the gods— due to the three kinds of remoteness characterized by space, time, and intrinsic nature,
he clarifies that very point with the words beginning "that which... and so forth.
The meaning is that it is neither of the nature of self nor of the nature of non-self; rather, it is of the nature of another.

That which is the manifestation (*pratibhāsa*), its "discrimination" (*viveka*) is its absence. By means of that [absence], whatever form—that is, whatever intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—has the habit of not manifesting in the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the cognizer, that form is described in that way.
Alternatively, by the word "form" (*rūpa*)...
A possessive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) should not be formed [with *upalambha*].
It is to be supplemented as "the completeness of other conditions for the perception of existence.
