That which appears in its own cognition by way of a nature devoid of similar and dissimilar [things], provided there is a conjunction of other causes—this is what is meant by "essential nature" (*svabhāva*).

"Such a thing" refers to an object that, despite being characterized by the three types of remoteness (*viprakarṣa*), is not remote in its actual form; yet, because it is not apprehended through the perceiver’s direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—which is free from the appearance of a non-self-form—it does not become an object for the linguistic convention of non-existence (*asad-vyavahāra*).
The meaning is that it becomes fit for the cognition of the linguistic convention of non-existence.

If it is asked: "Even though it exists, why does such a thing not become an object of the conventional usage of 'non-existent' when it is not perceived due to the absence of the sense organ, light, or mental attention? [The author] replies:
"While other causes of perception are present.

Now, one might argue that even a jar or similar object, though not distant and despite the presence of other causes of perception, is not perceived because it depends upon a transformation of the continuum (*santāna-pariṇāma*).
For it is not the case that the proximity of other causes alone constitutes a transformation of the cause conducive to the production of its own fruit;

for instance, even when the causal complex of earth, seed, water, and so forth is present, the transformation of a palmyra seed that is favorable to the arising of its own effect occurs only after a very long time,
whereas the transformation of a hemp seed or similar seeds occurs immediately thereafter— and the same will be the case here as well.

Furthermore, when an object is presided over by one possessing supernatural power—such as a piśāca or a magician—even though that object exists at that time, it is not perceived. How then can it be said that such an object, while other conditions for perception are present, is the referent of the conventional usage of "non-existent" because it is unperceived?
Surely you have [not considered this] in the *Nyāyabindu*.
[This is] not one for whom effort has been made [in this regard].
For it has been stated here: "That which is its own nature (*svabhāva*) becomes directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) when other causes of perception are present.
And that which depends upon the transformation of a continuum (*santāna-pariṇāma*), as well as that which is presided over by a powerful being, is not indeed a specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*).

Even when all other conditions for perception are present, because it does not produce the apprehension of its own nature, such a thing— whose form is indistinguishable from that of a piśāca or similar entities— is established as the object of the conventional usage of non-existence.
Rather, [this applies] to that which, being present, becomes directly perceived precisely when other conditions for perception, such as the sense faculties, are in proximity.
If you argue, "In that case, it is not established that there is an absolute non-existence [of the object]," then you are acting quite favorably toward our position;
for it was stated immediately thereafter:
"That very thing which comes within the range of vision when the totality of the sense faculties and other conditions is unimpaired."

And it is the non-perception of that [object] in its entirety that is established as the object of conventional discourse, but not the nature of something like a *piśāca* which is indistinguishable from such [an unperceivable entity].

Nor is it logical for such a thing to exist when it is not perceived despite the presence of all the conditions for perceiving it and everything other than it, because non-perception itself would then be impossible;
for there would be nothing remaining to be required for the production of perception.
This has indeed been clarified in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya* with the words, "Because there is no cognition of non-existence at the time of the effect," and so forth.

By this very [argument], it should be understood that everything urged by those who are skilled in caviling—while themselves not perceiving even the slightest [flaw] in the mind of the intelligent one who possesses a doubt—is ill-founded; therefore, enough with these unstable prattle of fools.
One desists [from further inquiry].

Therefore, it is established that only the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is the means of establishing the conventional usage of non-existence.
And since this is so, for that reason, otherwise [if it were not thus], there would be a relation of inherence (*samavāya*) in the logical mark (*liṅga*).

Having set aside non-apprehension characterized by the fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptānupalabdhi*), if another mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhimātra*) is employed as a logical mark (*liṅga*) to establish the conventional usage of "non-existent," then, when that [mere non-apprehension] is present, doubt arises.
There is no certainty regarding the conventional usage of "non-existent," because even upon the cessation of apprehension, the absence of the object remains unproven; such is the collective meaning.
Alternatively, it should be explained that doubt arises from the mark (liṅga) consisting of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*), provided that the mark is otherwise [present].
Therefore, the word "but" (*tu*) must be supplied at the beginning.

Or else, it should be explained as follows: when there is doubt regarding something other than that which has met the conditions for perception—that is, regarding something devoid of those conditions—that is the mark.
"What, then, is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in this case of non-perception?
To this he says: "In this case also," and so forth.
"Of such a kind" means that which is perceptible yet not perceived.
The inclusion of the term "all" is for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion through the universal application of all cases.

Now, one might object: "If indeed the status of being an object of the conventional usage of 'non-existent' applies to something like a horn—which, though meeting the conditions for perception, is not perceived on a rabbit's head—then by the same logic, other such things as universals (sāmānya), particulars (viśeṣa), inherence (samavāya), substances (dravya), conjunction (saṃyoga), and disjunction (vibhāga) must also be so [non-existent]. From what, then, does this restriction [that only some things are non-existent] follow? To this, he says: "Of something," and so forth.

When it is accepted that something non-existent—such as a rabbit’s horn—which has not been perceived despite meeting the conditions for perceptibility, is the object of the linguistic convention "non-existent," then it is stated that the object of such conventions like "non-existence" is itself non-existent.
This is because its characteristic is no different [from other non-existents].

The "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) of that non-existent is the aforementioned non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), which serves as its cause; and since the word *lakṣaṇa* is used here in the instrumental sense (meaning "that by which something is characterized"), it is because this [cause] is indistinguishable [in all cases], including in the case of universals, particulars, and composite substances. This is the completion of the sentence.
This is what is meant: why is even the rabbit's horn and the like accepted as an object of the conventional usage of "non-existent"?
If it is argued that this is because the aforementioned non-perception, which is the cause for such usage, exists in its case;
If it is argued that since it possesses the nature of both universal and particular, why is it not accepted as being the object of the conventional usage "existent"?
Otherwise, if one were to claim that this [existence] would apply there [to the universal] as well,
it would be improper to divide the objects of causes according to mere human whim.
By the words "no" and so forth, he clarifies this very point:
that if such a perceptible object were to exist, its non-existence could not be admitted when it is not perceived.
The meaning is that its non-existence is not admitted because it is the objective referent for linguistic usage regarding the non-existent and the like.
If it is argued that the term "non-existence" (asattva) indicates the determination of the conventional usage of non-existence— that is,
the non-perception of that very thing which would otherwise be perceived under appropriate conditions is the cause for its negation,
and so forth— then [this applies] elsewhere, such as in the case of the absence of a rabbit's horn, [just as one might see] a man with a staff.
The meaning is that this very [non-perception] is the *yoga*.
For such an object of perception (*dṛśya*), non-perception does not occur when the causes of perception, such as the eyes and so forth, are absent.
Rather, it is perception itself that occurs; this is stated by means of a double negation.
The sense is that there is an absence of any other requisite condition for perception. Thus, by this, he clarifies the very subject at hand.

However, such a thing, being unperceived despite having reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), does not exist; therefore, this much alone—the mere non-perception of what has reached the conditions for perceptibility—is the cause for the conventional usage of "non-existent. That [usage] is described as such. By this, he states that the conventional usage of "non-existent" has no other cause.
Why is this so? He says:
"Of another," and so forth.
The meaning of the conjunction is that, setting aside the aforementioned non-apprehension, there is no other ground for the conventional usage of non-existence.
But surely, for whatever has no capacity whatsoever in a given respect, the very absence of all capacity will be the cause for the linguistic convention of "non-existence.
Why is this being asserted by those who have uncovered their heads [in such a confused manner]?
Someone might say, "Because there is no other cause for that," and it is with this view in mind that he anticipates the objection.
If it is argued that the cause is the exclusion of all causal capacities (*sāmarthya*),
he states the resolution to this with the words beginning "In this way" (*evam*).

He thinks as follows: "It is well said that the exclusion of all causal capacity (*sarvasāmarthyaviveka*) is the cause [of the usage of 'non-existent']. However, how is this very entity—the exclusion of all causal capacity—cognized, setting aside the aforementioned non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), such that this exclusion of all causal capacity will become the cause for the linguistic usage of 'non-existent'?
Nor can it serve as its cause while remaining unknown."
Because this pertains to the context of indicative reasons (*jñāpaka-hetu*).
Why is it that for one who is devoid of all causal capacity, cognition occurs through the aforementioned non-perception alone? To this he says:
This is because there is no other means for its comprehension.
However, when through the aforementioned non-perception there arises the cognition of that [object] as being devoid of all causal capacity, then,
upon that comprehension, the conventional usage of "non-existent" occurs.
Thus, for this reason, this aforementioned non-perception is said to be the cause (*nimitta*) for the conventional usage of "non-existence.

Furthermore, the opponent might suspect that the statement "because of the absence of its cause" is at times untenable; therefore, [the author] anticipates this objection with the words beginning "cognition, designation," and so forth.
His underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) is as follows: [from] cognition, designation, and purposeful action...
Thus, linguistic convention regarding them arises;
for in this way, as they function, they establish the existence of a real entity,
and their difference or non-difference constitutes the difference or non-difference of the real entity— this is the intended meaning.

And those [cognitions], when they cease, cause the cessation of the conventional usage of "existent" regarding their own object, just as fire [ceases] smoke. Upon that cessation, there is the conventional usage of "non-existent.
This is because the conventional usages of "existent" and "non-existent" exist in a state of mutual exclusion; since the abandonment of one is necessarily concomitant with the adoption of the other.
And therefore, it is not correct to say that "in the cessation of cognition and so forth, [the absence] is the cause for the conventional usage of 'non-existent' for something else," and so on.
To this as well, he states the rebuttal:
"It occurs," and so forth.

The analysis of the compound *yathoktapratibhāsā* is as follows: it is a cognition (*buddhi*) whose appearance is the manifestation of a form appearing directly to the cognizer; "yathokta-pratibhāsa" means that which has the aforementioned appearance.
And this has been stated in the passage beginning with "that which is without self," and so forth.
From that [direct perception], the conventional usage of "existent" arises because of the direct apprehension of the object;
and since its opposite— non-existence— is absent therein, when that [perception] exists, the conventional usage of "non-existent" arises.
The sentence must be completed as "when other conditions for apprehension are present," because otherwise a doubt would arise.

For it has already been explained by us previously that when an object exists and all other causal factors for its apprehension are complete, that [non-apprehension] does not occur; such is the meaning.
Therefore, if such an understanding is what you intend by this, then there is indeed agreement between us; even so, nothing undesirable has been stated by us.
But if it is something else, then there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as he shows.
Demonstrating that very deviation, he says:
By the phrase "not an object of direct perception" (*pratyakṣāviṣaya*) and so forth:
"born from a mark" (*liṅgaja*) means produced from a logical sign (*liṅga*);
that is to say, inference (*anumāna*).

From that [perception], there would be the conventional usage of "existent" regarding an object even when it is imperceptible; however, he says "also" (*api*) to indicate that this applies only to that which has the form described above as being graspable by itself.
He asks: "Is this possible for every [cognition] arising from a logical mark (*liṅga*)? and answers: "No."
"From some [source]" means:
from that which has arisen through the power of both essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the logical mark (*liṅga*).
The underlying sense is that non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) establishes both non-existence and the conventional usage of "non-existent."
If it is asked, "Even if this is so, how then can there be a deviation (vyabhicāra)? he says:
"But the conventional usage of the non-existent," and so forth.
"Its reversal" means that when the aforementioned cognition born from the logical mark (liṅga) ceases, [the reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntika), which is to say, doubtful.

What is the reason? Because, even when the means of valid cognition consisting of the perceiver’s direct perception (*pratipattṛ-pratyakṣa*) has ceased due to the remoteness of the object—namely, through spatial and other forms of distance—there remains doubt; for this reason, [one cannot conclude] "the non-existence of the object. This is the ellipsis.
The term *pratipattuḥ pratyakṣam* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

And this [statement] is employed to explain that for one who has abandoned all cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), there is indeed no doubt regarding the cessation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "Of the other" refers to inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*). Furthermore, this is stated while accepting the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of scripture.

But they possess no validity, because words lack an invariable concomitance with real entities; therefore, the establishment of objects does not result from them, for they merely indicate the speaker's intention. (4)

Because of such statements as these, the intended meaning is this: even if the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have ceased to function with respect to an imperceptible object, how can there be the certainty that "it does not exist"?

For instance, things such as the sprouts of *dūrvā* grass and leaves existing within the thickets of the Malaya mountains remain bearing forms that transcend the scope of the three means of valid cognition.
Nor can it be asserted that these [absences] do not exist, because the non-existence of a means of valid cognition lacks the capacity to pervade the existence of all objects. Furthermore,

as has been explained, this would lead to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) due to the rule that the exclusion of one thing necessarily entails the exclusion of another, even if that other thing is devoid of the former's form.

Regarding that, it was stated previously: "How can there be non-existence through non-perception for many objects that are disconnected from the scope of treatises, whose forms are not perceived by the senses, and which lack [inferential] marks? (v. 5).

But surely, one might object: since the statement beginning with "the opposite of that" (*tadviparyaya*) has begun here to negate that a cognition born of a logical mark (*liṅga*) is a cause for the linguistic usage of a non-existent thing, why then is there an introduction of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and verbal testimony (*śabda*), which are indeed irrelevant?
This objection is valid.

It appears that the intention of this wise author is as follows: by demonstrating that the cessation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) results in a lack of communicative power, he shows that this [negation] cannot be absolute.

Now, it has been stated that since the positive linguistic usage (*sadvayavahāra*) and the negative linguistic usage (*asadvayavahāra*) are defined by their mutual exclusion, the absence of one necessarily entails the presence of the other; however, in the case of something remote, because the grounds for that [positive usage] are absent, the negative linguistic usage occurs through the cessation of the positive linguistic usage.
It is true that this has indeed been said, yet it is not logical.

For instance, regarding an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), there is the cessation of the conventional usage of "existence. How then, in the absence of its cause, can both of these non-apprehensions (*anupalabdhi*) equally result in the negation of the conventional usage of "existence"—one through doubt and the other through error—given the statement that they differ in having the presence or absence of a cause for their respective opposites? If you say it is by means of doubt;
If this is so, how then does a logical justification apply to the determination of the conventional usage of "non-existent" (*asat*) therein?

However, where there is a cessation of the conventional usage of "existent" (*sat*) through a definitive determination, there the conventional usage of "non-existent" is indeed appropriate, because it has been stated that it is another [usage] whose fruit is the engagement [of the agent]. Furthermore, in the exclusion of the nature of non-existence, there is no necessary implication of existence.

For in the case of the son of a barren woman, the sky-lotus, and so forth, there is no state of non-existence [as a positive entity] resulting from negation; rather, there would be only a mere negation.
This is because those two exist through mutual exclusion (*anyonyavyavaccheda*).
Likewise here, since the conventional usage of "existent" is negated regarding that which is imperceptible, there is no positive conventional usage of "existent."
The six [categories] would merely be the exclusion of that;
for the existence of one and the existence of the other are established through mutual exclusion.

And this was stated by Dharmakīrti himself—whose light of wisdom arose from the awakening to the reality of the stainless system of logic, thereby dispelling the darkness of all the doctrines of rival schools—even regarding the exclusion of impermanence, selflessness, and so forth.
Let us leave aside for now the discussion beginning with "it might be" (*syāt*) and so forth.
Now, stating that even the general cognitions and designations do not serve as the cause for the conventional usage of "existence," he says: "And not... and so forth.
And there, the connection is as follows in due order:
all those designations by means of the intellect do not establish the existence of a real entity;
nor do their difference or non-difference establish the existence or non-existence of the difference or non-difference of the real entity.
The inclusion of the word "all" (sarva), however, is for the purpose of demonstrating that some indeed establish [the existence of the past and future].
To the question "Why is this so?", he says:
"Because it functions even when [objects] such as the past and future are non-existent"—this is the verbal phrase.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), sky-lotuses and the like are included.
If it is asked how their occurrence with respect to those [objects] is logical in the absence of an actual object, he says:
"In some way," meaning that it occurs through the power of the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of that [object's] form.
And the sense is that there is no connection to a real entity (*vastu*) for them.
By the phrase "the conch-shell universal emperor" and so forth, he states the reason for the claim that they establish the existence of a real entity (*vastusattā*) in this manner.
Those whose nature it is not to perform a single or manifold purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) are described as such.
And because there is a causal function even toward those [particulars].
For what purpose is there a function toward them? It is for the sake of making known their existence.
That is, for the sake of making known the existence of those [particulars] which do not perform a single common purposeful action.
This means: for the purpose of explaining both the performance of various causal functions and the performance of a single causal function by that thing.
[Objection: "In that case, the reality (*tattva*) of that object must indeed exist. To this he replies:
"Even in the absence of a manifold or unitary nature (*nānaikātmatā*), of that object... [End of fragment].

It should be understood that by this [argument], he establishes that the various designations of cognition (*buddhi-vyapadeśa*)— which possess diverse forms— do not prove the difference or non-difference of real entities (*vastu*). He brings this very point to fruition by demonstrating an illustrative example.

King Mahāsammata is an example of a past occurrence; the word "just as" (*yathā*) should be supplied here. Śaṅkha the Cakravartin and so forth are examples of a future occurrence. Regarding words such as "horn," when the form of what has been apprehended is visible—because it generates visual consciousness—it is "with visibility" (*sanidarśana*).
And it is "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) because it obstructs the arising of another in its own location;
this is an illustration of [the principle] that [a thing] functions with respect to various purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*).

For, although that [object] is of a single nature due to its being the producer of effects such as visual consciousness and so forth, it is nevertheless made the object of various terms such as "visible" (*sanidarśana*) and so on by means of various forms.

Therefore, these [reasons] are not capable of proving a difference in the nature of things. "A jar" is an example of those things that perform a single purposeful action; for instance, many [qualities] such as color, odor, taste, and touch, because they are capable of accomplishing a specific effect such as the holding of water, are assimilated by it as its objects through their commonality.
Therefore, they are not capable of establishing non-difference.
And it is well known that the cognition of such things as the past, the future, or a rabbit's horn does not establish a real entity.
Now, how is it understood that cognitions and words such as "visible" (*sanidarśana*) do not establish a difference in real entities? To this, he says:
"No," and so forth.

Why? Because in this very case, due to the application [of the terms] to the object such as visible form (*rūpa*), there is co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—that is to say, "visible form is that which is demonstrable and possesses resistance.

Otherwise, because they would have different referents, there would be no co-referentiality at all for words such as *vakula*, *utpala*, *kamala*, *mālatī*, and *mallikā*. This is the intended meaning.
But those who follow the doctrines of Kaṇabhakṣa and Akṣapāda, whose inner vision is defiled by the loss of right discernment produced by an attachment to false views, declare:
"Even if it is admitted that they have different objects, their synthesis in a single [substratum] is not at all contradictory;
for the causes thereof—such as visibility and so forth—inhere therein, in that [substratum], such as color-form."

Intending to show that all of this is a doctrine that provokes the laughter of wise men—because it is charming only so long as it is not investigated and because it cannot withstand the scrutiny of critical analysis—he says:
"Alas, this [is] labor," and so forth.
The word *vata* expresses compassion; to the question "Whose [labor]? he replies:

The intention is as follows: since it is impossible for those [qualities] to have a relationship with that [universal] in the absence of mutual assistance— given that the universal assists multiple related properties such as visibility and so forth—
the cause for falling into this exhaustion is the one who, from those related properties such as visibility and so on, attempts to sweep [the universal] into itself by means of various words.

Now, one might object: "By means of those very same distinct powers through which the state of having a common form (*sarūpatva*) assists a single relatum that has multiple connections, why does it not likewise produce multiple words such as 'intellect' (*buddhi*) and so forth? If this were the case, what benefit would be gained? To this, he says:
For in this way, the labor of following a causal chain is avoided.

The meaning is that this poor fellow [the Grammarian] abandons the effort of following a causal chain—namely, that [a substance] assists its relatum through various powers (*śakti*) and words proceed from those [powers]—by means of [postulating] forms (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Now, you too must necessarily accept that all entities possess specific causal powers; otherwise, why does a rice seed produce only a rice sprout and not a barley sprout?
When one is challenged by another, what can be said except for the nature of reality (*bhāvaprakṛti*)?
Therefore, for you, taking recourse in the nature of the categories of existence (*padārthaprakṛti*) alone is the only refuge, because otherwise it would be impossible to avoid this fault.
And this [position] is not something forbidden to me either by the royal court.
For it might be argued that even I can state this: its capacity consists solely in assisting various related things, not in producing multiple words.
This is true; however, he thinks as follows.
To begin with, properties such as visibility and so forth do not exist, because causal efficiency is impossible through either succession or simultaneity.

Furthermore, since those things that meet the conditions for perception are not perceived, it cannot be asserted that something which meets the conditions for perception exists while being unperceived; for such a claim would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Or, if [the universal] has not reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatā*), how could cognitions and designations based upon it proceed in the case of cows, gavayas, and so forth? By this, it is also shown that even for those things that are perceived, there is no perception of a universal as distinct from the individual, just as in the case of momentariness and the like; for if the universal were seen in its entirety, it would not fail to be clearly distinguished [from the individual].
If [the universal] exists, how can that verbal function (śabdavṛtti) which arises through its power exist?

In cases such as "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin), that basis for both cognition and the word does not exist in the absence of the [universal]. Therefore, even that [position] of yours does not cohere by any means of reasoning.
Furthermore:

In your view, it follows that all entities would occupy the same location, because they are non-different from their existence in every respect; or else, this [entity] would be excluded from a different location at once.
For if it were to exist [in both], it would not be one, since that which possesses existence in multiple locations cannot be single in every respect.
In the case of fruits such as the palmyra and others, there is a single nature despite their many and diverse substrates.
Alternatively, even if they were existent, that [single nature] would not be determined by the presence or absence of the capacity to produce a cognition or a word.
For this very reason, because it is not perceived, and because those [fruits] exist even in the absence of that [nature], as is the case with "cooks" and the like.
And this has been established in the *Pramāṇavārttika* (1.160):
"In the case of 'cook' and the like, [the word] is expressive even without an undivided object;
because there is a distinction, action is not its cause, nor is the genus residing in the action."
This and more is not stated here.
Furthermore, these [universals] cannot be recipients of assistance (*upakārya*), because being eternal, they cannot have any excellence added to them (*anādheyātiśayatva*).

Nor can they be brought into proximity by the intention of a person through the capacity of the universal—such as its resistance (*sapratighatva*)—which is assisted by the individual; for even when such a capacity is present, activity would follow regardless of whether there is a desire to speak (*vivakṣā*).
Or rather, let that very intention of the person (*puruṣābhiprāya*) be the regulator; what is the use of universals (*sāmānya*) residing in the objects?

For it is observed that the universals follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of those [intentional states], since eternal things cannot possess negative concomitance due to their lack of exclusion.
Therefore, all this is a mere conceptual construction based upon a false view.

And that very conceptual construction (kalpanā) should be adopted which cannot withstand further scrutiny; for among the various constructions possible in that context, this one is preferable because it is free from the faults of conceptualization and possesses positive qualities.
This may be the thought: "This conceptual construction is indeed logical."
For a single [word] does not possess the capacity to produce various meanings;
if this is so, he says: "In this case as well, we shall speak."

The intention [of the author] is this: if there were no capacity to produce various sounds, then there should also be no assistance rendered to various related entities, because it is accepted that there is a contradiction in one thing being the benefactor of many.
If it is argued that "no assistance is accepted precisely because the related entities are eternal," he says:
For if visibility and the other [qualities] were accepted as being ultimately unhelpful to those [entities], their relationship with them would not be established;

indeed, a cause that is not assisted by something else cannot properly be considered related to it. Since the non-differentiation of the objects of words has already been proven, those very same people, bearing the burden of their own exhaustion, raise this objection once again.

Now, let it be granted that words such as "name" (*nāman*), "visible" (*sanidarśana*), and so forth, have non-distinct objects. But how is it determined that words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and "cloth" (*paṭa*) have multiple objects as their referents?
To the extent that there exists another, distinct substance different from form (*rūpa*) and the rest,
it is precisely that which is made the object of words such as "pot" and "cloth.
For instance, a cloth that has become the subject of investigation is distinct from its threads, because it has a different maker, just like a pot and so forth.
Likewise, [the cloth] is not the object of either collective or individual cognitions, like a cow or similar things;
for the cognition "threads" or "a collection of threads" with respect to a cloth is not erroneous.
Furthermore, it is produced by other means, like a jar or similar things.
Furthermore, because it is produced by those situated in different locations,
and because it possesses a distinct dimension, just like a jar or similar objects,
such as the *vakula*, *āmalaka*, and *bimba* fruits.
And for this reason, because they exist at prior and subsequent times, like the seed and the sprout;
or else, threads are other than the cloth because they are its cause, like the shuttle and so forth;
or [the reverse] between the threads and the cloth.
Since you [assert that things] possess distinct powers, like water and fire,
so too this other object under investigation— the blue lotus— is entirely different from its fragrance and other qualities, because it serves as their delimiter,
just like Caitra and others.

In this context, whatever is the delimiter of a given thing is other than that thing; for example, Caitra is other than the body of a cow. These are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish their mutual exclusion. How, then, could these have different objects? || 0 ||
Anticipating that even this [objection] is but a slight manifestation of the darkness of those whose inner faculties are shrouded by the veil of adherence to false views, he says:

"Let even the pot be nothing but color and so forth, which, performing a single purposeful action, are denoted by a single word; what is the use of postulating a separate entity? Thus, the term "effect" (*kārya*) is supplied [to the objection]. His intention is that there is nothing at all of such a kind [as a pot], since it is not perceived apart from blue and the other [colors].

However, he considers that these means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which have been stated to establish that [distinction] are incapable of proving its differentiation because they are afflicted by defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus, it is as if a shadow is cast before him.
For instance, when this first means of valid cognition is examined, it does not even withstand the preceding examination.
For in this regard, two alternatives arise for these [opponents]:
either the distinctness of the cloth from the threads is being proven while they remain in their other state, or while they are arranged in a specific configuration.
Of these, the first alternative cannot withstand the heavy burden of critical analysis.

Because this would entail the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). For, since those whose pure intellects have been attained through the power of relying upon the system of the Sugata’s doctrine—which has thoroughly realized the reality of all things—and who [hold that] "all entities perish immediately after their production," it follows that you yourself actually desire their distinctness [from the cause]. Thus, how can the demon of the impending fall into the fault of proving the already established not seize you?

The second alternative as well finds no foothold for the soles of the feet upon the surface of a heated stone slab, as if scorched by a fierce fire; for the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the opponent.

Indeed, the fact that a cloth has different makers from those situated in specific locations does not enter the path of proof for the opponent, who—due to its very non-existence—does not even admit any difference from such types [of makers].
How, then, could he possibly accept that there is a difference in their authors?
Even though it was stated immediately prior, it is not sufficient to fulfill the desired objective by means of valid proof, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For the cognition "cloth" occurs only with respect to threads existing in a particular state of arrangement.
If it is argued that [the reflection] is seen in crystals and the like because its form is distinct [from them], even though the eyes are completely closed, we shall refute this later.

As for the arguments that [the reflection is not real] because it is accomplished by other means, because it is produced by those situated in different locations, because it has a different dimension, because it exists at earlier and later times, and because it possesses different powers— [these will also be addressed].
Here, the opponent—like one whose eyes are averse due to intense reflection—cannot endure the excellence of this [position], for it exposes the defects of the alternatives stated in the first proof.

"In the first case, there is the proving of what is already established; in the second, the reason is unestablished, because the production of [entities] as qualified by momentariness is what is intended. This is the summary verse.
Furthermore, as for what was stated— that the blue lotus has fallen within the scope of investigation and so forth—
that too is not tenable.

Because [it is said] "the fragrance and so forth of the blue lotus," this means that the fragrance and so forth, which are the very nature of the blue lotus, are capable of producing specific effects such as the cultivation of honey.

They are described in this way because they are distinguished by a particularity known as the "accomplishment of an undifferentiated effect," expressed through general terms such as "fragrance" and so on, which denote the accomplishment of an undifferentiated effect.
However, there is no other substance here possessing the characteristics previously described; for it has already been stated that such a thing is not perceived.
And thus, in this manner, it serves as the delimiter of those [cases];
yet, since that delimiter of theirs is not absolutely distinct [from them], what contradiction is there between these two?
A reason whose exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful is one in which the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is unestablished.
For there is no proof from a mere example, as that would lead to the over-extension [of the argument] to all things. Furthermore, [the example] "the body of a stone statue" [is used].

Even in the case of "the intrinsic nature of form" (*rūpasya svabhāvaḥ*), since there exists a distinction between the stone statue (*śilāputraka*) and its form (*rūpa*) by way of excluding [the former] from being the intrinsic nature of the body (*śarīra-svabhāva-vyavacchedakatva*), a difference between those two would also follow from that [reasoning];
yet this does not occur, because it would entail the consequence of their lacking intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*).
Therefore, you must clearly state that this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by means of this very point.

Now, do these words— such as "the fragrance and other qualities of the blue lotus"— proceed based solely on the actual nature of things, independent of the operation of human intention, by those whose intellects are possessed by the demon of false views and excessive conceptualization?
Or rather, do they, regardless of the actual nature of things, convey that object through a false attribution exactly as they are employed by them?

If the first alternative were the case, then there would be the consequence of constant denotation; furthermore, there could be no application [of words] to the past and so forth, or to other things, based on the will of a person. Moreover, it would follow that there could be no engagement with meanings that differ according to various other systems of doctrine.
And there would be no statement whatsoever that lacks a true referent. Now, if the latter [case] were so, then for those whose basis is the thing...
Words are not dependent on another for the sake of what is intended to be expressed;
[therefore,] objections such as the use of the genitive case or differences in number are appropriate only against those who raise them.
As they say:

In whatever way a word is designated by speakers as a signifier, that word is a signifier for that [meaning] regardless of any external object. At that time, there is no dependence on the power of words functioning according to the speaker's prior intention. (10)
Since the reality of the object is established through its subordination [to the cognition], the reason remains in a state where its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful.

By this, the following argument is also refuted: "We maintain that the other qualities—color, taste, smell, touch—and properties such as being something to be abandoned, which are distinct from sandalwood that has become the subject of dispute, do not exist [in the latter], because they are not designated [as such]."
It is like [the case of] a stone, a balance, an *āḍhaka*, or a *prasēvikā*.

Therefore, it is established that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever to establish its existence. For us, however, this very [lack of a means of valid cognition] is the proof establishing its non-existence.

Those things whose bodies are embraced by an existence characterized by mutually exclusive intrinsic natures do not produce a specific excellence of the self (ātma-atiśaya) through a form that conforms to a distinct composite substance (*vyatirikta-avayavi-dravya*).

For example, many such things as ashes, supports, saliva, and spittle; and likewise, threads and so forth possess the properties as they have been taught. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*).
By way of dissimilarity, [the examples are] the sky-lotus and so forth, because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).

If one does not admit that even those things which are mutually excluded possess a single intrinsic nature, then the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is the impossibility of that [single nature] existing in them either in its entirety or otherwise.

For how could that [single nature], while existing simultaneously in many places in its entirety, not lead to the inference of a multiplicity of its own self—just like a container situated upon multiple supports? Thus, how can it be attributed with a non-differentiated intrinsic nature?

Furthermore, at the time of perceiving a single part, there would follow the consequence of perceiving the whole, because the whole is entirely contained therein. If perception occurs by way of perceiving multiple parts, then even when only a few parts are seen, there would be perception [of the whole]; however, if perception were to occur by way of perceiving all the parts, it would follow that it is never perceived, since its bright middle portions are not perceived simultaneously.
Furthermore, it must be stated that if there were a vibration of a single part, it would follow that there would be a vibration of the whole and so forth;
nor can it be [the case] by way of a single portion, because that would entail having parts,
and because those portions themselves would entail an infinite regress.

For if those [parts] are indeed its components, then even in the case of things residing in a component such as a hand, it would have to reside in something else, and so forth; thus, there exists some single whole (*avayavin*) that is devoid of any other parts.
Consequently, let it be merely a collection of atoms and the like—what is the insistence on [the existence of] components that are identical with its own self?
Alternatively, it does not reside anywhere at all, for the individual parts are not each the whole. Enough with these well-established false prattlings; I shall desist.
Thus, considering that this [opponent's] supreme position will dissolve—like a fragment of a snow mountain rock struck by the intense rays of the sun—one who thinks so says:

"What is the point of postulating another object? This might be the response of one who holds such a hope; however, it is not the case that multiple things lack the capacity to perform a single purposeful action. Therefore, he says:
"Even many," and so forth. Like what?
Like the eye and other [senses].
Just as form, light, attention, the eye, and so forth, together produce a single visual consciousness,

so too will form and the other factors perform a single purposeful action, such as the specific act of holding water. Since this is the case, we consider it logical that for the sake of indicating that capacity for a single purposeful action, there may be the application of a single term— such as "cloth"— to those [factors] like form and the rest.
The word "also" (*api*) indicates that it is not only the performance of a single purposeful action that characterizes them.

If one asks how this is logical, the following is intended: certain words are employed for some specific purpose; in such cases, whatever is useful for multiple things in a single context must necessarily be enjoined there.
Furthermore, if it were enjoined separately in each case, there would be excessive prolixity (*atigaurava*).
Nor is it possible to enjoin its unique form, which is not shared by anything else.

Moreover, this effort would have no fruit whatsoever; rather, by this [effort], only those objects suitable for that [action] are to be enjoined, and the speaker has the freedom here as to whether they are enjoined by a single word or by many.
Thus, this single scriptural statement, proceeding with respect to many [meanings] by virtue of the intention of the speaker, does not deserve censure;
nor is it impossible to apply, because it depends upon the will [of the speaker].

For if there were no desire of the agent, how could this [universal] apply even to a single instance? Or, if there is such a desire, who is capable of obstructing it even in many instances? Nor should it be suspected that it does not function due to a lack of purpose.
Since it has been stated that even when [words] are distinct, there may be a cognition from a single word according to the difference in its purposes, we have rightly observed that this is well-said;
for people employ words in some way or another even without a purpose.
If it is argued that therefore this is not tenable, he says:

Furthermore, the application of words to objects in the world is not without purpose. For it is not a mere whim on the part of people that they employ words in an unrelated manner; rather, every undertaking of theirs is dependent upon a purpose, and it is considered that this [application of words] has such a purpose. Thus, it is said to be "by way of having a purpose."
The meaning is that just as visible form, odor, taste, and so forth, having a single common purpose, are combined and perform a single function.
One might raise the doubt that even when things are brought together, sometimes only one of them is active toward the effect while another remains indifferent; therefore, he says:
"or separately" (*pṛthak vā*).
The word "or" (vā) has the sense of "and" (ca).
The meaning is that all [of them] possess activity.
Others, however, explain it differently.
And they first refute the explanation [of the opponent].

In this regard, regarding the sequence by which objects are communicated through words—those objects such as form (rūpa) and so forth, whether together or separately, have a single purpose; that is, those forms and so forth, when combined and established in the shape of a broad base and belly [as a jar], have one purpose.
That is to say: either the fetching of honey, water, and so forth, or the production of cognitions with their respective individual forms from each of those very things.

Furthermore, since a single purpose observed in one case is not necessarily present in another—given that even among co-existent factors, indifference is sometimes observed—the phrase "or separately" (*pṛthag vā*) was stated in order to demonstrate that all [factors] possess activity.
Others maintain that the word *vā* (or) signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*).

However, since the expression "having a single purpose" (*ekaprayojanāḥ*) already implies that all [factors] exist in that manner, the inclusion of "or separately" would be redundant; moreover, this is not the intended meaning of the word, so such an objection is trivial.

They have not perceived the context; for here, the discussion has begun to explain how there is no contradiction in the application of the singular number to a collective term. In that case, what occasion is there for stating "separately"?
Furthermore, this term "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth is a generic term (*jāti-śabda*).
In that case, the process will necessarily be of a different nature.
As for what was stated—that because they are designated as having a single purpose, there is indeed a cognition of all [the constituents] being of such a nature—that too is not logically consistent.
For instance, although those intent on defeating an enemy force share a single purpose, not all of them are actively engaged in every operation;
the same would apply here as well.
It is for this very reason that the possibility of such a doubt has been explained.
However, when this term "separately" (*pṛthak*) is stated for the purpose of indicating that all [the factors] possess activity, then the denial (*apahnava*) is set aside.
By this very [explanation], the claim that it is not the meaning of the word is also refuted; thus, this [objection] is merely trivial.
Or let this interpretation stand, if it can somehow be established.

If a single word, such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*), were applied to designate those very things of such a kind—which, despite having different names, perform a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākārin*)—then what would happen? There would be no fault whatsoever;
rather, only a benefit would be obtained. Thus he says:
[regarding] that purposeful action...
There is no contradiction whatsoever with the singular number even for a collective term employed to indicate a power that is non-different [from its possessors].
Why? Because that power is one and non-different when [the factors] are combined; it does not belong to each individually, meaning it does not exist in those that are separate.

Thus, therefore, when that aggregate-word denotes a single aggregate such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) or the like, the singular number occurs—as in "a jar" (*ghaṭaḥ*); this is the remainder [of the argument]. Or rather, the verb "it would be" (*syāt*), which is to be mentioned later, is the verbal form.
Now, one might ask: "Is not this word 'jar' and so forth a genus-word (*jāti-śabda*), like the word 'cow' (*go*) and others? How then can this have been stated?"

This is true; there is no fault because of the following intention: this word [e.g., "cow"] is a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) with respect to its internal functioning within a collection, but it is also a collection-word (*samudāyaśabda*) with respect to the constituents of that collection, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
For instance, there are three ways of understanding words: some are exclusively genus-words.
Just as words such as "pleasure" and so forth [denote their objects] because pleasure and so forth lack parts;
whereas some are indeed collective terms (*samudāyaśabda*), such as the words "Vindhya," "Himavat," and "Sumeru," because there exists no other collection belonging to that same class.
Furthermore, there are other words that denote a collection,
such as these very words "pot" and so forth, which [denote] a collection in relation to another collection of constituent parts.
Thus, for now, the absence of contradiction regarding the application of speech with respect to words denoting collections has been explained.
Now, he asks: "How is it with respect to genus-words (jātiśabda)?
He says: "With respect to genus-words," and so forth.
Because of the capacity of objects such as jars, both individually and collectively, there is both a manifold capacity and a single capacity.

This is what is meant: because even a single tree is capable of performing purposeful actions such as providing material for a house, and many trees are also so capable; therefore, since they are individually capable, there is a manifold capacity, yet since they are collectively capable, there is a single capacity. This is due to the metaphorical attribution of unity, based on their being the cause of a single reflective conceptualization (*pratyavamarśa*).

And since this is so, therefore, when there is a desire to express various powers (*nānā-śakti*) in their respective order, the plural number occurs as "trees" (*vṛkṣāḥ*) because of the multiplicity of powers;
however, when there is a desire to express a single power, the word would be stated in the singular because of its oneness.
This would be the case if this rule were accepted by you, whose minds are agitated by the possession of the demon of false attachment.
The plural number occurs when many things are to be expressed, and the singular number occurs when only one thing is to be expressed. Thus, even when this view is adopted regarding many things—
There is a rule: "The dual and singular endings are used for two and one [respectively]" (Pāṇini 1.4.22). Thus, he shows that even in that case, there is no fault whatsoever.
But how is it for you? To this he says:
"For us," and so forth, by the power of convention (*saṃketa*).
In words ending in the plural number, such as *dārāḥ*, *sikatāḥ*, *pādāḥ*,
and *guravaḥ*, the grammatical operation occurs even though plurality does not exist in the referent.

Even though there is thus a multiplicity [of instances], the fact that words ending in the singular number—such as *eṣā nagarī* ("this city") and *ṣaṭ pūlīvanam* ("six groves")—occur in such usage is simply a matter of non-insistence (*anabhiniveśa*).
For what conscious person indeed would venture to insist upon words whose application depends merely on the intention of a speaker? This is the intended meaning.
He presents the opponent’s position as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*):
"If it is argued that multiple things, such as color and so forth, are not capable of producing a single word,
because a relationship between the manifold and the one is not tenable."
The refutation begins with the words "Why, etc. There are two alternatives: do objects, being independent of them, themselves produce words?
Or are they somehow applied by persons to objects for the sake of linguistic usage? Such is the dilemma.

In that case, those [sounds] are employed by persons according to their will; otherwise, there would be no employment of past sounds in cognitions immediately following the perception of their source, or in other instances—this is the sense.

Consequently, when objects themselves, independent of human desire, give rise to words, one might indeed consider whether a thing possesses power or lacks power, as expressed in the verse beginning with "nāmaika" (only one name).
If it is argued that there is indeed self-arising, he says:
"And that is not tenable," the intention being that this is due to the three reasons just mentioned.

Therefore, since those persons have the power to assign those words to objects even without [grammatical features] such as singularity and so forth, those persons may, according to their will, employ a word ending in the plural even for a single object, or a word ending in the singular even for multiple objects. What reproach can there be in that regarding those words? The objection that "a non-unitary thing, such as color and so forth, is not capable of producing a single word" is entirely without merit; one considers it to be nothing more than the manifestation of excessive delusion.
It might be asked: "Why would they assign a single word to multiple things? To this he says:

Since the ground for the restriction has already been stated, [the author] says "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth to demonstrate its capacity, at this point where it might be argued that there could also be a restriction of a single word therein.
He states the reinforcement.
"By that which is accepted as the substratum" means by the composite substance (*avayavidravya*), because they [the parts] are connected to it through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
How is there a connection? There is no connection at all between the manifold and the one, because the contradiction [between them] is admitted.
The intention [of the opponent] is that otherwise, it would follow that [the universal] coexists even with a single word.
The other replies:
"If this is not so, because of the contradiction in its relation with a single [word], we do not accept that the universal 'one-ness' resides in color and the other [sensory objects]."

However, there is a contradiction regarding this manifold purposeful activity— such as holding water, providing clothing, and so forth— which belongs to form and other qualities that are non-different and indistinguishable [from one another] in objects such as jars, blankets, and couches. Thus,
because of the contradiction of the word [used to express them], its capacity [to denote such distinct activities] is revealed.
And there is no distinction between them because there is no distinction in the substance that serves as their substratum. He clarifies this very point:

those [elements] such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, being of a single nature, would perform that same purposeful activity—such as the specific capacity to hold water—which is impossible in another collection like a woolen blanket (*kambala*). For that reason, of that...

These [entities] manifest for the sake of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); those others do not perform that causal efficiency which is impossible for them, just as those very same qualities such as color (*rūpa*) residing in a woolen blanket [do not perform the efficiency] of those belonging to their own kind [when residing elsewhere].

And likewise, the qualities such as color residing in a jar also possess a nature no different from the qualities such as color residing in the woolen blanket; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
In this manner, it should be applied elsewhere as well; such is the formulation of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). To this, he states the reply beginning with "Let it be so," and so forth.
By this, he points out the non-establishment of the reason (*asiddhi*).

The meaning here is as follows: there is indeed no non-difference among color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities] within things such as a blanket, because they are determined by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) precisely as being mutually distinct in their own forms.
And this being the case, why does this perception disregard this desire?
[The word] *kim* is used here in the sense of a question or a censure; it means that [perception] ought not to tolerate [the claim] but rather rejects it.

Furthermore, this is undesirable for us, because we maintain that color and the other qualities are non-different from the pot, the blanket, and so forth, since—by the force of the reason that they constitute a collection—we admit their own internal differentiation while disregarding the substance.
Thus, by means of this admission as well, he points out the fallacy of the unestablished (asiddhatā);
the distinction from the previous case is that it was pointed out by way of perception.
Again, the opponent, full of envy, says:
If the pot were indeed something other than its form and so forth, what would happen?
The intention [of the opponent] is that no fault whatsoever would arise;
we do not refuse to accept this out of stinginess.
However, he says that this much must be stated here:
because that whole (avayavin), being perceptible, is admitted to be graspable by the sense organs of sight and touch;
[it would follow] that it has no form and so forth—that is to say, it would be devoid of the nature of color, odor, and the rest.
Because of the admission of the difference between quality and substance.

The meaning is this: by means of its distinction from those [qualities], that is, by means of its distinction from color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, when it appears to the intellect born of the visual or tactile sense-faculties, what obscuration could there be? There is no obstacle whatsoever. Furthermore, even one whose faculties are unimpaired, though examining with great care, is not able to perceive a substance such as a jar as a distinct entity possessing a form separate from blue, sweet, fragrant, hard, and so forth.
Abiddhakarṇa, however, says:

"Even when color and so forth are not apprehended, the apprehension of the substance itself certainly exists; for in very dim light, a substance is perceived even while its color and other qualities are unperceived, such that one is uncertain whether it is a cow or a horse."
But is it not the case that even there only the configuration (saṃsthāna) is perceived?
True, it is perceived, but it does not consist of color-form (rūpa) and so forth.
For if it consisted of color-form and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving specific distinctions such as blue, yellow, and the like.
Likewise, when a man is inside an iron suit of armor, although his form and other qualities are not perceived, the cognition of "man" is observed.
And at night, when the form and other qualities of a crane perched on a branch are not perceived, the cognition of "bird" is observed.

Similarly, in the case of a crystal gem that conforms to the differences of various adjuncts such as blue objects, although its own form and other qualities are not perceived, the cognition of "crystal" occurs.

Likewise, it is observed that when the color of a cloth is overwhelmed by the color of a dye, even though the color of the cloth and so forth are not perceived, the cognition of the "cloth" still occurs.
All of this speech merely reveals the manifestation of an intellectual dullness born from the long-term habituation to false views.

For instance, regarding what was said—that in very dim light or at night, and in the presence of a blue or other colored substrate, the substance is perceived even when its color and so forth are not grasped—it must be asked: of what kind [is this substance]?
If it is argued that "the substance is perceived there,
and its nature is indeed seen exactly as it is perceived," [we reply: surely,
in very dim light or at night, neither the color of the crystal nor the color of the substrate is perceived there.
And it is not of that same nature;
for if it were of that nature, the consequence would be the collapse of the position just stated,
and because it is not perceived as such by those standing nearby or at its side.

Nor can there be an understanding of a real entity through a cognition that does not possess its form, because that would entail the absurd consequence that any cognition whatsoever could determine all entities.

Therefore, this cognition is erroneous; arising from its own beginningless material cause which is the seed of error, it is produced as being devoid of an object, appearing as such just like the perception of two moons and the like.
Even though it is devoid of an external object, it occurs at specific places and times,
because it depends upon the awakening of its own material cause (upādāna-vāsanā) and external dominant conditions (bāhya-adhipati-pratyaya),
just like the cognition of two moons and so forth.
Even though it is erroneous, there is non-contradiction with the object because of the presence of a specific dominant condition,
just like the illusion of a jewel in the luster of a jewel.

Nor is it logical to maintain that this [cognition] possesses an object solely because it does not contradict the object, for this would be subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of inference and by the illusion of a gem (*maṇibhrānti*).
If it is argued that "it is precisely that substance which is grasped as such; therefore, anything other than that is objectless," we reply:
indeed, it has already been stated that a substance is not of that nature, nor can a cognition permeated by one form be the determiner of another.
And this being the case, even if there is dependence [on other factors] while having "the existent" as its object, it indeed remains that it has the existent as its object.
For it can be said in this way: those very things such as blue appear in that manner.

However, when there is no cause for error or doubt, and when one is in a state of light, situated in a suitable location, and in a state free from external adjuncts (*nirupadhāna*), it is not perceived.

That substance appears as having a non-self-nature when distinguished [from others] at other times; however, when there exist causes for error or doubt—such as the state of eyes shrouded in the darkness of night, staying in a distant place, or being in a state of using a bolster—it appears as distinguished from the form of anything else. Who other than a materialist (*bhautika*) could say this?
The cognition of a person inside an iron armor is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Rather, it is inferential (*laiṅgika*).

For instance, from seeing a bodice situated in a specific shape produced by the strength residing in the limbs of a male body, there arises a cognition based on an effect as a logical mark (*kāryaliṅga*); this cognition depends upon the recollection of the [invariable] relation (*sambandha*) regarding such a cause.
Immediately after [the perception of the body], the cognition "this is a person" (puruṣa) arises.
For this very reason, that recognition is of indistinct form, and there arises the doubt, "What is this?

Furthermore, the causes for the production of such a configuration—the "mantle" (kañcuka)—are precisely the color, shape, and so forth of the person; it is not some other composite substance (avayavidravya).
Because that [entity] is unestablished, and it is impossible to accept the causal status of something unestablished;
whereas the causal relationship between form and so forth is established through perception and non-perception,
since they alone are perceived when arranged in such a manner.
In the case of a cloth, however, due to contact with substances such as *kaṣāya* or *mañjiṣṭhā*, that very [cloth] is seen to have become something entirely different;
it is not, however, a perception resulting from the inseparable conjunction of two substances possessing distinct forms.
Furthermore, its cessation occurs through the severance of the causes for the persistence of that substance’s configuration.
Furthermore, since water, fire, and so forth arise from other causes that depend upon their own respective material bases (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), this [objection] is refuted.
By this, it is also clearly demonstrated that even when an iron ball and its color are perceived, the cognition of them as distinct is observed.

Thus, since the perceptibility of a substance (*dravya*) is unestablished, the proclamation that "cows, horses, buffaloes, boars, and elephants, having entered into a state of mutual exclusion, are distinct from color and the rest" is merely empty talk.
The argument that "because it is sensory while being unconditioned by the sense-faculties (vākya-indriya) that grasp all [objects] such as form— just like pleasure and so forth"— is thus refuted.
The formal arguments (prayoga), moreover, are as follows:
Whatever is visible and does not exist apart from its substratum must either be admitted as non-different from it or accepted as non-existent.

For example, a horn on a human head is not perceived; likewise, while blue and other such qualities are visible, universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), priority (*paratva*), posteriority (*aparatva*), and so forth, are not perceived as existing apart from them. This is a case of the non-perception of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*);
thus, there is no proof for their existence.

Because it is itself admitted to be visible; and because substance, as accepted to be distinct from the fivefold objects such as form and so forth, is not apprehended by visual cognition— given that it is accepted as meeting the conditions for perception— due to its lack of the nature of an object such as blue,
like sound, smell, or taste.
And anticipating the objection that "this [distinction] is not indeed non-different from that, and thus this same fault applies there," he says:
"That excellence, characterized by exclusion, being identical with the substrate possessing that excellence, is non-continuous;

thus, when it necessarily ceases, since it lacks pervasiveness, how does it—while proceeding as something non-existent—not bring about a plurality of natures, just like the cognitions of pleasure and pain?"
The meaning is that it indeed draws [the effect] along.

Furthermore, the application [of the reason] is as follows: whatever is the very nature (ātmabhūta) of something necessarily ceases when that thing ceases, and it proceeds only when that thing proceeds, just as the essence of that very excellence (atiśaya) does. And since the possessor of excellence is of the same nature as the excellence itself, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).

Furthermore, there is a difference between the two states belonging to the substratum (the self), because they are occupied by mutually contradictory qualities, just like pleasure and pain; this is indeed a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

If it is argued that this excellence does not proceed or cease without being connected [to the self], and therefore the example in the former case lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*), while in the latter case the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*), he replies:

If it is admitted that excellence (atiśaya) possesses a lineage [of causal continuity] and thus undergoes cessation and emergence, then what is the cessation of what, or what is the emergence of what?
There is no cessation or emergence of anything whatsoever,
because everything exists at all times.
And thus, by the statement "everything would be applicable everywhere," etc., the fault previously mentioned applies; this is the intended meaning.
He states the reinforcement:
"If you yourself admit that there is the occurrence or cessation of some intrinsic nature (svabhāva) called 'excellence' (atiśaya)."

Because it is stated that "the distinction in conventional usage arises from the cessation of one excellence and the production of another excellence," the opponent—whose mind has been purified by the repeated study of the Tathāgata’s words—does not accept this very point. He would indeed agree with Bhadramukha if the engagement and withdrawal [of activity] were authorized by him in the same manner as they are by me.

However, since he accepts the arising and destruction of things without any underlying substrate (*niranvaya*), there is no manifestation of the substance apart from those [qualities], just as in the case of light or blue, or because it is perceived by the same sense organ as they are; therefore, he says:

Furthermore, objects are perceived through direct perception as appearing with distinctness—such as "this is blue," "this is fragrant," "this is sweet," or "this is rough"—even though they do not occupy separate locations; what are these [objects], such as visible form and so forth?

This was stated according to worldly convention, but for them there is no non-distinctness of location. For it is said in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "The ten material [elements] possess resistance. (AKB 1.29)
Because of this statement [in the *Pramāṇavārttika*],
and likewise because [the examples] such as the touch of wind and sunlight are apprehended by non-distinct sense faculties, this response is given in due order.
By this, he demonstrates the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason (*hetu*).

And having approached [the argument], it was stated that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the property of being perceivable by distinct sense organs (*sabhinna-indriya-grāhyatva*) with respect to its connection with the subject of the thesis (*dharmin*); however, this [deviation] does not apply here because of the "unestablishedness in one part" (*ekadeśāsiddhi*).
How so?
Because fragrant, sweet, and other such qualities are not perceivable by the sense organ that perceives the substance (*dravya*).
[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence that a single substance would possess all the sense-faculties.

However, light, blue, and so forth are indeed non-different, because when a lamp or similar source is present, they arise as having the nature of illumination, their bodies being permeated by such an intrinsic nature; thus, there is no difference between them. Therefore, he considers that the example is also devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikalpa*).

Therefore, by those who accept its perceptibility, it must necessarily be admitted that it appears as distinct from form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects]; otherwise, its status as perception would be unestablished.
Why? Because of the passage beginning with "this very [object]," which is easy to understand.
Furthermore, this jar and so forth are accepted by you as being distinct from form and the rest.
What is this "purchase for the price of one's own self"?
By this, he indicates that such a thing does not enter into the path of worldly transaction.

Furthermore, he does not show its nature as something superior, because it does not appear [to the senses]; yet he wishes to accept its perceptibility, since the established doctrine (siddhānta) states that substance is both visible and tangible.
One should supply the phrase: "Friends who possess uninterrupted love for this Self will accept this.

The commentary states: "One who is a buyer by means of payment of a price (*mūlyadānakrayī*) is not like that [the friend]. Alternatively, one whose nature is to buy is a "buyer" (*krayī*); such a buyer by means of payment of a price is not like that [the friend].
To the question "How is this so?", he says: "He who [attains] direct perception," and so forth.
He concludes that "the payment of the price" here means the surrender of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

If it is argued that [the pot] must indeed exist—just like color and other qualities—because of the existence of the cognition and designation "one pot," how then can it be non-existent? To this, he replies with the words: "Cognition, words, and so forth have also been explained; and not all... and so on.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), its distinctions and non-distinctions are included.
If it is claimed that its establishment as a proof is achieved through those [attributes] such as cognition and designation, one might argue:
"Even though a substance is manifest, it is not perceived when its salty taste is overwhelmed, just like the taste of sugar;
therefore, a logical mark (*liṅga*) is stated in order to establish it. To this, he says:
Furthermore, it is not logical for the form of an object that is directly perceived to be unperceived,
provided it is not overwhelmed by another substance; however, if there is such overwhelming, then [its non-perception] is indeed logical.
It is like the juice of sugar-cane;
nor is there any suppression of it by anything here.
If it is argued that there is [suppression] by blue and so forth—
There is no perception [of a substance] due to its being large, possessing a single substance, or having such a nature;
likewise, it has been stated that there is non-perception because of the absence of the manifestation of color (*rūpa*).
And when that [color] is not perceived, those [other qualities] are also not perceived.

This leads to the consequence that [the whole] would lack defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Consequently, it is thought that because all categories of things would be uncharacterized, worldly discourse (*lokavyavahāra*) itself would be utterly destroyed.
It is precisely by means of such non-characterization that a logical mark (*liṅga*) is stated for the purpose of proving that [alleged] whole.

If it were accepted that the logical mark (*liṅga*) is a means of establishing the existence of that [nature], then that [nature] would be expressed; however, there is no logical mark whatsoever that makes it known.
As was stated previously:
if it is argued that "even in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it, that [nature] certainly exists," he says:
It is improper to accept the existence of that which lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), even if it is not perceived.
By the term "of that which lacks a means of valid cognition," he states the absence of any proof-establishing means of cognition other than perception.
One must admit that whatever lacks a means of valid cognition to establish its existence does not exist.

Just as there is no lotus in the expanse of the sky, and since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish the existence of a whole (*avayavin*), he considers non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) to have the result of negating the conventional usage of "existent.
Having thus established in detail the absence of a single substance, he concludes the current topic with the words beginning "That... (*tad...*).
He concludes the fundamental treatise as well with the words "Thus far... and so on.
For this very reason, there is no reversal—that is, no absence—of those [qualities] such as existence and so forth, due to a reversal of those [entities] such as cognition and so forth.
The intention [of the author] is this: how can that which does not even establish the existence of something establish its non-existence while it is present?
If it is argued that although cognition and so forth do not establish existence, difference, or non-difference, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) will nevertheless establish them, he replies:
"But the conventional usage of 'existence' would arise from causal efficiency," because existence is defined by that very characteristic. This is the meaning.
By this, he shows that there is indeed equality between us two in this regard;
however, he states that there is disagreement elsewhere, saying:
"there is no conventional usage regarding the difference or non-difference of existence."
How so? Because even a single thing is observed to perform multiple functions.
