Having thus explained in detail the justification of the members of the proof regarding the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), [the author], wishing to describe the remaining types of non-apprehension, says:

"In the case of the non-apprehension of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhau*), and so forth. Having established by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the relationship of pervaded and pervader between two properties—such as being a *śiṃśapā* tree and being a tree—the establishment of the absence of the pervader (e.g., "tree-ness") is the justification; the term "of the member of the proof" (*sādhanāṅgasya*) is to be supplied.
For example: "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here because there is no tree.
Now, one might object: "In that case, its absence is established by the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) alone; so what is the use of this [other reason]?
For a means of proof (*sādhana*) is not truly effective if it merely adds a distinction to an object for which the action has already been accomplished."

According to the statement of Pāṇini (1.4.42), "The most effective means is the instrument," and because valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been described as having the nature of making known an object not yet apprehended, or as the illumination of an unknown object,
this is indeed true.
For this [reasoning] is not applied everywhere;

rather, it applies only where there is a lack of certainty regarding the specific distinctions of trees such as the *sāla*, *sarala*, *palāśa*, and *śiṃśapā*—namely, in that which has gone beyond the sky (is invisible).
In every case, this is employed precisely where the absence of the pervader is not ascertained due to some cause of error.

The non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) should also be employed only in those cases where the absence of the effect is not ascertained, and not elsewhere, for [otherwise] it would be futile. For example, when smoke is not ascertained in the darkness, one cannot say, "There is no smoke here because of the absence of fire," because there is doubt regarding the absence of the effect.
And because [the absence of the effect] is certain when the cause is absent,

the perception of what is incompatible with the nature [of the cause] (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*) must also be employed only in reference to that which exists in space and so forth, where the body is situated in a state of contact and is being licked by a mass of flames agitated by a cluster of locks of hair. Furthermore, the perception of what is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*) can only be applied to a spot of ground occupied by a person standing nearby— where it is impossible to perceive the presence or absence of specific states such as the bristling of hair or the teeth-chattering caused by cold— and not elsewhere.
Because of their fruitlessness.
Following this same method, the scope of application for other types of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) should also be understood.
This refers to those [non-apprehensions] of essential nature (*svabhāva*), pervader (*vyāpaka*), and cause (*kāraṇa*).
The analysis of the compound is: "those perceptions of them [the two] are contradictory.
Between two contradictions, there is the presentation of one.
Furthermore, the two contradictions are: the occurrence of one thing when its causes are unimpaired, and the non-occurrence of another.
And [this refers to] that which is characterized by existing through mutual exclusion.

Following this same direction, the establishment of the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) in cases such as the perception of an effect contradictory to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*) is likewise easily understood; thus, it has not been stated.

Nevertheless, due to slight differences in formulation, even among those [reasons] distinct from the eleven types of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), such as the perception of what is pervaded by what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), the perception of what is pervaded by what is contradictory to the effect (*kāryaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), the perception of the effect of what is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*), and the perception of the effect of what is contradictory to the effect (*kāryaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*), etc., [the members of the proof are established].
The establishment of the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) has been stated; their examples, moreover, should be understood in their proper order as follows:
"There is no smoke here, because of the touch of frost."
"There are no causes of fire here with unimpeded capacity, because of the sensation of frost;
nor is there a sensation of frost here, because of smoke;
therefore, there are no causes of cold here with unimpeded capacity, because of smoke."

The presence of a cause, an effect, or something incompatible [with the negandum], as well as the absence of a pervader or an effect, and another type consisting of the effect of something incompatible—these are the means of proving a negation.
(15) Here there is no smoke because of the sensation of cold; nor is there a capable cause of fire.
"Here, from smoke there is no touch of snow; it is not possible [to infer] a cause of cold"—these are the summary verses (*saṃgrahaśloka*).
Thus, first of all, it has been demonstrated in one manner that the statement of what is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) and so forth constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

He establishes that very point by means of another formulation as well, beginning with "Or else" (*athavā*). This entire compound, "na ceti," functions here through repetition (*āvṛtti*) to include an additional meaning while setting aside the previously stated meaning. It does not, however, function like the expression "Either the *dhava* tree stands, or else the *khadira* tree," where there is a disjunction (*vikalpa*) involving the abandonment of the prior meaning; for in this case, both meanings are intended to be expressed.
In this context, the word *sādhana* (means of proof) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
Here, the word *aṅga* (limb/member) signifies a constituent part (*avayava*), whereas in the previous [verse] it signified a cause (*kāraṇa*); this is the distinction.

By employing the term "collection" (*samudāya*) for the statement of the three-featured reason (*trirūpahetu*), [the author] subordinates the status of being a means of proof to the statements of the definition and so forth within those [three features].
One might think: "In a formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya*), the absence of the reason in the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*) is stated;

and in a formulation based on difference (*vaidharmya*), the presence [of the reason] in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is not [stated], because it is precisely what is to be negated immediately thereafter.
Therefore, how could the non-statement of even one of these two constitute 'the statement of a non-member of the proof' (*asādhanāṅgavacana*)? This would not contradict what is about to be said."
And this is not explained in that way alone;
for the reason (hetu) possesses three forms and has such a nature.

When it is established in its ultimate sense, the statement of it consists of those two expressions which reveal it—namely, the expression of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and the expression of its presence in the similar class (sapakṣasattva), or the expression of the property of the subject and the expression of its absence from the dissimilar class (vipakṣāsattva); the collection of these two constitutes [the proof].

The statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth is a member (*aṅga*) of that collection of two statements. Thus, first of all, the statement of the property of the subject is constant for both [the other members], while either one of the other two may be occasional.
Therefore, the member of that which consists of the collection of two statements is always twofold; now, the non-statement of even one of these members constitutes a non-probative statement.
By the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that this applies not only to the case of both [members] being absent, but according to the first explanation as well.
For silence is the absence of speech regarding two things; and since that has already been mentioned under the heading of "lack of ready wit," he states another synonym as well,
beginning with "Or else," and so forth.
"Of that very [statement]" refers to the collection of statements possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*); that which is not a limb, not a constituent part (*avayava*), of it.
If it is asked, "But how is it that the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth are not limbs of the proof (*sādhana*)? it is said in reply:
The statement of the thesis is not the means of proof,
because it does not produce the establishment of that [thesis] either directly or indirectly; for it is the object itself that leads one to understand the connection,
whereas the verbal expression does not, as it is devoid of any connection with the object.

Therefore, neither the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) nor the statement of the reason (*hetu*) is a direct means for the establishment of the object. Furthermore, since doubt regarding the object is observed from the statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*), and not certainty, it is for that reason also not a direct means of proof.
It might be argued: "Doubt itself is unestablished, because the proponent and the opponent have certainty [regarding the matter], even though it may arise for others."

If this were so, then even upon hearing the statement "because of being produced" (kṛtakatva) and the like, doubt would arise for those who are unlearned; thus, [the reason] would be inconclusive (anaikāntika).
This, however, is irrelevant.
For the certainty of both the proponent and the opponent must exist either when they have begun to communicate regarding a single property, such as impermanence, or regarding two opposing properties.
Firstly, it cannot be [the case] in a single [locus], because there would be no dispute;
for that would entail the consequence of the uselessness of employing a proof. Nor can it be [the case] in two properties.
First, it is not [the case that a thing is one], because there would be no dispute regarding a single entity,
which would entail the futility of employing a proof;
nor is it the case that it is both, because it would entail the superimposition of two contradictory properties upon a single real object.

For when two contradictory properties regarding a single object are ascertained by the proponent and the opponent through the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that object would result in having a dual nature. Alternatively, if those two are not ascertained through the power of valid cognition but rather from their respective scriptures (*āgama*),
even so, since the two properties have been ascertained by means of valid cognition, it must be explained why doubt does not arise from the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*).

Therefore, the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*) is not a direct means of proof, nor is it an indirect one; for, by virtue of merely expressing the probandum (*sādhya*), it cannot indicate what is possible—just like the statement of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*). On the other hand, the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*) is said to be established as a means of proof through its capacity, because it indicates what is possible. Furthermore, while being the statement of the thesis, it is an auxiliary member of the proof because it assists the proof, just like the statement of the reason.
And by means of illuminating the object of the proof (*sādhana*), it assists the establishment of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Otherwise, that proof would operate without an object.

Since even [factors such as] the contact between cognition, the self, and the mind (*jñānātmanmanaḥ-sannikarṣa*) are assistants to the proof, the qualification "provided it is speech" (*vacanatve sati*) is added.

Furthermore, [the opponent argues that the statement of the example is a member of the proof] because it illuminates the object of the probandum and the means of proof, just like the statement of the example itself.

This too is utterly worthless, because the request "prove that sound is impermanent" is an external utterance; while it assists the proof, it does not illuminate the opposite of the means of proving the probandum, nor is it an internal member for the establishment of the probandum.

Or what is the use of pointing out the object (*viṣaya*) if, without it, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) would not occur? Indeed, everything would be appropriate (*śobheta*), since even without this, [the probandum is established] as long as [the reason is present].

Whatever is produced is all impermanent, like a pot and so forth; and since sound is produced, even if the thesis "sound is impermanent" were not explicitly stated, it would still be merely a part of the meaning.
Therefore, its formal statement is entirely purposeless.

This might be a misconception if the reason (*hetu*) were not employed as a verbal expression just like the thesis (*pakṣa*) for the purpose of indicating the object of the reason's operation; in that case, how could it receive the designation of being dependent upon the thesis?

The properties such as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth are established [only when the reason is already known]. Alternatively, if these [properties] were to depend upon themselves, the occurrence of the subject would be impossible due to the power produced therein.
It is also untenable to say that the properties such as being a property of the subject are established by the force of the subject which is obtained through implication (*sāmarthya*).
For if those [other factors] were absent, the very thesis (pakṣa) obtainable by implication would be impossible.

Furthermore, this involves mutual dependence: the status of being a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) and so forth are established by virtue of the thesis which is reached through their own force; and the thesis is established by the power of the status of being a property of the subject and the rest.
To this it is replied:

Indeed, at the time of the formal proof (*sādhana*), there is no conceptualization regarding the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth; rather, it is simply that in whichever particular subject (*dharmin*)—be it sound and the like whose specific nature is desired to be known, or a fire obscured by a wall, or a vessel and the like—in which a property characterized as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), "smokiness" (*dhūmatva*), or the like, is apprehended either through inference or through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Or it is made known;

or, by virtue of its connection with specific qualities, it is ascertained in another object such as a jar or a kitchen and remembered as being present there; or it is remembered precisely as non-existent in things devoid of those specific qualities, such as the sky or the ocean.

Like a property of the thing itself (*vastudharmatā*), even without the formal designation of "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth, it makes the subject understood as qualified by the property sought to be known, solely by its own efficacy.
And that object of capacity is called the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) for him.

Subsequently, for the sake of conventional usage in the treatises, designations such as "property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth—which arise in dependence upon that [thesis]—are elaborated according to one's preference.
Alternatively, by the force of the context of retrospective reflection, these conceptualizations such as "property of the thesis" may indeed occur even at the time of the proof (*sādhana*).

How so? For that property of a subject which a proponent intends to prove as being qualified by the subject under dispute—that is the *pakṣa* (the thesis). Any other property belonging to that [subject] is the *pakṣadharma* (the property of the subject). And a *sapakṣa* (similar instance) is an object that is similar by way of the generality of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) under discussion.
The phrase "the thesis is the locus of the absence of that" means as follows:
even for one who employs the thesis at the time of the proof, it is not the case that the thesis is merely the initial statement, such as "sound is impermanent.
Rather, [it is the subject] through another context of introduction.
Even by means of the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth must also be stated;

and that [force of the context] is common even to one who refutes the formulation of the thesis (*pakṣa*). Therefore, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is not a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*).
As for why the statements of the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*) are not members of the proof, that will now be explained.

In this context, the application (*upanaya*) of the proof is the connection [to the example], expressed as "it is thus" (*tathā*) or "it is not thus" (*na tathā*), which depends upon the illustrative instance (*udāharaṇa*).
The phrase "just as... so too" (*yathā tathā*) is for the purpose of reflection (*pratibimbana*).
What, then, is reflection here? It is the establishment of the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the property residing in the example.
Therefore, there is a commonality of property with that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
And thus, the meaning of the application (*upanaya*) is the presence [of the reason] together with the thing to be proven, as in: "And this [sound] is produced.
But is it not the case that this presence has already been stated by the [reasoning] "because of being produced"?
It is not stated [explicitly], because there is only a mention of the property to be proven (sādhya) and the proving property (sādhana).
The mention of only the property to be proven and the proving property is as follows: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced."
Furthermore, the presence of "being produced" (kṛtakatva) in sound is understood through the application (upanaya) as "it exists," or [in the negative form],
"it does not exist in sound."

And thus, it could be inferred that the application (*upanaya*) conveys a meaning distinct from the statement of the reason (*hetu*), because—while possessing an identical form and being distinct from well-known synonyms—it is employed after the statement of the reason, just like the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). [The definition of conclusion is:
"The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the re-statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the presentation of the reason" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.39).

Furthermore, regarding the conclusion (*nigamana*): it is the restatement of the subject matter of the proposition (*pratijñā*)—namely, "the forest"—once that subject has been established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for the purpose of negating the possibility of the opposite consequence. It is not, however, merely a repetition of the proposition itself.
What is the reason? Because the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is the indication of that which is to be proven, and the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the indication of what is established.
Furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) is observed to signify multiplicity; for example:
"Again, this radiance of lightning flashes forth."
Furthermore, it is said: "And this city of Gandharvas is seen.

Here, by implication, what is understood is the statement of the reason (*hetvapadeśa*) occurring immediately after the application (*upanaya*), not that which occurs immediately after the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Because it is impossible;
for no one employs a conclusion after stating another proposition and adducing a reason, such as:
"Sound is impermanent because it is produced."
Therefore, sound is impermanent.
For this reason, the statement of the conclusion has a meaning distinct from the meaning of the proposition;
because, while possessing a form distinct from the proposition, it is stated at a time subsequent to the statement of the reason, just like the statement of the example.
Furthermore, the conclusion (*nigamana*) does not establish the meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*),
because it functions as a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) upon that which has already been conveyed by another word.
It is like the statement "Therefore, this is not a horse," when someone has said, "This one who is coming here has horns."
Therefore, a sentence accompanied by a word does not convey a meaning that is established for the purpose of investigation,
because it is employed only after the instruction regarding the cause has occurred;
the illustration is as before.
This is what is being refuted: indeed, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is not stated in this manner—
namely, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced"—
because such an application of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has already been rejected immediately following [the previous discussion].
Moreover, sound is produced;
and whatever is such is entirely impermanent, like a water-jar and so forth;
or rather, whatever is produced is entirely impermanent, like a pot and so forth.

And thus, the formulation "sound is produced" may be employed in either way as desired, because the proof of the probandum (sādhya) occurs in both cases. In that regard, having stated, "Sound is produced; and whatever is such is entirely impermanent, like a jar or the like," the statement of the application (upanaya) is then uttered for the purpose of reflecting that [concomitance] back upon the subject: "In this same way, sound is produced."
This [example], moreover, is useless, because even without this reflection, comprehension occurs through the mere application (prayoga) just described.
Furthermore, that which is useless should not be adopted by the learned in a proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*).

For example, a statement such as "ten pomegranates" is useless; likewise, the statement of the application (*upanaya*) for the sake of a reflection is useless. This is established by the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).

This same principle is observed even in inference for oneself; for no conscious person, having apprehended the existence of "producedness" in sound and recalled its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*), proceeds to form a mental reflection (*pratibimba*) such as, "And thus, sound is produced.
Rather, [they reason]: "Whatever is produced is all impermanent, like a jar."
And thus, the statement of the application (*upanaya*) is uttered for the purpose of demonstrating the possibility [of the reason] in the subject, namely, "and so sound is produced.
We accept both of these [the reason and the application].
However, we do not accept the mere indication of the proof occurring immediately after the thesis (*pratijñā*), such as simply saying, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced."

Because there is no application of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*) stated for the purpose of establishing the upanaya as a distinct member of the syllogism is simply incapable of curing the "snakebite" of the unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*). Furthermore, that which is described as the conclusion (*nigamana*), characterized by the restatement of the established meaning, cannot be justified; for it is impossible for one who maintains that the proof consists of five members to avoid redundancy unless the conclusion is present, since the establishment of the meaning would otherwise be incomplete.
Otherwise, since the matter would already be established prior to the conclusion (*nigamana*), the conclusion would be rendered useless and could not be considered a member of the proof (*sādhana*).
Consequently, this [conclusion] need not be included in the statement of the proof; for it is not a thesis (*pratijñā*) because the matter is already established.

It might be thought that there is a delusion on the part of the opponent who, being in disagreement, requires other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, it is said that "impermanence is established."

The conclusion (*nigamana*), however, functions for the purpose of ascertainment by means of a review of all the constituent members once the object of each respective means of valid cognition has been established through the application of all the means of valid cognition, [concluding] "it is indeed impermanent.
If, then, there is no dependence on other means of valid cognition, then that which is to be proven (*sādhya*) is indeed ascertained by implication alone.
For instance, that which is unproduced is necessarily non-eternal;

just as the word "pot" and so forth are produced, so too, when the state of being produced— which is invariably concomitant with non-eternality— is made known in the case of sound, by the very force of that [cognition], the certainty arises that "sound is non-eternal."
Therefore, this statement is redundant and unworthy of being employed, because its capacity for conveying meaning is already established by its very nature as a communicator of an object.
Nor is even a trace of the possibility of the opposite case to be suspected here,
such that its inclusion would be fruitful for the purpose of excluding it.
Because the pervasion of "being produced" by "impermanence" itself is established,
the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
That which is understood through its own inherent capacity need not be explicitly stated by a discerning person.

Furthermore, that statement is a redundancy, such as saying, "The boy is not in the house, yet he lives," which is a statement of his being outside the house— already understood through the force of those words.

And because [the conclusion] is understood through the force of the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the object intended to be proven again by such statements as "therefore, it is indeed impermanent" is, with respect to the first probandum, an observation of something incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), and with respect to the second probandum, an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).

For this very reason, the "perception of the contradictory of the non-pervader" (*avyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*) in the conclusion (*nigamana*) is a "reason based on essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*) with respect to the second probandum (*sādhya*).
For this very reason, the reasons stated to demonstrate that the conclusion is a separate member (*avayava*) of the syllogism are unestablished (*asiddha*).
That [objection] too has been refuted by this very [argument]. As he said:
When the conclusion (*nigamana*) is stated for the sake of comprehending the meaning of the sentence— following the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth—
it does not constitute a mere repetition (*punarukta*). (17)
Furthermore, a single meaning is not established by scattered statements;
therefore, for the sake of establishing the connection, the conclusion (*nigamana*) must be stated separately. Enough with this overly prolix discussion.
The phrase "or [the mention of] positive and negative concomitance" is another way of stating what is meant by "appropriation" (*upādāna*), as it continues from *Nyāyasūtra* 2.1.12.
Regarding the second [cause], it lacks efficacy because the proof has already been produced and cannot be produced again.
As for the commentators on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, they say "But surely," and so forth.
"No," and so forth, is the reply.
Furthermore, "if" serves as the reason for the accumulation [of faults]:

the member of proof known as the proposition (*pratijñā*) would necessarily become a means of proof (*sādhana*), because it is the cause for the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*), just like the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth.

If it is argued that the reason (*hetu*) has a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*), he replies: "For [this applies] even to the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
This is because the contradictory (*viruddha*) and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reasons, despite the presence of the property of the subject, lack probative power (*agamakatva*).

If it is argued that the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is not a means of proof because doubt arises from it— just like the statement of a common [inconclusive] reason and so forth— the author replies:
"By this, the arising of doubt is refuted," beginning with the words "that is equal to that" (*etena tattulyam*).
He clarifies this very point with the words, "even from the statement of the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmavacanāt*).
By this, he indicates that the immediately preceding reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*).

[Objection: But surely, since a property of the subject such as audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) constitutes a member of the proof only when its relationship [to the probandum] has not yet been demonstrated, there can be no inconclusiveness because of the absence of a counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
But once the relationship has been demonstrated, it then becomes a member of the proof; and since there is no doubt arising from that, it is all the more not inconclusive (*anekānta*).
He thinks as follows:
this [objection] applies equally even to the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*); thus, that too would be a means of proof (*sādhana*).
Now, if one were to proceed [on the basis of the reason], it would be true provided that there were something to be proven; yet there is no proof of what is to be proven from anything else.
Furthermore, once the action has been accomplished, tools such as axes and the like do not serve any further purpose regarding the wood.

However, since the relationship [between the reason and the probandum] has not been demonstrated, this was stated because it serves as a cause for the arising of doubt; thus, it is said: "from that very [reason], doubt arises."

If this were so, then since the establishment of the probandum would not be impossible without that formal application (prayoga), that application would be entirely useless; otherwise, who would be capable of excluding the statement of the thesis (pakṣavacana) from the means of proof?
Consequently, the words of the Teacher—such as "inference for others is the non-statement of the three-featured mark"—would be contradicted.
How, then, was it stated [that the thesis is not to be stated]?

There is no contradiction in the statement that "the exclusion of others" follows from the mention of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), the relation (*sambandha*), and the probandum (*sādhya*). This is because the explanation is as follows: "exclusion" (*ākṣepa*) refers to the illumination of the probandum through the mention of its status as a feature of the subject and its relation [to the reason]; therefore, other elements such as the statement of the application (*upanaya*) are excluded from the proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*) as they are not to be employed. This same point is found in the *Vivaraṇa*: since it is logical that only the statement of the property of being a feature of the subject and the relation—along with positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*)—is the cause for establishing the intended object, and nothing else.

Therefore, the refinement [of the argument] is that the statement of the *pakṣa* (the thesis) must be employed for the purpose of demonstrating and establishing the object of inference, and nothing else. It is called *pakṣa* because by means of it the [object] is drawn toward (*ākṣipyate*), or manifested (*prakāśyate*). Thus, the *pakṣavacana* is the three-fold logical mark (*liṅga*). For "drawing toward" (*ākṣepa*) is equivalent to "denoting" (*abhidhāna*); thus it is called "statement" (*vacana*), or because the root *vac* has multiple meanings. But for us—
In this regard, even the statement that "the indication of the object of inference is considered to have the meaning of the reason as its domain" (19) is contradicted;
for by the word "therein" (*tatra*), the connection of the treatise on logic (*tarka-śāstra*) is here being stated.
But if it were connected with the application (*prayoga*), many inconsistencies would arise.
This has been stated regarding that very [subject] by way of its definition;
and specifically for the purpose of refuting the various misconceptions of others. (20–21)
Thus, enough of this digression.
The means of proof (*sādhana*) consisting of that [reason's] presence is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) by virtue of being its object.
That relevant matter which is under discussion is the "member of the proof" (*sādhanāṅga*); its manifestation is effected by the subsequent two words.
By the phrase "not desired by the opponent," such as "under the pretext of not relying on the treatise" and so forth, the inclusion of irrelevant digressions is intended.
"Addition" (*prakṣepa*) refers to a detailed proclamation by means of a mere name.
For example, when it is merely desired to know whether or not there exists a self distinct from the collection of intellect, sense-faculties, and body, the Naiyāyikas offer the following proof:

"My cognitions, such as perception and the rest, which have as their objects generalities like existence (*sattva*) and so forth, and which have as their objects things to be known, are perceived by a perceiver distinct from my own body and so forth, because they possess birth dependent upon their own causes, and so on."
"Like the cognition of another person.

From this [it follows that] substance, quality, and action are indistinguishable from one another because they share common properties such as "existence" (sat), "impermanence," "possessing substance," "being cause and effect," and "possessing generality and particularity. Thus, they explain [this] at great length based on the non-distinction of existence and so forth. However, in this context, the qualification of the property (*dharma*)—namely, that its object is the object of a cognition whose content is existence and so forth—is in no way helpful for establishing the probandum under discussion.

In the phrase "for the sake of [causing] the obstruction of the power of confusing others, repeating [the opponent's words], and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the cause for obstructing the power of understanding the subsequent [reply]. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a consequence (*prasaṅga*). What does the example of the proponent of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*) indicate? Even in a case where [the doctrine] is prescribed or prohibited, and even regarding the faults and virtues of the Sugata’s Dharma and Vinaya, one is intent upon washing away all the impurities such as pride; yet, in this very instance, it is not [possible] for the proponent of a self (*ātmavādin*) to achieve that [purification] through the proof of a self.

There is an attachment to dancing, singing, and so forth; in that case, what need is there to mention others or anything else? But surely we are Buddhists who speak thus—how can this be, since you have stated a negation accompanied by a qualification?
One must say, "I, a Buddhist, speak.
Just as one says, "I, Gārgya,
speak" or "I, Paṭu, speak," this is not a case of the plural number being used only when there are many [as prescribed by Pāṇini 1.4.22].

21) Because of the statement, "It is possible to say something," it is not the case that he [the proponent] has applied [this argument] in such a way with respect to himself, his own followers, or many others; rather, it should be understood that this example was stated specifically when the proponent intends to speak in this manner, and not in any other context.
Alternatively, this was stated in this manner to ward off the dogmatic adherence of dull-witted grammarians; accordingly, he will demonstrate the futility of the science of grammar (śabdānuśāsana).
For this very reason, it has also been employed by another great chariot-warrior (mahāratha) as follows:
"You are the king, and we too are elevated by the pride of wisdom derived from having served our gurus. (22) Thus the courtier mocks those esteemed as virtuous; the word "aho" is to be supplied here.

Having formulated a proposition in this manner—"That which is the treatise called Mīmāṃsā for the purpose of illuminating the expansion and detailed exposition of the twelve characteristics such as 'means of valid cognition' (pramāṇa), and that which was propounded by Jaimini himself—the statement of its eternity;

and the substratum of that [statement], namely the word 'pot'—of these two, one or the other; by that [word], he is the second pot"—he proceeds to provide an exposition of the twelve characteristics and so forth.

First, he explains the single definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) over a long period of time: "Dharma is that which is characterized by injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇo dharmaḥ*, Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.1.2). They say that an injunction (*codanā*) is a statement that impels one toward action; for an injunction [makes known] what has been, what is being, and what will be, as well as what is subtle, concealed, or remote.
It alone is capable of making the object known, and no other sense organ [is so capable]. For it is said:
"When there is contact with a present object, the arising of cognition in a person through the sense organs is perception."
The signless (*animitta*) is established by such [Mīmāṃsā Sūtra] passages as "because there is perception of what exists" (1.1.4).

Without the establishment of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), impermanence is not established, because that which has not arisen dependently cannot possess momentariness.
In that case, should such a property be stated separately? No, he says:
"But of such a kind," and so forth.

Even for such a property—which is invariably concomitant with the probandum under discussion, yet is not desired to be known by the opponent, and which is asserted apart from that [probandum]—and which is neither a reason nor an example, when, then, would this be a statement of a non-member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*)?
He states that this is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) as previously described:

when the opponent has demonstrated that [the argument] lacks a constituent part of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*), yet the proponent does not demonstrate this, then neither of the two—neither the one nor the other—attains victory or defeat. Why? Because there is no victory for the proponent due to his failure to state the proof.

Furthermore, since the opponent has not established that state [of the reason being inconclusive], there is no defeat at all; for defeat depends upon such establishment. For this very reason, those two [defeat and non-defeat] are likewise absent in the case of the opponent as well. || 4 ||
Now, concerning the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the opponent, he says:
"The non-utterance of a fault," and so forth.
The intention is that there is no offense even if a fault is not pointed out in a matter that was either sought to be known or not sought to be known.
What, then, are these defects of the proof (*sādhana*)? He says: deficiency is of six kinds, occurring when one or two of each pair of forms is not stated.

One might think: "If there is no simultaneous application of the presence and absence [of the reason] in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), how can deficiency be said to occur from the various types?"

When there is no implication [of the probandum] through the inclusion of all cases by means of both positive and negative pervasion (*vyāpti*), then this [fallacy] is established. Now, it might be argued that even then, there is the fault of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for which the positive and negative concomitance have not been demonstrated. Let this be another fault of his; for proofs are not necessarily afflicted by only a single fault. There are three types of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and eighteen types of fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) in the *Nyāyabindu* (in the third chapter).
These [points] should be examined in detail with examples. He explains their non-mention by means of two synonymous terms.
Furthermore, he states that this non-mention is due to three causes.
Then again, [the text says] "because the proof (*sādhana*) is faultless," and so forth.
Now, it may be argued: it is indeed appropriate that the opponent (*prativādin*) suffers defeat for failing to point out a fault when the proof is faultless;

however, when the proof is faulty, even if the fault is not pointed out due to ignorance or incapacity, it is logical that the defeat belongs to the proponent (*vādin*) alone, because he employed a defective proof, and not to the opponent.
To this, he says:
"For even when a faulty means of proof (*sādhana*) is stated...
If this is so, since the proponent has defeated the opponent even by means of a faulty proof, why does victory not belong to him? To this, he replies:
"Only," and so forth.
If this is so, why is there no defeat?
The objection is that it is because of the loss of the establishment of reality (*tattva*).
The answer begins with "not because of non-refutation," and so forth.

The phrase "the misconduct of the wicked" refers to improper behavior; the ellipsis to be supplied is: "therefore, no so-called *vitaṇḍā* (destructive debate) enjoined by yoga—which is conducted through quibbles (*chala*) and other such means—is just.
This is because, once the reasoning has been stated, if the opponent seeks the truth, he would accept that meaning endowed with logic.
Now, if— due to the strength of attachment to one's own position— one should not understand even when the reasoning has been stated,

then, because the assembly of people present nearby who know the self would not disagree when that opponent fails to understand the meaning of that reasoning, it follows that for the virtuous, the pursuit of reasoning alone constitutes debate.
Another [interpretation] holds that it is for the purpose of protecting the truth (*tattva-rakṣaṇārtham*).

As it has been said: "Sophistry (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) are for the purpose of protecting the determination of the truth, just as the covering of thorny branches is for the purpose of protecting the growth of seeds" (Nyāya Sūtra 4.2.50).
"No," says the Teacher, and so forth.
In this way, reality (*tattva*) becomes well-guarded;
the sense is that it is because the opposing factors have been uprooted by means of absolute certainty.
"Absence of that" means the absence of both the demonstration of the proof (*sādhana*) and the refutation of the fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*).
"Even otherwise" means even in the absence of idle chatter (*mithyāpralāpa*) and so forth. || 0 ||
He explains how this is not a fault of the proof:
because even if that which is intended as a fault were present, there would be no obstruction to the establishment [of the conclusion].

When it is intended to prove mere impermanence through the property of being an effect in the case of sound—even though qualities such as being a quality of space (ākāśaguṇatva) are undesired—the followers of Kaṇāda (Kāṇādas), ignorant of logic, raise an objection.
Because one accepts the treatise, everything intended therein should be the probandum (*sādhya*).

Furthermore, it is illogical to claim that there is a fault in the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis (*pratijñā*) when the treatise is the primary authority; for even when relying on a treatise, only that which has been [previously] rejected is the probandum.
Otherwise, this very same reason, when used to prove the opposite of "being a quality of earth" regarding odor, would result in being contradictory (*viruddha*) with respect to that very same thesis.
Likewise, there is this further pointing out of a fault:

as Bhāradvāja stated, there is a mutual contradiction between the two terms of the proposition, namely, "the self" and "does not exist. For "self" denotes a real entity, while "does not exist" is its negation.

This too is incorrect, because it is intended to refute the fact that the referent of a word—which consists of a distinct appearance established by conceptual constructions of a self arising from beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)—has as its material cause the existence of a self characterized by such attributes as permanence and consciousness, as postulated by others.

For it is precisely regarding this subject (*dharmin*) that wise people investigate its existence or non-existence, asking: "Does this object appearing in the conceptual construction of a self have as its material cause an entity as it is conceived, or not?"

However, it is not the case that the object appearing here as a conceptual reflection is denied, for words are employed precisely to bring that very object to mind, and because it is personally experienced within oneself.

But the external particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is distinct from the conceptual reflection, is not at all the referent of words; therefore, there is neither its affirmation nor its negation. Otherwise, if words were restricted solely to the ultimate [particular], they would be without basis.
There would be no engagement with objects that differ according to various philosophical systems;
nor would there be truthfulness for any speech regarding things past or yet unborn. Therefore, this [speech] is considered to have mental constructs (*buddhy-artha*) as its object. (23–24)

Furthermore, this conceptualized entity, which is intended to be refuted by virtue of its being the material cause [of the notion], does not lack an objective referent (*aviṣayatva*) simply because it is the object of a conceptual reflection, regardless of its restriction by space and time; for the word "self" (*ātman*) does have an object.
Consequently, that which is negated in a certain place must exist elsewhere.
For example, the word "pot," when not in grammatical coreferentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), does not exist; yet it cannot signify the non-existence of a pot.
Rather, the understanding of a negation arises due to specific distinctions of place and time.
For instance, "the jar does not exist" is a negation with respect to a specific place, such as "it does not exist in the house";
or it is a negation with respect to a specific time.
Now it does not exist; previously it did not exist; hereafter it will not exist.
This universal negation is not tenable for one who has not experienced the existence of a jar.
Likewise, regarding the statement "the self does not exist," is it a particularity of place that is being negated,
or a particularity of time?
If, first of all, it is a negation of a specific location,
that is not appropriate for the self, because the self is non-spatial.
Furthermore, the self is not thereby negated by the negation of a specific location.
Moreover, this is not your intended position:
[namely,] "the body is not the self.
For of whom is the body the self, such that there is a negation directed against it?
If you say that there is a negation such as "there is no self in the body," then of what [self] in the body is this negation? Where, then, is the self?
The self does not exist anywhere.
Is it then non-existent altogether? No, it is not non-existent, because there is a specific negation.
What is this mode of expression? It is neither in the body nor elsewhere, yet it is not non-existent.
This indeed is that mode of expression.
Since a thing is taught exactly as it exists in reality, and this self does not exist anywhere at all,
its teaching must be precisely in that manner;
moreover, a denial restricted to a particular time is not logical.
Furthermore, by one who denies the self on the grounds that the three times are not manifested in it, the referent of the word "self" must be stated;
for we do not observe a single word to be devoid of meaning.
Furthermore, even if you were to understand the word "self" as referring to the body and so forth, there would still be a contradiction if [the self] is not thereby excluded. How so?
At that time, the statement "there is no self" would mean that the body and so forth do not exist.
Much of this and similar [arguments] is irrelevant and thus discarded.

Furthermore, the claim that [the reason] is a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*) is also incorrect, because there is no such thing as a "particular universal" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*).

Alternatively, the property of "being immediately subsequent to effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is not a part of the meaning of the proposition, because it ceases once it has characterized the locus (*dharmin*).
For that which serves as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaka*) of something else cannot be a part of it; just as a crow is not a part of a vulture.
(73) Furthermore, what was stated by Akṣapāda—that there are twenty-two kinds of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), such as the "abandonment of the thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*)—is not tenable.
Shifting the thesis, contradiction of the thesis,

abandoning the thesis, shifting the reason, shifting the meaning, the meaningless, the unintelligible, the incoherent, the mistimed, the deficient, the redundant, the repetitive, failure to restate, lack of understanding, and lack of ingenuity.

"Deflection, admission of the opponent's view, neglecting what requires inquiry, inquiring about what does not require inquiry, a counter-tenet, and fallacious reasons are the points of defeat" (Nyāyasūtra 5.2.1).
"These twenty-two types will now be explained in detail.
Admission of the property of the counter-example constitutes the abandonment of one's own proposition.
(Nyāya Sūtra 5.2) Having refuted the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra in that regard, this Vārttikakāra states the established position: "We shall explain that very [position]."
The sense is that since the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya* has already been refuted by Bhāradvāja himself, our share of the burden is, for now, at an end.
In this regard, the opinion of the author of the *Bhāṣya* is as follows:

"When one who has been countered by a property contrary to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) admits the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) into one's own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*), one abandons the thesis; this is 'abandonment of the thesis' (*pratijñāhāni*)."

When the demonstration has been made—"Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a jar"—the opponent says: "The universal (sāmānya), though perceptible by the senses, is eternal; why then is sound not so? Thus opposed, [the proponent] says this: "If the universal is perceptible by the senses, then let the jar also be eternal.
Indeed, this [proponent], by implying the eternity of the example used in the proof, falls into this [logical] error.
One who abandons the very position (*pakṣa*) for which one is arguing— while another is abandoning that position— is said to suffer a "loss of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*),
because the position is the locus of the proposition.
And this has been refuted by the author of the *Vārttika* in the following manner:

“But we do not understand how the proposition (*pratijñā*) is abandoned here. The opponent objects that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by means of a general example (*sāmānyadṛṣṭānta*).

Without stating the removal of that fault of inconclusiveness, [the proponent] establishes permanence (*nityatā*) in his own example. Since the establishment of permanence is unproven, there is the fault of the example being unestablished (*asiddha*). Thus, this is a defeat (*nigraha*) either by way of a fault in the example or a fault in the reason, but it is not a ‘abandonment of the proposition’ (*pratijñāhāni*).”
The point that one who abandons the example also abandons the proposition is a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
Since a metaphorical designation cannot be applied when the primary [referent] is absent, the actual subject matter of the abandonment of the proposition must be stated.
Now, he himself presents the opinion of the author of the *Vārttika*:
Regarding the phrase "of the counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭāntasya*) and so forth: what, then, is intended here by "example"?

If it is the technical definition—namely, "an example is that wherein there is a consensus of understanding among ordinary people and experts" (*Nyāya Sūtra* 1.1.25)—then this is no different from the view of the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*), and that has already been refuted.
Now, he says that another [element] is not understood [therein].
In that context, since this [example] is observed through the five-membered proof and is established at the end as the conclusion (*nigamana*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the subject (*pakṣa*).
Therefore, there is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) with its own word.

The counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) is the opposite of that. For instance, when a proponent says, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and the opponent [points out] that universals (*sāmānya*) and the like are both perceptible by the senses and yet permanent—thereby showing that the reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) because it exists even in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)—and when the opponent has thus countered by means of a general principle, the proponent replies, "If that is so, let sound be likewise [permanent]. This is the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "abandonment of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*).
Why?
Because of the abandonment of the impermanence of sound, which was previously asserted as the thesis (*pratijñā*).
By the word "thesis," the property (*dharma*) that serves as a qualification of the locus (*dharmin*) is expressed, because it is a constituent part of the whole [proposition].
This [verse] refutes that [position].
Here, according to the view of Bhāradvāja, because there is an abandonment of the accepted proposition (*pratijñā*),
what is the basis for the specific restriction regarding that which has been established as "loss of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*)?
In this manner, by way of admitting the property of the opposing side within one's own position, there is a loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*).
It might be thought that this alone is the mode of losing the thesis and no other exists; therefore, it is stated for the sake of restriction.
For it is indeed possible [to lose the thesis] in another way as well.

Now, if it is thought that the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is the cause of this [intellect], and therefore when that is demonstrated, the other is also necessarily revealed— then to this he replies: By means of what has been established through the pointing out of fallacies in the reason (*hetudoṣa*) and so forth, the opponent must abandon their proposition (*pratijñā*), because of the articulation of a valid refutation.
Regarding what was stated—that since it has been said that a universal is eternal and perceptible by the senses, let sound also be so—he offers this rebuttal:
"But this is entirely irrelevant.

For what person of sound mind, merely upon the presentation of a universal, would investigate whether a universal exists and whether it is perceptible and eternal, and then conclude that sound is eternal?"

Furthermore, even if this much were granted—that the universal (*sāmānya*) is perceptible by the senses—it would remain doubtful, because that same perceptibility is observed in a jar, which is impermanent.
Moreover, it is not proper here to concede the property of the counter-example; thus he says:

"Nor is its property"—that is, the property of that universal, namely permanence—[established] by one who says "sound is impermanent," for such a person would clearly be saying "some sound is permanent."
[The term "near" (*pratyāsanna*)] means that it would be a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*), but not a general one, because it pertains to a different subject (*dharmyantara*).
For indeed, the contradiction between permanence and impermanence exists only when they reside in the same substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*), not when they reside in different substrata.

The inclusion of the word "directly" (*āñjasa*) is for the purpose of indicating that this too is a counter-argument because it is the locus of contradictory properties, yet it is not as closely proximate as the [proposition] "sound is permanent."
It continues: "In this manner, one is not subject to defeat on account of abandoning the proposition.
To the question "By what means? he says:
"By admitting the property of the counter-position."
Alternatively, "by this" refers to the statement of a non-essential member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*).
As it has been said: "This alone is the primary cause."
Without having stated the removal of the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) regarding that [reason], he attempts to establish permanence in his own example.

Since the establishment of permanence is unproven, there is the fallacy of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*). Thus, this defeat occurs either through a defect of the example or a defect of the reason, and not through the proposition (*pratijñā*). And by abandoning the example, he abandons the proposition; therefore, it is designated as a "point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*) by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

Furthermore, since a metaphorical usage cannot be established when the primary sense is impossible, one must state the primary object of the proposition; thus, there would be a loss of the original thesis. Now, he himself sets forth the view of the author of the Vārttika, beginning with the words "of the counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭāntasya*), etc. What, then, is the intended example here? If it is first [the case] where... "among ordinary people and experts" (*laukika-parīkṣakāṇām*)—[and so on].

If [the definition] "that which is a similarity of cognition is an example" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.25) is taken as a technical term (*pāribhāṣika*), then there is no difference from the view of the author of the Bhāṣya, and that has already been refuted. Alternatively, he says: "That other [example] is not understood."
In this context, that which is "seen" (dṛṣṭa) is established at the end of the five-membered proof as the conclusion (*nigamana*); thus, the "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the "subject" (*pakṣa*).
Thereafter, a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) is formed with its own word [i.e., *dṛṣṭa*].
That which is contrary to it is the "counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭānta*).

For example, when a proponent states, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and the opponent objects that universals (*sāmānya*) and the like are also perceptible by the senses yet are eternal—thereby showing that the reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) because it exists even among the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*)—the proponent replies, "If that is so, let sound be likewise [eternal]. This is the point of defeat called "Abandonment of the Proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*). Why? Because [he has abandoned his original claim].
Because of the abandonment of the non-eternality of sound, which was previously asserted;

for by the word "proposition" (pratijñā), the property that serves as the qualifier of the subject is denoted, since it is a constituent part of the whole [of the proposition]. This [point] he refutes.
In this regard, according to the opinion of Bhāradvāja, since there is a relinquishing of a proposition that has been accepted,
what is the basis for establishing this specific restriction regarding that "loss of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*)?
What constitutes "loss of the proposition" in this manner, namely, in the form of admitting the property of the opposing side within one's own position?
It might be thought that this alone is the way in which there is a loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) and no other; therefore, it is stated for the sake of restriction.
For it is possible [for the loss of the thesis] to occur through another way as well.
Or, if it is thought that this is the primary cause, then by demonstrating this, the other way is also necessarily demonstrated.
Regarding this, he says here as well:

This very thing is the reason for the manifestation of faults in the logical reason (*hetu*) and so forth; because when the opponent has thus established [the point] by manifesting faults in the reason, the proponent must abandon the thesis (*pratijñā*) due to the statement of a valid refutation.
And as for what was stated—that when it is said "the universal is eternal and perceptible," one might reply "let sound be likewise"—to this he provides a rebuttal.
This, moreover, is entirely irrelevant.

For what person of sound mind, upon the mere presentation of a general property (*sāmānya*), would—without investigating whether that general property exists and whether it is perceptible and eternal—accept the word to be eternal?

At most, one might become doubtful; for even if the general property were eternal and perceptible, since that very perceptibility is observed in a jar, which is impermanent, one would remain in a state of uncertainty.
Furthermore, he states that in this case, the mere admission of the property of the counter-example is not appropriate:

"Nor is that property— the property of that universal, namely eternality— [admissible], because for one who says 'sound is impermanent,' the counter-thesis 'some sound is eternal' would be too closely proximate [to his own position], whereas the universal [itself] is not, since it is a different substratum (dharmin)."
For indeed, the contradiction between permanence and impermanence occurs only when they reside in the same locus, not when they reside in different loci.

The inclusion of the term "directly" (*āñjasā*) is for the purpose of indicating that this too is a counter-position because its properties reside in contradictory loci, but it is not as immediately proximate as the case where one says, "Sound is permanent.
It follows that one is not subject to defeat on account of the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) in this manner.
By what means is this [done]? He says: by the admission of the counter-position (pratipakṣa-dharma).
Alternatively, "by this" refers to the statement of a non-essential member of the proof (asādhana-aṅga-vacana).
As it has been stated: "This alone is the primary cause."

"When the meaning of the proposition is refuted, the indication of another meaning by means of a modification of the property is 'shifting the proposition' (pratijñāntara)" (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.3). This second defining sūtra [is stated];
the term "point of defeat" (nigrahasthāna) follows everywhere [in this context].

The meaning of this is as follows: the negation [of the reason] in the counter-example (vipakṣa) is the statement that the reason exists therein; when that is the case, by means of the distinction between the properties of the similar example (sapakṣa) and the counter-example, one formulates another proposition for the sake of establishing the meaning of the original proposition. For example: "Just as a jar is non-omnipresent, so too is sound non-omnipresent; like a jar, sound is likewise impermanent. The remainder is easily understood.
This [objection] is refuted by the words "atrāpi" and so forth.
Abiddhakarṇa, however, raises this doubt in his commentary on the Bhāṣya and seeks to resolve it with the words: "But surely, provided that [the self] is not omnipresent..."
The qualification of the reason has been stated;
and since the qualified reason does not exist in the counter-example (vipakṣa), this is not the point of defeat known as "shifting the proposition" (pratijñāntara).
For it is not the case that by adopting a different proposition, such as "sound is thus non-omnipresent," one commits a fault.
To claim that the inclusion of a qualification for the reason (*hetu*) constitutes the defeat-ground (*nigrahasthāna*) called "another reason" (*hetvantara*) is far too crude.

For a person of refined intellect who qualifies the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in this manner does not put forward a different thesis (*pratijñā*), since [the original thesis] is already established.

As for the claim that the introduction of a qualification to the reason constitutes a different reason (*hetvantara*) and is thus a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), that too is utterly flimsy; for in that case, let it simply be called a "different proposition" (*pratijñāntara*), as it is connected to that.
This is because of the phrase "due to similarity with the example, etc. (*udāharaṇasādharmyādeśca*).

Because of the absence of the definition of the thesis (*pratijñā*)— namely, that "the statement of the probandum is the thesis" (*sādhyanirdeśaḥ pratijñā*)— in the rule "The reason (*hetu*) is the means of proving the probandum through similarity with the example" (*udāharaṇasādharmyāt sādhyasādhanaṃ hetuḥ*,
Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.34), by accepting [this rule], one does not intend for proof to be achieved by the mere thesis, devoid of reasoning, for the sake of establishing the thesis.
Consequently, even prior to that— that is, immediately after the first proposition— he would not state the reason (*hetu*) "because of being perceptible" (*aindriyakatvāt*).

Therefore, since it is impossible to enumerate such childish ravings as these, where another proposition is stated for the sake of proving a proposition, a restrictive definition (*lakṣaṇaniyama*) is indeed incoherent.
What is this? It is the point of defeat called "shifting the proposition" (*pratijñāntara*), which occurs when one states a different proposition [after the original has been refuted].

But is there not such a restriction on the definition as follows: "When the meaning of the proposition is refuted, the restatement of that same meaning by means of a modification of the property (*dharmavikalpa*)"? Indeed, it is so defined.
There is no fault, because that very point is being stated by means of a different formulation.

Now, it might be argued: "Just as the learned do not state a proposition (*pratijñā*) as a means of proving the proposition, so too they employ unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reasons for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*); therefore, [the definition] 'stating what is not a member of the proof' (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) and so forth should not be stated even by you. To this, he says:

3) "Even for the wise" means that in my own system, the acceptance of a scripture without a [valid] means of knowledge (*apramāṇaka*) is not demonstrated as being established as it truly is in general; this is the meaning.

For indeed, those sages who are heroes in their determination to perceive reality do not respect the obstruction of the established systems of others when their minds have emerged [from meditative absorption].
A statement lacking authoritative basis is not to be disregarded by the wise, because an assertion supported by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) must not be violated.

Furthermore, this would be the case: even if the proponent does not become a victor because he has stated a proof not established by valid means of knowledge, he still does not [truly] defeat the opponent because he has failed to refute the counter-position. || 4 ||

Contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) is the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodha*), as defined in Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.4:
"The proposition is that 'substance is distinct from its qualities'."
The reason given is that no object distinct from color and the other [sensory qualities] is perceived.
This constitutes a contradiction between the proposition and the reason:
if the substance is distinct from the collection [of qualities], then the non-perception of any object distinct from color and the others would be untenable.
Now, since no entity distinct from color and the other [qualities] is perceived, it is untenable that substance exists as something separate from its qualities.
By this very same contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), the contradiction with one's own words is explained.
This was stated by the author of the Sūtras merely as an illustration of that [contradiction].

There is a contradiction with one's own statement: [the claim] that there is sexual intercourse with men who have not abstained from the life of a *śramaṇa*, yet the embryo does not exist without sexual intercourse with a man.
By this, it is stated that there is a contradiction with the reason (*hetuvirodha*).
First, [the claim] is that "everything is separate and manifold; there is no single entity."
The meaning is that because the word *bhāva* is used in the sense of a collection (*samūha*), it is expressed by words such as "pot" which denote a collection;
for by one who speaks of a "collection," a single entity is necessarily admitted,
since a collection is indeed a unification of many.
For instance, by one who perceives substances such as cows as aggregated, a collection must be admitted.
Yet this collection—namely, that "these substances, existing in the form of cows and so forth, constitute a collection"—is not established.

Furthermore, regarding difference, which exists in degrees of being more or less minute, that which is the ultimate minimum and indivisible is that from which difference ceases; and that from which this difference ceases is the One.

Now, if you think that even that which you consider to be an indivisible atom is itself a collection of form and the other [sensory qualities], then according to this view, since those form and other qualities that have come together constitute the atom, it must be stated: "In the atom there is form; of what, then, is that a collection?
The same applies to the remaining qualities.
Now, if you do not accept that collection [as the atom], then the treatise stating that "the eight substances combined constitute an atom" would be contradicted;
for it says in the *Abhidharmakośa* (2.22): "In the desire realm, an atom consists of eight substances when it is without sound."
22) Therefore, to claim that because one [unitary] production is untenable, multiple productions must follow, is extreme folly.
Furthermore, this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For it is established that a single entity exists as connected with qualities (*guṇa*) such as odor and so forth, which possess manifold characteristics, as well as with parts (*avayava*) such as the base and so forth.
Therefore, when a single object is understood from a word, the remaining related meaning is apprehended as a consequence.
But is this not a contradiction between the proposition and the reason? Indeed, it is no different from the first [case].
It is not so, because contradiction depends upon both [the thesis and the example];
for Bhāradvāja himself has stated that the mention of either one occurs according to the speaker's intention.

An example of the contradiction of a proposition by a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) is as follows: "The manifest world has a single primal material cause (*ekaprakṛti*), because it is finite, like a bowl and such things. Here, the corroborative instance—the bowl and so forth—subverts the state of having a single primal material cause.
Because the material cause (*prakṛti*), which serves as the illustrative example, is itself a distinct material cause;
or, if there were only a single material cause, the examples such as the clay bowl would be inappropriate.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction between the reason and the examples and so forth, as in the case: "The object is distinct from its qualities, because it is not perceived as a separate entity."
"Like a jar," etc.:
because jars and so forth are perceived as distinct, the example subverts the reason.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the application (*upanaya*) and conclusion (*nigamana*) of the reason are [implied].
By these two, contradiction is apprehended. An illustration of these is: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced.

[The opponent argues: "Whatever is produced is impermanent, like space; and sound is likewise produced"—thus, by means of the application (*upanaya*), there is a contradiction with the reason (*hetu*).
For it has been stated [in the Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.38] that the application (*upanaya*) of the probandum is "the conclusion 'it is so' or 'it is not so'," depending on the example;
here, since the example is not reversed, there is no contradiction of the reason (*hetu*) by the application.

And in such an application, when there is a conclusion with the words "therefore it is impermanent," there is a contradiction of the proposition and the reason by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For example, [the argument] "fire is not hot because it is a substance, like water" contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
[This applies to] the opponent's position and so forth.
And this [point], as well as "that which is independent of one's own position" and so forth—

it shows that since both of these are already subsumed under the very category of "contradiction between the proposition and the reason," they should not be stated as separate points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Regarding the phrase "the positions of others":

When another person has established a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), Kaṇāda points out its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). However, in the case of the statement "and independent of one's own position," it is the Vaiśeṣika himself who provides the means of valid cognition, while the opponent demonstrates its deviation; such is the distinction.

If, then, a contradictory response has been made by citing the deviation [of the reason] through "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, [the opponent] says: "In that case, the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) [reason] would be without an object," and so on—beginning with the words "both" (*ubhaya*).

That which is established for both the proponent and the opponent, yet not admitted by either side, is the inconclusive; because it has that as its object, it is metaphorically designated as such, and thus there is the "charge of being inconclusive."
Regarding the phrase "here too" and so forth:
this also refutes that [position]. That which has that as its basis means that contradiction for which that proposition (*pratijñā*) is the basis;
or "produced by that" means produced by that proposition.

The remainder is very clear. Even for non-distinct entities such as piśācas and the like, which are remote from certain things such as mountains, this alone constitutes the ground for defeat (nigrahādhikaraṇa).
Namely, the employment of a proposition (*pratijñā*). The phrase "contradiction of the proposition is a ground for defeat" continues [from the previous rule]. Why is this so?
"Because it has that as its locus";

the meaning is "because it is the basis for the proposition. He says this [to show] that if, on the other hand, it did not have that as its locus, it would become a locus for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
"Yadi" and so forth:

the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) of the discussion (*prastāva*), that is, the completion of the debate, is its termination; the formulation of the thesis (*pratijñāprayoga*) is the cause for that [termination].
For by that alone, because of the proponent's failure to state a member of proof (*asādhanāṅga*), there is defeat (*bhanga*).

In some places, it is read as "because it is the occasion for the conclusion of the topic. Even there, the meaning is that when the discussion is concluded and the proposition (*pratijñā*) has been stated, there is the "occasion" or "scope" [for further argument].

Now, just as you [prove] a single property of an object, such as its momentariness, by means of many reasons—such as existence, having an origin, being differentiated by the difference in cognitions, and so forth—[so too is this case].

In the same way, even a single member of a proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*) proposed by another that is to be refuted is refuted either by means of the inclusion of a proposition (*pratijñā*), by means of its contradiction, or otherwise.
And thus, this fault does not apply, because there is no defeat of one who has already been defeated.
To this, he says:

As for those reasons that are stated, they possess the capacity [to prove] because they function toward the establishment of the probandum— either through an alternative conceptualization that does not depend on the previously stated reason, thinking "it is thus," or else by establishing it in another way.
What, then, is the reason that there is no application [of the term] in the sense of a conjunction? He says:

otherwise, if the application of another distinct reason were not intended in the sense of a conjunction, then the second [reason] would be redundant; thus, the phrase "the universal by way of option" follows.
He demonstrates this very redundancy:
For if, even in that case, the employment of the second were not possible without the employment of the first— since the determination of the rule would result from the negation of both—
then the meaning is that if the employment of the second were possible through conjunction with the employment of the first.
In that case, there would be no purpose for a second [reason], because there is no need to demonstrate what has already been understood.

This is to say that, just as an axe or similar tool has no status as a "most effective means" (*sādhakatama*) once it is applied to wood whose action has already been accomplished—since it is already occupied with the very object established by the first reason—the same applies here.
Now, one might object: "But surely, just as there is an analysis of the 'means' (*sādhana*), there will likewise be an analysis of the 'refutation' (*dūṣaṇa*)."
He thinks as follows:
"It is not appropriate for another to accept [this] in such a manner;
for in doing so, he would himself have admitted that the thesis is not a constituent part of the proof."
And consequently, this [sūtra] is contradicted:
"The thesis, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion are the members" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.32).

By means of other reasons— those previously mentioned methods that negate the existence of a composite substance— it has been established that the word "jar" and others do not denote a specific composite substance characterized as a single entity such as a pot,

but rather denote the generality of multiple objects such as color and so forth, which consists in their capacity for a single purposeful action; and it has been shown that every word-meaning, such as color and the like, which is capable of a single purposeful action, possesses a manifold nature by way of being the instrument [of that action].
