It is a single thing, and its nature is that of a specific entity consisting of a composite substance (*avayavidravya*); the state of being such is "the nature of being a single specific entity. By demonstrating the absence of that [nature], the Buddhist would assert that "there is no single entity," but he does not thereby reject the forms (*rūpa*) which are the objects of the senses. It might be thought: since capacity (*sāmarthya*) is not distinct from form and the other [sensory qualities], it too must be manifold; how then can it be called "one," or how can it be the referent of a word?

It is not said that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the referent of a word. Even though [particulars] are diverse, because they possess the capacity to perform a single purposeful action through their non-distinction from themselves, they are called "one" by way of a causal chain, since they are the cause of a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*). As it has been said: "Because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness, it is non-differentiated."
In one way, there is also non-difference among individuals by virtue of their being causes [of the same cognition].
(25) As long as the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the person (*puruṣa*) is not ceased, that [universal] is not established as the referent of a word.

For the person, through the power of the maturation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from beginningless false habitual practice, superimposes upon external objects a form that exists only within the internal domain; thus, he apprehends the identity between the perceived and the conceptualized. However, in ultimate reality...
Verbal expressions are indeed devoid of objective referents;
for individual instances and the forms of cognition lack connection with any external object, and thus they are beyond the scope of verbal designation.
Furthermore, the form exists only in accordance with conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"For by whatever name any phenomenon is expressed, that [phenomenon] does not exist therein; for that is the true nature of phenomena. (26) Thus, the summarized meaning here is as follows: form and so forth, as well as a jar, possess respectively multiplicity and unity, because they are denoted by plural and singular terms.

For example, by means of fallacious inferences such as "the stars are the moon," that very object which the opponent accepts as the referent of words like "pot"—namely, a single entity called a "composite whole" (avayavin)—is refuted;
however, color, taste, and so forth, which are of the nature of atoms, are not [refuted], for it is indeed accepted that each of these possesses a singular nature.

It is stated [in the text] to illustrate their necessary simultaneous arising, on the grounds that they do not form a collection unless they are present together, just as a seed that is barren when alone.
A subtle atom (*paramāṇu*) in the realm of desire that lacks sound consists of eight substances;
one possessing the body-faculty consists of nine substances; and one possessing any other faculty consists of ten substances.
(Abhidharmakośa 2.22ab)
However, how atoms possess both perceptibility and impermanence has been explained by us at length elsewhere.
As for the argument that [atoms must be many] because they are denoted by plural and singular number, that is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*).
For instance, even with respect to a single woman, water, or sand, one employs such expressions as "wives" (*dārāḥ*), "waters" (*āpaḥ*), and "sands" (*sikatāḥ*).
If it is asked: "In that case, what plurality is there therein by which such a distinction of power occurs?
[The answer is: Now, the singular number is everywhere abolished because of the absence of a single power.
If it is argued: "The singular number occurs elsewhere due to the non-difference of the object," [we reply:]...

Let it be so here as well. Thus, this rule being established without a real basis demonstrates the independence of one's will regarding the employment of words. By this, that which Kumārila said is also refuted: [The text continues with Kumārila’s verse: "Since there is no fixed relation between the word *go* and the dewlap, etc., how can there be a restriction [that the word denotes only the cow]? This is answered by the following: even if there is no intrinsic connection, the restriction is established through convention (*saṅketa*). For instance, when a person who knows the convention says, "Bring the cow," another person brings only the animal possessing the dewlap and so forth, and not a horse or anything else. Therefore, the restriction is indeed established. Furthermore, since the convention is made by someone who possesses the power of independent will, the independence of the speaker’s will is thereby demonstrated. It is for this reason that the Master [Dignāga] stated: "The relationship between a word and its object is based on convention. This very point was also stated by the venerable Ācārya [Dharmakīrti]: "The relationship between a word and its object is established by convention; it is not natural. And it has been said: "The relationship between a word and its object is created by the will of God. Thus, the independence of the speaker’s will is clearly shown. In that regard, if the word *dārāḥ* is applied to both the individual and the genus,
it functions by taking the number of either the individuals or their constituent parts.
And how is it that there is the singular number in the case of "the city of six" (*ṣaṇṇagarī*) when there are many [cities]?
Cities themselves are not anything at all; how then could there be a collection of them?

Since there is no production of heterogeneous things such as palaces and persons, how could their aggregate be a substance? Furthermore, it cannot be a conjunction, because there is no mutual conjunction between the palaces and so forth.
Because the palace itself consists of conjunctions and is devoid of qualities, it cannot be conjoined with anything else;
for that very reason, number is also absent. If it is argued that "city" is the existence (*sattā*) qualified by those conjunctions and the person [occupying them], [we reply: ...

What is the qualification for this unsurpassed [excellence], given that existence (*sattā*) is a single entity? Furthermore, even when there is a plurality of cities, why would the plural form "cities" (*nagarāṇi*) be used?
If it is argued that it is because the two are mutually accompanied, [we reply: no.
What kind of assistance can there be between two things that do not benefit one another?
Furthermore, since the person (puruṣa), conjunction (saṃyoga), and existence (sattā) are multiple, how can the term "city" (nagara) be used in the singular?
If it is argued that the cause is some undifferentiated power belonging to those elements in certain cases, we say no.
Because power is not distinct from the nature of the entity;

for if it were distinct, that which is not assisted could not be dependent upon another. Or, if there is assistance, then since there would be a further power assisting that power, there would be an infinite regress, resulting in the impossibility of establishing [the original power].
"If it were not distinct from that, the same consequence would apply to other [cognitions] as well"—this is trivial.
He states another alternative as well:
"And this is a demonstration of what has been observed."
But how can there be an example even when the [reason] is stated in the ablative case?

To this he says: "Just as it was said by someone: 'Because of being produced, [it is] impermanent'—wherein the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason with the probandum and its absence when [the probandum] is absent are stated."
In that context, the example belongs to the fifth [member], while the reason consists of the application (upanaya).

When there is a dispute regarding a certain object, such as a substance like a jar— concerning whether it exists as something distinct from its qualities like color and so forth— one points to the established usage of words for a universal (*sāmānya*) such as "Ṣaṇṇagarī" (The Six Cities), which is superimposed by the intellect upon many mutually exclusive objects like cities. By means of this, and having indicated the application of the word to a collection formed by the intellect that unifies mutually exclusive things into a single conceptual unity, one anticipates the final synthesis of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) through the subsequent application (*upanaya*), and being thus situated within the point of dispute, concludes with a general summary.
"Everything is distinct"— this is the analysis of the compound, meaning that by this [text], the locus of realization has been established.
This is what is being said:

Since there is a dispute as to whether [the object] exists or does not exist apart from the skull and so forth, this example is presented for the purpose of indicating the three characteristics [of a valid reason], not as a logical reason (*hetu*) itself.
The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, is formulated here as follows:
Those things which are mutually distinct do not possess forms that are followed by a single, separate, composite substance;
for example, like the six cities and so forth.
And likewise, the potsherds and so forth are mutually distinct.

Now, if this is indeed an application of an example (*dṛṣṭāntaprayoga*), why was it not formulated by the straightforward method of that application—as in "whatever exists is momentary, like a jar," and so forth?
Why is there this indication using the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*)?
And why has the object of the dispute (*vipratipattiviṣaya*) not been shown, namely the potsherd and so on as qualified by the negation of the composite whole (*avayavin*)?

Just as elsewhere [it is stated], "Sound is impermanent because it is produced and impermanent," by the word "and" (*ca*), why is the reason clearly not shown to be concomitant with the probandum? For in this case, since mutually exclusive things that do not follow a single object are mentally brought together, the completion of the sentence is effected by inferring the application of the term "collection" (*samūha*).
To this, the reply is: "No, because it is a concise indication," meaning because it is an abbreviated statement.
Even so, such usage is observed in cases like "because of being produced" (*kṛtaka*) and "because of being impermanent" (*anitya*).

Furthermore, since it is not a formal proof (*asādhana*), this sentence is merely indicative of an intended formulation of a proof, being a statement that suggests the conceptualization of a syllogistic application.
The meaning is that this is not a statement of proof (*sādhana*).
"For this very reason" means precisely because it is a statement of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
This reason (*hetu*) is: "The forms of the threads and the cloth have different causes because they possess distinct qualities, like color and touch."

This [argument] also fails to establish the desired conclusion, because since the difference between the threads and the cloth is not established, the quality residing therein is also not established as distinct; thus, it has an unestablished substratum.
For others explain that "possessing particularity" consists in the inherence of subtle and gross substances, or the inherence of substances produced at different times.
Indeed, speakers have diverse intentions.

Regarding those who employ speech solely with the intention of a logical reason (*hetu*), we state that the reason is sublated by the thesis (*pratijñā*); however, this does not apply to those who take pride in their examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). To this point, he says:
"And not," and so forth.

The summary of the point is this: you have raised this objection against those who rely on the doctrine of the Blessed Tathāgata, yet such a contradiction does not exist for us, even in our dreams, O follower of Akṣapāda.
It might be thought: "There certainly exists a Yogācāra who [holds that] because of the simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom would become a mass of dust."

By the statement beginning with "Because the six [atoms] occupy the same location, the aggregate would be the size of a single atom," it is said that even one who does not accept the unity of the atom nevertheless accepts the aggregate—which is synonymous with a collection—as being real.
As for the phrase "And whoever... and so forth, what is intended here is rather to establish the non-existence of the atom by this very method.
How so?
Because of the negation of both unity and multiplicity.
First, unity is negated by such arguments as the impossibility of its being like mud.
Since that [multiplicity] does not exist, even its collective form— namely multiplicity itself— is not found,
for it has been stated: "Indeed,
whatever entity is examined, that very thing lacks unity."
"Therefore, there are not even many [things], because even a single one does not exist."
But surely, how can even unity be destroyed by contact with mud and so forth,
since in that case its possession of parts has been established?

Furthermore, those very parts of it are the smallest atoms (*paramāṇu*), because atoms are characterized by having division as their ultimate limit. Now, if it is argued that even those parts must possess parts according to this same method [of analysis], then the same response applies there as well; in this manner, it is impossible to negate the unity of the atom.
[This is so] because division [presupposes] that which is being divided...
[This is] not so, because it is not a treatise (*tantra*).

Furthermore, how can one who does not accept the existence of atoms accept such things as the conjunction of a row [of atoms]? Thus, in establishing their non-existence, all reasons are *asiddha* (unestablished) with respect to their locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) by their very nature.

And this is not the case, because capable disputants [proceed] by reducing that which has attained its minimum limit through the division of parts. And this is not the case, because capable disputants [proceed] by reducing that which has attained its minimum limit through the division of parts.
They call [the self] "the one who wanders" (*bhāmaṇu*); by that term, its identity with the five elements is excluded due to their lack of conjunction and so forth.

And if, having been thus refuted, they were to admit the possession of parts for that which has been accepted [as partless], then they would fall away from their own doctrine. For those who do not accept the possession of parts are not entitled to object in such a manner.
"Let those very parts be the atoms. Since that definition must be established by them alone and refuted by the Yogācāra, they are thus confuted.
For this very reason, there is no infinite regress.

Furthermore, because this is a *prasaṅgasādhana* (a reductio ad absurdum), the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) does not apply; enough of this. Now, if it is argued: "We are not saying this to you, sir; rather, we say it to whoever might be a proponent (*vādin*) who has not washed his feet and speaks thus"—that is incorrect.

For [we have already refuted this] in the context of the verse beginning with "kāmeṣṭadvayaka" and so forth in your own work, where it was stated: "Because of the distinctness characterized by separate existence, there is no production of a single entity from multiple characteristics. All of that [objection] is invalid.
Even though he has stated this by setting forth our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*),
nevertheless, having provisionally accepted it, he points out another fault:
"And this [difference] does not differ from the previous one indicated by the words 'distinct from the qualities' and so forth, because it consists merely in the mutual attribution of meanings."
There is no difference in meaning between the two types of sublation—those pertaining to the reason and the thesis and those accompanied by examples—other than a mere difference in words.

Furthermore, if such cases were to be cited separately, then statements such as "sound is unproduced because it is produced" would also have to be cited either together or separately; this is the meaning of the reading found in some versions: "saha pṛthag vā" (together or separately).
In that context, "saha" means simultaneously, and "pṛthak" means individually, as in the first case.
Thinking that even the consideration of contradiction here is improper, he says "Moreover" (*api ca*), and so forth. [The opponent argues:
"Everything is distinct; the word 'entity' (*bhāva*) is applied to a collection."
This is the reason:
[the reason] "because it is a property of sound" is unestablished (*asiddha*), as it is not a property of every subject (*dharmin*).
Thus, due to its lack of co-referentiality (*vyadhikaraṇatva*), the very fault of being unestablished applies, just as in the example: "sugar is sweet because the crow is black."

In that case, there is no contradiction because the meanings of the reason (*hetu*) and the proposition (*pratijñā*) have different loci (*bhinnādhikaraṇatva*). One might think that there is no lack of common locus (*vyadhikaraṇatva*) because of the formulation used by Bhāvivikta in his commentary on the *Bhāṣya*: "Because it is denotable by a word expressing a collection (*samūha*). He thinks as follows: "We have not begun to point out this fault against one who has formulated [the argument] in this way by Uddyotakara himself; even for those who now formulate it differently, if this..."

There is no fault. Let it be; however, the fault just mentioned and that which will be stated hereafter cannot be avoided even by Brahmā himself. Furthermore, I have asserted this while accepting that the contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) constitutes a distinct point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
However, that [classification] is not appropriate for this [category], because it is already subsumed by the rule: "And fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are points of defeat" (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.24).
Desiring to explain this, he says:
"Furthermore," and so forth.
That class of faults, that type of defect, which possesses two members (*avayava*), is "twofold" (*dvayī*). To what does he refer? He says:
[It refers to] contradiction (*viruddhatā*) and unestablishedness (*asiddhatā*). How, then, is there contradiction? He says:
"Contradiction," and so forth.
This is the summary of the meaning here:

where a contradiction between the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) is raised in an argument, there must necessarily be an established subject (*dharmin*); and when that subject is established, [the contradiction can be examined].
The presence of either the reason (*hetu*) or the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) must exist in the subject (*dharmin*), or both must exist there.
Among these, it cannot be the case that both exist [in the same locus], because they are mutually contradictory; like cold and heat, they lack a common substratum.

Otherwise, because they would exist together in one place, there would be no contradiction at all—just as between taste and form—and thus a contradiction between the thesis and the reason would follow most certainly.
As he will state:
"Because two contradictory natures cannot exist in one place, there is no contradiction otherwise."

Now, even if the reason (hetu) exists there, it is clear that this [reason] is contradictory (*viruddha*), because where the reason is present, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is absent, while its opposite is found—
as in the case: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced."
Thus it is said: "The contradiction [of the reason] consists in its presence in the subject (*dharmin*) at the time when the proof [is required].

However, when the existence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in that subject has been ascertained by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the reason does not apply there, because it is subsumed by its opposite.

Therefore, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), just as in the case: "Sound is produced because it is not an effect. Furthermore, there is non-establishment regarding the subject (*dharmin*) and so forth when that [reason] is applied to what has arisen from that.

Now, you might think: "The contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) is established only when the substratum (*dharmin*), such as substance, is already proven to exist as distinct from its qualities by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, this fault does not apply. To this, he raises the following objection with the words beginning "asiddhe" [unestablished]. Even so, although the contradiction has been avoided because the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is impossible due to the non-existence of the substratum, [the fault remains].
Reflecting that the state of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*) remains exactly as it was, he says:
"In the case of 'lack of valid cognition' (*pramāṇābhāva*), however, there is doubt regarding the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in the locus (*dharmin*) for both the proponent and the opponent;
for even when valid cognition is absent, the non-existence of the object is not established."

Therefore, it is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*) because its locus is doubtful, as in the example: "There is a peacock in this bower, because of the sound of its cry. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates that when there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish [the existence of] the subject (*dharmin*), the reason's locus is clearly unestablished once a means of valid cognition subverts that subject.
The phrase "like the quality of being perceived everywhere" is intended as a cumulative argument when the self is to be proven as being omnipresent.

For, in the case of the [fallacy] of unestablishedness (*asiddhi*) regarding the nature of the subject (*dharmisvabhāva*), the subject would be intended as unestablished due to the absence of a proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Or [it is due to] the operation of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*).
In the former case, the fault has been stated explicitly; in the latter, it is joined by the word "and" (*ca*).
Here, he anticipates the response of Audyotakara.
By the passage beginning with "because it has both as its basis," etc.,
all of this is easily understood since its meaning has already been explained.
He refutes [the objection] with the passage beginning with "not in all cases," etc.

As was stated previously regarding the phrase "not two types of faults," if it is now established that contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) occurs independently of a reason—being a fault consisting merely of the thesis itself—as in the case of "O Śramaṇas, there is no self; [yet] she is pregnant," then he says:
"In the case of independence, the mention of a reason is not connected."

Because it is of no assistance. Furthermore, regarding this example of contradiction with the reason (*hetuvirodha*) given by the statement "sound is eternal" and so forth, he says "na cet" and so on, in order to explain that it is improper [to classify] that as a contradiction with the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) by means of the reason.

It might be thought that, since contradiction depends upon both [the thesis and the reason], even in this case it does not follow from the reason alone; therefore, it is said: "Even though it rests on both," and so forth.
Having introduced the examples thus demonstrated, he states the following in order to refute the desired position:

"And as for what was said—that by this [same principle], contradictions with the example and so forth regarding the thesis must also be stated according to the 'clown’s chalk' (bhaṇḍālekhana) method."
The word "iti" is to be understood here as "it must be stated"; otherwise, because the other [speaker] would not have employed a reply, it would be poorly constructed.
The mention of a "jester" (bhaṇḍa) is for the purpose of illustrating the permanent male character (nityapuruṣa).

For just as jesters, in order to amaze common folk, might paint a lifelike image such as a large doll (viśālabhajikā) endowed with various characteristics, thereby displaying their skill in diverse artistic crafts—so too [is this usage].

The Śālins likewise extend this principle: that even such places for dramatic representation as the *hasya* (comic) and others, fashioned by our own skill, are to be understood [by analogy] in a single moment; such is the case with this work of Uddyotakara.

For indeed, this very same point has been demonstrated: that it possesses the characteristics of a fallacy of reason (*hetvābhāsa*) distinct from the contradiction of the stated reason (*upadarśita-hetu-virodha*) and so forth. What further need is there for deliberation regarding what has already been extended by analogy?

He begins to explain that the extended definition (atideśa) likewise lacks a characteristic distinct from the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), such as contradiction with the example (*dṛṣṭāntavirodha*) and so forth, by means of the passage beginning with "In that case also" (*tatrāpi*).

In that context, where there is a contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñā*) with the example, the contradiction of the proposition with the example would occur only if the example possesses the opposite of the property established as the subject (*pakṣīkṛtadharma*). This is the implied sense.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which possesses the opposite of that property which has been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*)";
and by "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*), a homogeneous example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is intended.
Since a dissimilar instance (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) necessarily possesses the opposite of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), what contradiction is there in that? An example of this is:
"Sound is eternal, like a pot."

And when the example is contradictory, if the occurrence of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is established by means of valid cognition as being "not shared with others" (*ananyasādhāraṇā*), then that is the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as the contradictory (*viruddha*).
The term "not shared with others" (*ananyasādhāraṇā*) means not common to others.

By the word "other," one who possesses the opposite of the property under consideration (*pakṣīkṛtadharmaviparyayavat*) is intended as distinct from the subject itself; thus, if it is established that [the reason] occurs only in that which possesses the opposite of the property under consideration, then it is the contradictory reason.
This is the meaning.

For example, in the case of these two—the probandum (*sādhya*) and the instance (*dṛṣṭānta*)—the property "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) does not exist in external space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, which are the counter-examples (*vipakṣa*), whereas it does exist in a jar, which is the opposite of those.
When the common presence (*sādhāraṇā vṛttiḥ*) has been established, the remainder [of the definition] is "in both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the counter-examples (*vipakṣa*)."
The inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) is that which is called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*).
For example, in these very same two cases of the probandum and the illustration, [the reason] is "because of being an object of cognition" (*prameyatvāt*).

Since the restriction of its non-occurrence in those two—the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—has not been established, namely the restriction of its occurrence as "it occurs only in the similar instance" or "it occurs only in the dissimilar instance," it is indeed inconclusive; thus, it is one where both the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are doubtful.
Or, for example: "The person intended [as the subject] is either omniscient and free from passion, or he is not, because he is a speaker, like a street-sweeper.
When there is no occurrence of the reason in either of those two—the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—it is the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) [inconclusive reason].
For example: "Sound is eternal because it is audible.

An opponent says: "When there is an occurrence of a contradictory instance (*viruddhadṛṣṭānta*) and an occurrence of the opposite of the reason (*viparyayavṛtti*), there is no fault in the reason whatsoever. For instance: 'Sound is non-eternal because it varies according to differences in its conditions, like space'—this by way of similarity (*sādharmya*)."
And by way of dissimilarity, "like a jar.
Here, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhatva*) because the reason (*hetu*) exists in the subject (*dharmin*);
nor is there inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), because it does not occur in both [the similar and dissimilar instances].
And because of the existence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Nor is there contradiction (*viruddhatva*), since there is an absence of occurrence in the opposite manner in both the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). However, as for the contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñā*) with the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), this is a case that does not exceed the category of defects of the reason (*hetudoṣa*), namely, "contradiction of the proposition by the example."
This [objection] is refuted. No;
because even then, it does not transcend being a cause for doubt.

For in the case of a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is no contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñā*) when the instance is based on similarity (*sādharmya*); it is not a fault in the case of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Why? Because of the contradiction with what is intended.
The intention is that a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is defined as one that possesses the opposite of the property established for the subject (*pakṣa*).

Even if this were the case, how does it still fail to transcend the category of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)? To this he says: "And in a similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) that possesses a contrary property, such as space (*nabhas*), it is impossible to demonstrate the property of being non-transient."

And an example is presented for that purpose. As it has been said: "It was stated that the reason has three forms; when it is established as a property of the subject (pakṣadharma), the remaining two forms are demonstrated by means of an example. (32)

But how can it be impossible, given that being differentiated by the variation of conditions is, in reality, non-deviant from impermanence? To this he says: "Even though there is non-deviation in reality. The meaning is that even if non-deviation exists, it is as good as non-existent because it has not been established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the ascertainment of the probandum does not arise from a reason that is not connected through the demonstration of an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*).

Consequently, even the contradiction of the example with the proposition (*pratijñā*) does not escape the category of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), because at that time, this [contradiction] also possesses a doubtful exclusion from the counter-instances (*vipakṣa*); this has been indicated.
The word "also" (*api*) indicates that there is not only a contradiction with the reason (*hetu*), but also with the opponent's position.
This applies in both ways: by way of the reason and by way of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

It is not by way of the reason, because once a proponent has been defeated through the incidental mention of faults in the example, there is no need to state another fault—namely, a contradiction with the example—since there is no further defeat for one who is already defeated; such is the intended meaning.

This is especially true for the Naiyāyika, who asserts a specific sequence for the members of a proof; for he maintains the fixed order of the proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*).
But what is his excellence? To this he says:
"The similarity with the example," and so forth.
Even granting this, there is no contact with the fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) consisting in a contradiction with the example,
as stated immediately above.
By this, the formulation of the fault through alternative options (*vikalpataḥ*) is applied.
Thus, it is established that a contradiction with the example does not escape the category of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

As for what was cited by Aviddhakaraṇa in his commentary on the *Bhāṣya*— "The manifest world has a single primordial cause because it is finite, like a jar and so forth"— in that case as well, the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), since the reason "finitude" either does not exist in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) or exists only there.

Furthermore, because [the reason] occurs in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa)— such as a clay bowl and the like— which consists of multiple constituent parts, and because the clay itself undergoes differentiation at every moment and in every part,
he now states that the contradiction of the reason by means of the example is included among the fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).
If there is a contradiction with the example, the reason is also either unestablished (*asādhāraṇa*) because it does not occur in either [of the two cases],
or it is contradictory (*viruddha*).
When does there arise the state of being contradictory (*viruddhatva*)? He says:

if it were [stated] in terms of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), then the following example would be stated by that very same [author]: "Substance is distinct from quality, because it is not perceived as a separate entity, like a jar. Even here, if the qualification "while being visible" (*dṛśyatve sati*) is applied to the reason, it becomes contradictory, because it does not exist in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Furthermore, because [the reason] exists in its own nature within the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth;
and because, if a qualification were not employed, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since even things like *piśācas*—which are not perceived as distinct entities—are mutually exclusive.
Moreover, the example "like a jar" is not appropriate here, because that very jar has been made the subject (*pakṣa*) precisely on account of being a distinct substance.

The apprehension of that [entity] as distinct from form and so forth has already been refuted; and since the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of such apprehension, our own position remains firm.
Now, he asks: when a reason contradicts a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what kind of fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is it? He says:
Because the coldness of fire is unestablished, being non-existent.
Furthermore, the other example given here—that fire is not hot because it is a substance, like water—is incorrect;
for direct perception does not subvert the reason (hetu) that it is a substance.
Because that [heat] is established in the subject (dharmin);
however, non-heat is the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā).

Now, since the meaning of the thesis is sublated by perception, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by that [perception]; thus, it is said that the reason contradicts a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If this is so, then because the reason is not pervaded by the contradictory property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), the reason-fallacy (*hetvābhāsa*) is one whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful; thus, our own position is supported, for a contradiction of the reason by a means of valid cognition does not exceed the category of reason-fallacies. (33)
As it has been said:
"Those [objections] which contradict perception and so forth,
occurring at a time when [the pervasion] is established..."
All of them do not employ a pervading property that is contradictory.

It might be thought that because contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the thesis (*pratijñā*) arises solely from that [contradiction], it cannot be subsumed under the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*); therefore, he says:

"Contradiction with a means of valid cognition regarding the thesis is explained by contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*); its refutation has already been provided there [in the section on *svavacanavirodha*] by the passage beginning: 'The employment of a thesis—which is not a constituent part of the proof—in a proof-statement is the very basis for defeat (*nigrahādhikaraṇa*),' and so forth."
Thus, he concludes with "therefore, all [of them] indeed.
As for the other objection raised by the proponent—that the response is contradictory—that is entirely irrelevant;
for [he says] "if indeed," and so forth.

When one person—whether a Buddhist or another—puts forward the argument, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a pot," a Mīmāṃsaka or a Vaiśeṣika might seek to establish the fallibility (*vyabhicāra*) of the proponent’s reason (the Buddhist) by means of a universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*), which is established for their own position. They would do so by superimposing [this point] upon the opponent and asserting: "Cowness is also perceptible by the senses; therefore, according to you, it too would follow that it is impermanent. This is how they would speak.

In that case, for that Buddhist, that universal (*sāmānya*) would be both perceptible by the senses and eternal; however, this contradicts his own position, because he does not accept eternal entities and thus does not intend such a thing. Therefore, how could there be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)? [The opponent replies: "Contradiction" (*virodha*) means "obstruction" (*vyāhati*), which is to say "inconsistency. One must supply the words "it is consistent with the answer" (*yujyate uttarasya*). But he does not raise the charge of deviation by merely casting a burden upon the other party as if it were his own; so how can there be a contradiction for the answerer? For that respondent himself has already accepted [the point].

Since the reason "being beyond the senses" (*aindriyakatva*) applies to "cowness" (*gotva*) as something eternal, one who is doubtful might express their own lack of comprehension or non-ascertainment by asking: "Is sound impermanent because it is beyond the senses like a jar, or is it eternal like cowness and the like? By speaking thus, he reveals his own position that even though cowness is beyond the senses, it is indeed eternal; therefore, this [reason] is currently inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, by putting forward his own very own admission, he raises the charge of inconclusiveness. Consequently, the rejoinder is correct; such is the meaning of the whole passage.

It might be thought that for a Buddhist, eternal cowness (*gotva*) simply does not exist, and therefore the response is indeed contradictory; to this they reply: whether cowness exists or does not exist in reality, that reason—namely, "because it is perceptible by the senses"—is certainly inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since its capacity to prove [the thesis] remains unestablished and it functions as a cause of doubt due to the absence of any subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: its capacity for proof (*sādhanasāmarthya*)—characterized by the state of being inseparable from the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhāvitva*)—has not yet been established.
The word *sādhana* here functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*).

However, when one establishes the inseparability of the reason through the force of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) by means of a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), such as: "Whatever is graspable by sensory cognition is impermanent, because it produces a cognition that bears its own image," then [the reason is established].
If [the self] were eternal, it would follow that the cognition having that as its object would either occur at all times or never at all; for instance:
"That which is capable of producing a cognition within itself must always be capable;
or else, if it is incapable even once, it must be incapable at all times. (35)
Whether he possesses power or lacks it, that which is established by his very nature cannot be remedied because of its permanence; who is capable of exhausting it?

At that time, since even eternal universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) are—as it were—shattered all at once, the reason does not subsist in "cowness," and thus there can be no doubt [regarding its pervasion].
This and what follows are easy to understand.
The summary is that even in those cases, one does not escape the status of being a fallacious reason (*anaikāntika-hetvābhāsa*).
The inconclusiveness [of the reason] arises by way of its being a cause for doubt when the reason has not been established;

since this applies "elsewhere" as well—that is, equally even to an object admitted in one position—there is no distinction in the inconclusiveness between an object established for both parties and one that is otherwise.
This is exactly as was stated immediately prior.
And that reason [is classified as such] by the words "whether it exists or does not exist," and so forth.

Furthermore, the other type—which is not admitted by one of the two parties—is explained as being "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) because its object is inconclusive. It might be argued: "This is not a fault, for it is undesirable [to us]; however, what is established for both parties is indeed a proof."
Or how is it that this [objection], namely "it is a refutation," is not contradicted? That is not so, because the statement was made with the intention of pointing out a certain refutation.
For that very reason, another [author] stated immediately after that: "On the other hand, some regard [the probans] as being yet to be proven."
But this might be the case:
then there would be neither victory nor defeat for either of the two.

Furthermore, what was stated by Udyotakara while explaining the very sūtra on the contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*)—namely, that these are fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) and so forth—that too is incorrect for the Naiyāyika who maintains that there are other members [of the syllogism].
The intended meaning is that the Buddhist shines only when speaking in this manner;

for by his statement—namely, the statement of a fallacious reason—it would follow that the fallacious example, which is understood from that [statement], lacks the status of being a separate means of proof (*sādhana*) distinct from that reason.
The word "of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Now, one might object: "If it is taught that fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) are included within fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), then the statement that 'there is no other member [of the syllogism] beyond the reason and the example' would be entirely incoherent. To this, he says: "Of the fallacious examples," and so forth.
This application of his reasoning unfolds in the mind:

if X is a different entity from Y, then it is not logical to refer to X by means of a term that refers to Y; nor is it possible for those things appearing as X to be included within those things appearing as Y.
This is just as, for example, fallacious perceptions (pratyakṣābhāsa) cannot be included within fallacious inferences (anumānābhāsa).

And thus, for your reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be a separate entity; this is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Therefore, the inclusion of the example within the reason must necessarily be accepted. In that case, the example would not be a separate member of the proof (*sādhanāvayava*).
This means that because it is not distinct [from the reason], it possesses a single function.
He explains this very point with the words "the example," and so forth.

Having stated that since the elaboration of the contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) is already subsumed under the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), no separate mention need be made of it, he now says [the following] to demonstrate that the same principle applies to cases such as the removal of hostility (*pratighahāni*).
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "api ca":

the mention of the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) is for the purpose of stating that the opponent of the final position (*uttarapakṣavādin*) possesses defects such as ignorance and so forth, which are touched by fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). Alternatively, "connected with those" means connected with the fallacious reasons and the proponent of the prima facie position.
Now it is said:
since shifting to another subject (*arthāntara*) and the like do not touch upon the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), they are not included among them.
And that is incorrect;

for even in the case of a reason such as "going to another object" (arthāntara), it is equally possible for an incapable [reason] to function in this way. Why? Because, by the force of logic, there is the capacity of the proponent to establish the probandum—this is the ellipsis.
The intention is that [the fault arises] because of proceeding falsely by going immediately to another object and so forth. || 4 ||

The subsequent [point] is that which will bear fruit later; and "that and this" refers to the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*). With respect to that, "what is not something? means "nothing at all. Those whose determination regarding number is incapable—referring to the activities of those who engage in the prattling of eunuchs—and those disputants whose [speech consists of] the prattle of eunuchs and the like, their activities such as the abandonment of the thesis and so forth: what is proposed by them? (What fault, then, exists when this is the case? He says: [The rest of the passage follows: ...the word *vā* ("or") is used in the sense of "and"; the word *api* ("even") is used in the sense of "also"; and the word *hi* ("for") is used in the sense of "because. Therefore, the intention is that this too is incoherent, because such a manner of expression is too crude for an assembly of learned men. Regarding this, Bhāvivikta himself, having raised an objection, indeed provides a rebuttal on the grounds of its crudeness: "This..."
If it is argued that this constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because one denies the meaning of the proposition asserted in the presence of the judges and the opponent, we reply:
that which is stated is irrelevant, for it is not understood what the intention was.

We do not say that sound is perishable; rather, the intended meaning of the proposition is that it is not manifested by conjunction and disjunction. He says this because a universal is manifested by its own substratum, and thus there is no dispute [on that point].
However, as for the ground of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), it is because the opponent has not previously stated the intended meaning.

When the reason is refuted by the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he is defeated because he abandons the intended meaning of his proposition. In that regard, it must be said: if the proponent was still expecting [an answer] when, in the interim, some ill-informed person pointed out the fault of inconclusiveness...
Being thus challenged, he reveals his own position by bringing the fruit of the promised meaning to fruition;
at that time, there is no fault whatsoever,
much less the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*).
Now, being free from further desire [to elaborate], he later qualifies his proposition when prompted;

yet, since he is defeated by the very fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), what is the point of waiting for the abandonment of the subsequent proposition? Thus, nothing has been resolved. Furthermore, it is clear that this is included within "shifting the proposition" (*pratijñāntara*) and need not be mentioned separately. 4.
The sūtra beginning with "aviśeṣokte hetau" (when the reason is stated without distinction) serves as an illustration or example here; this is the meaning.
The follower of Kapila (the Kāpila) offers this proof in the hope of establishing the existence of the Pradhāna:
"This manifest world has a single primordial nature (prakṛti), because it is finite in its various manifestations, just like a jar, a bowl, and so forth."
The analysis of the compound is "that which has a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Primordial nature (*prakṛti*) means the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). And that which is indeed the primordial nature of the collection of transformations is called *pradhāna*; this is a false attribution.
[The Sāṅkhya's] [example] is "limitedness," such as "quadrangular" or "circular," and so forth.
By the phrase "of those preceded by clay," he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
The opponent (*prativādin*) raises an objection against this reason (*hetu*) on the grounds of its deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

When the opponent has raised an objection, stating that "magnitude is observed in things of diverse natures such as elephants and horses, as well as in things of a single nature such as jars and water-jars," the Proponent of Primordial Matter (Pradhānavādin), having been thus challenged or refuted, says:
"Because magnitude is observed when there is a correlation with a single primordial nature. His thought is that because the reason is thus qualified, there is no fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra).
But how is there an endowment with a single primordial nature? To this he says:
"For this manifest world, which is limited, is perceived as being endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion;
for its effects are seen everywhere. This is the intended meaning.
For instance, for those in whom *sattva* (purity) predominates, there arise joy, satisfaction, serenity, and attachment;
for those in whom *rajas* (passion) predominates, there arise exhaustion, feverish distress, agitation, and aversion;
and for those in whom *tamas* (darkness) predominates, there arise concealment, intoxication, lethargy, loathsomeness, dejection, and dullness.
And all these [qualities] are observed everywhere, without distinction, according to their aforementioned increase and decrease.
Therefore, this universe has the three qualities (*triguṇa*) as its material cause (*prakṛti*).
By the words "this very [universe]," etc., he states the reason for [the opponent's argument being] a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
In this case as well, the negation of the first [position] is easily understood;
the meaning is that because there is no cessation, no interruption, and no completion of the statement of the proof. || 0 ||

The phrase "possessing the characteristics as previously stated" recalls the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) as two contradictory properties residing in a single substratum.

When the acceptance [of the debate] has been made by the proponent and the opponent, and the task at hand is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) through the reason (*hetu*), then within this context— where the establishment of the probandum proceeds by virtue of the reason— the subject under discussion is the permanence of sound (*śabdanityatva*).
Because it is irrelevant;

By saying "having abandoned the subject at hand," he demonstrates precisely its logical propriety.

What is relevant here is the statement of the probandum, the means of proof, and the reason; failing to perform that, [the argument] is not capable of countering the fault when it has been raised. The meaning is: of that which is a constituent part for supporting the means (sādhana) already presented.

It is neither a word nor a sentence;
for it is said that in this context, speaking of a different meaning—that is, stating something irrelevant—is merely the utterance of phonemes (varṇa), this being the remainder [of the definition].
He speaks precisely of the state of being unconnected.

For it is not merely from the presentation of a sequence of syllables that there is pointlessness; rather, whatever statement is made regarding that which is not a member of the means of proof—such as the unestablished (*asiddha*) or the contradictory (*viruddha*)—or regarding the establishment of the form of words and so forth, that alone is pointless.
What is the reason?

This is because there is no subject matter that serves to establish the thesis (*sādhya*). Furthermore, one should not think that there might be some other purpose even in the absence of anything that serves to establish the thesis; this is what he expresses by saying, "and because it would be purposeless."

The intention is that since the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) alone is the subject at hand, even if there were another purpose, it would be entirely irrelevant to the present context. That which is intended as "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*) is not that which is useless for the establishment of the thesis (*sādhya*) because it is not an integral part (*anaṅga*), but rather that speech which has no meaning whatsoever, like the cawing of crows and the like. The claim that "for him there is no meaning whatsoever" is also incoherent; because even the indication of the sequence of phonemes is not meaningless, as it possesses meaning in certain contexts, such as in the formation of pratyāhāras (abbreviated terms).

The phrase "stated thrice" indicates that the rule of logic (*nyāyatva*) requires the utterance to be made three times; for even when spoken once, the meaning may sometimes not be understood despite being clear, and thus the recitation must be performed three times. The meaning is that [the order follows] according to their definitions for the sake of practical purpose (*arthavaśāt*).

For, lest the application of the means of proof (*sādhana*) be without an object when the object has not been shown, the thesis (*pratijñā*), which is defined as the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*), is stated first.
Immediately after that, the reason (*hetu*), defined as "the proving of the probandum through similarity with the example," is stated for the purpose of establishing that [probandum].

Therefore, for the purpose of demonstrating external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*), the example (*udāharaṇa*) is defined as: "The instance which possesses that property due to its similarity to the probandum" (*sādhyasādharmyāt taddharmabhāvī dṛṣṭānta udāharaṇam*).

Following that, the application (*upanaya*)—defined as "the application of the means of proof (*sādhana*) by way of 'it is so' or 'it is not so,' depending on the example, for the purpose of reflection or for the purpose of showing the possibility [of the reason] in the subject of the probandum" (*udāharaṇāpekṣas tathety upasaṃhāro na tatheti vā sādhanasyopanayaḥ*)—is the application.

Thereafter, following the examination of all the constituent parts, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is defined as "the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) after the statement of the reason (*hetu*), for the purpose of removing any erroneous implications" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.39).
Such is the definition of the conclusion.
This is the sequence according to the characteristics [of the process], by virtue of the purpose;
for even in the world, it is the established rule that first the material cause, such as a lump of clay, is taken up, and only afterwards the instruments, such as the wheel and the staff.
In this regard, regarding this sequence...

When [the members of the syllogism] are established in their proper order, the statement of the constituent parts, such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, in reverse order is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
For example: "Because it is produced, like a jar, it is impermanent."
Bhāradvāja himself raises and then resolves this objection with the words, "Even so, [the goal] is established" (*naivamapi siddheḥ*).

He does so by means of the phrase "not like the word 'goṇī' when divorced from its actual application" (*na prayogāpetaśabdavad etat syāt*), using the term *goṇī* as an example. For instance, it is like a child being taught who utters the sound "Amba-amba."
By one who knows that [unmanifest], certainty arises regarding the manifest.
(38) Thus, indeed, words such as *goṇī* and others are, by means of inference from the correct [words],
the causes for the production of comprehension.

This is indeed the description of a madman by a mad grammarian, just like the description of one madman by another madman; for in that case, one madman describes a second madman, and this [work] is likewise so.
That is to say, if it is the description of the madman Uddyotakara by the mad grammarian.
For instance, the grammarian himself is first of all insane, because he propounds things that contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, how could his grammatical procedure possess the status of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for an investigation into valid means of knowledge? This is what is intended [by the author].
But how is it that the grammarian propounds what is incorrect? To this he says:
The passage beginning with "yad" and so forth is easy to understand.
The words *strī* and *śūdra* are terms for a fool.
For one who knows the word *nakka* only as the word *mukka*, that is, merely as a synonym for the nose.

How could he, having understood the correct word from an incorrect word (*apaśabda*), understand the meaning from that correct word? It is asked: "Is it not said that he does not understand the cognition in that way?
[The author] replies: "And it is observed that even for Sanaka and others who know both, there is comprehension; therefore, the comprehension of the meaning is not through a traditional succession."
This is the summary here:
it might indeed be that non-virtuous things indicate virtuous ones,
provided that their possession of the three characteristics (trairūpya) were as certain as it is for smoke and the like.
And that is not possible;
for Sanaka and others, who do not possess knowledge of both [the pervaded and the pervader], do not perceive this relationship of pervaded and pervader even though it exists.
Nor can that [relationship] be a prover when unknown, because it must be known in order to function as a signifier.

Even those who are skilled in distinguishing between correct words (*sabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*) conceptualize them as such precisely because they do not [inherently] exist. For instance, the relationship between incorrect words and correct ones would have to be either identity (*tādātmya*) or a cause-and-effect relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*);
since both of these are absent, there can be no rule of non-deviation (*avyabhicāraniyama*).
In that regard, identity (tādātmya) cannot be accepted, because a real difference is clearly perceived through direct perception;

furthermore, it would follow that even an incorrect word would be expressive due to its non-difference [from the correct one]. Nor can the relation of origination (tadutpatti) be maintained, as it has already been cast far aside.
For the wicked do not arise from the virtuous,
because their existence is caused solely by the qualities of the cause and the desire to speak;
nor are they eternal, since they are perceived only occasionally.

Or rather, in reality, there is an even greater absence of its arising; or even if the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) and the knowledge thereof were present, because of the deficiency of the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), there can be no inference from "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*) and the like, just as there is none from corrupt words.
For the property of being a characteristic of the subject does not exist here in this case, by virtue of which it could be established.

For it is not the case that only the virtuous (sādhu) possess the property of being the subject (dharmin), since they alone are what is being inferred. Nor is it logical to establish the subject itself [as the probandum],
because a property that exists, does not exist, or both would be afflicted by the fallacies of the unestablished (asiddha), the contradictory (viruddha), and the inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Or how could that [non-existence] be a property of the virtuous?
For they do not exist at that time. And it is well said: "To be a possessor of a property and to be a subject of verbal expression belong only to things that exist."

As for the claim that "the person is the subject (*dharmin*), the intention to speak the word 'cow' (*go*) is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), and the word 'goṇī' is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)," that too is incoherent,
precisely because there is no relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*).
For we do not perceive an intention to speak the word 'cow' at the time of employing the word 'goṇī'.
Now, it might be argued:
"Just as even an indistinct utterance by a child can lead to the inference of a distinct one despite being deficient in properties such as being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharman*),
so too do the ungrammatical forms lead to the inference of the grammatical ones."
That is incorrect, because the same objection applies there as well. We, however, maintain that even from that unmanifest [source], the objects such as the *mātrās* are perceived directly.
Furthermore, one should not think that this perception is impossible because the relationship between the name and the named has not been previously experienced.
Because in beginningless saṃsāra, such a relationship has been indicated through a continuous succession of linguistic usage.

For instance, even in the case of words such as "cow," the restriction of their meaning is generally not established by explicitly pointing to each individual object; rather, the learned determine it through the tradition of linguistic usage.
And this is exactly the same in the present case as well.

Therefore, this is like the wailing of one in the wilderness; just as a child, while being taught, utters "Mama, Mama," so too is that which is unmanifest. Through the manifest, the certainty regarding it arises for the knower. (39)
Thus, when a correct word ought to be employed, whatever corruption is used instead, by that corruption some intended meaning is understood, though it is mediated by the correct form.

As for what was further stated by Kumārila: "When the word 'go' is established for us, the cognition of a cow arising even from words such as 'gāvī' is produced by that [primary word] through its incapacity [to denote], and it follows the original word. (41)
This very same rebuttal applies to that as well, and having encompassed all of this, he concludes:
"There is no cognition through a succession. He provides further reinforcement on this very point.

Because that which is corrupt (*asādhu*) is incapable of conveying meaning, and because even when the word is correct (*sādhu*), it lacks the capacity to produce comprehension [if the speaker is corrupt].
To this, one might object: "We do not deny that corrupt words generate comprehension regarding their meanings; rather, we deny their status as *vācakas* (denoters).
A corrupt word certainly generates comprehension, but it is not a *vācaka* at all. To this, he says:
For it is not the case that the denotative power of a word with respect to its meaning is something entirely different [from its power with respect to itself], and so forth.
If you maintain that even an incorrect word (*asādhū*) produces the cognition of the meaning,
then we are fully satisfied by this much.
The underlying intention is: "What is the use of our postulating a distinct denotative power (*vācakatva*) for these [words]?
If it is argued that this [word] is not at all capable of producing the cognition of the meaning, but rather it is the *śabda* itself [that produces it], he replies:
"If it is an *apaśabda*..."

Now it is said: the word has an inherent connection with that [word-form] itself, not with the object; therefore, it conveys only that and not the object. For example, by its very nature, the eye illuminates visible form and not sound and so forth.
To this he says: "of one for whom no convention has been made," and so on.
"Because they are not observed":
for words such as *siṃha* (lion) do not function in the linguistic usage of Āryas unless their relationship [to the object] has been apprehended;
rather, it is convention (*samaya*) alone that brings about comprehension.
And since that relationship [between word and meaning] is conventional, its referent cannot be denied.
Why should a non-standard form (*asādhu*), by virtue of convention, not function as a standard one (*sādhu*) when it denotes an object such as a cow?
For there is not even the slightest fault; rather, it is exclusively a virtue—so he says with the words "For thus," and so forth.
This is what is meant:
Those things which are illuminators by their very nature do not depend upon a convention (*samaya*),
such as the eye, a lamp, and so forth, in relation to visible forms and the like.
If the word "incorrect" (*apaśabda*) were an illuminator of the word by its very nature, [it would likewise not depend on convention].
Consequently, even that [connection] would not be independent; yet it is indeed dependent. Therefore, the capacity of this [word] for denotation is not inherent in the word itself.
In this way, the following can also be inferred:
those [cognitions] that function by depending on convention are, in all cases, unimpeded in their extension according to convention and thus become direct conveyors [of meaning].
Just as bodily intimation and so forth function,
so too do corrupt words (*apaśabda*) function in dependence upon convention; thus it is established that their capacity to convey meaning occurs precisely without any mediation.
And there is another reason for this accumulation, namely, the observation of misconceptions.
For instance, when "tree," "fire," or "lotus" is uttered, children of unrefined intellect remain engaged in inquiry, beginning with questions such as, "What is this tree? and so forth.
And because there is no other means of instruction, they are instructed by means of corrupt words alone, such as *rukkha*, *aggī*, and *uppala*.
Thus, in this case, it is observed that only the ungrammatical forms are expressive, while the grammatical ones are not, even though they exist; this is a reversal of the expected rule.
Now, if you maintain that the refinement of words is a means for accomplishing *dharma*, as it has been said:
"That which is established through the tradition of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) is the means, and the means is the accomplisher of *dharma*."
"Even when there is no difference in the communication of meaning, ungrammatical forms are indeed erroneous. Likewise:
"A mantra that is deficient in accent or phoneme, when wrongly employed, does not convey its intended meaning."
That thunderbolt of speech destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [did] due to the transgression of the accent; those gods, having uttered "He! Alaya! Alaya!", fled away. (43)
"Even a single word, when correctly employed, leads the virtuous to the heavenly world;
for one who has maintained the sacred fires, having uttered an incorrect word (*apaśabda*), must perform an expiatory sacrifice (*prāyaścittīyā iṣṭiḥ*)," and so forth.
(Mahābhāṣya, Āhnika 1)

This removes [the objection that] the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words is not a means for realizing the Dharma; the word "it follows" (*vartate*) is understood. He asks, "What is the reason? and says:
"Because they enjoin false conduct," and so forth.
The compound *mithyāvṛtticodanā* is to be analyzed as: "those by which false conduct is enjoined."

For instance, even when it is said that "having cut off the head with a sword-blade darker than a blue lotus of a twice-born man lying beneath an Ashoka tree, which is resplendent with rows of beautiful clusters and tender sprouts as lovely as a profusion of fresh coral shoots," the instigator indeed incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin. This occurs because he has directed others toward an act that was not otherwise likely to happen, by urging them toward a correct course of action through a contrary means.
"Just as a cow might be given to that brahmin.
All of this, because it lacks authoritative basis (*apramāṇatva*), is merely a statement by you who harbor a different intention;
he says this as an accumulation [of arguments], beginning with "simply from the correct employment of words" and so forth.
[The opponent says: "Such [statements] are thus devoid of any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).

But surely, in cases such as 'If one causes a shrine (*caitya*) to be built on a consecrated spot of ground, one produces Brahma-merit and rejoices in the heavens for an eon (*kalpa*)', this same consequence applies to you as well, since there too there is an absence of a means of valid cognition."

Because in this case there is no parity— since the purification of both objects is for the sake of another, and because there is non-correspondence (visaṃvāda)— discerning persons proceed with satisfaction even toward the third category.
But it is not so in your view, for even the two [categories] just mentioned are contradicted by valid cognition (pramāṇa), and that contradiction has been demonstrated immediately above.
Therefore, this is equivalent to the rivalry between a pauper and a lord;

the expression "employed by qualities such as the knowledge of what is to be known" (*viditavedyādiguṇaprayuktāḥ*) is a designation in which the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is implicitly contained.

Those by whom that which is to be known—the nature of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—is known are described as such; by the inclusion of "and so forth," compassion and other qualities are encompassed.
These very [qualities], when cultivated, are the others, while those not so cultivated are the non-cultivated.
This is what is meant:
For speech has as its purpose worldly transaction, which results in the communication of meaning.
Since that [communication] is achieved through the power of convention from refined words just as it is from unrefined ones, why are the learned so intent on what is irrelevant?
For this very reason, I believe that because they are intended for those who possess discernment, their names were given with such meanings as these.
Or rather, what concern is it of ours if they are rejected?
Because there is no certainty in this regard—that they employ only these [words] and not others—as it has been said:
"And in this matter, there is no imperceptible witness by which we might determine from that witness: 'They employ only these and not others.'"
But was it not stated [in the *Mahābhāṣya*, *Āhnika* 1] that the purpose of its grammatical exposition is "protection, modification, addition, brevity, and absence of doubt"?
How then can it be said that there is no excellence of quality? To this he replies:
protection of the Vedas and so forth is indeed not a purpose for a follower of the Tathāgata who does not abide by that [Vedic] tradition.
Because it does not conform to logic;
that is, because its intrinsic nature consists of correct words.
"Even from another source" means from the traditional lineage of the elders' discourse.
He clarifies this very introduction of the illustration with the words beginning "prākṛta" (ordinary).
Having thus demonstrated the madness of the grammarian, he now states [the view] of Bhāradvāja.
"Even when the members [of the syllogism] are inverted," and so forth.
"Cognition of the relationship" means that the relationship is the state of being mutually benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*).
"By implication, the intended meaning is communicated"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Now, it might be argued that the sequence of the members of the syllogism, such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, is not being altered here in order to maintain the methodological principles of the system established by Akṣapāda; to this, he replies: "For there is no convention, established doctrine, or rule here that is supported by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Another also says:
The probandum is not understood from the contrary;
rather, it is understood from that contrary in its proper sequence.
This is the refutation of that [position].
"There is no cognition of sequence from those whose relations are not perceived.
He explains this very point with the words beginning "Of those... and so forth.

Furthermore, we have already previously rejected the employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*) within the proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*). Therefore, how could there be a reversal [of the order] caused by those?
This he explains with the words beginning "it has been established" (*pratipāditam*).
The mention of the "proposition" (*pratijñā*) is for the sake of illustration.

Now, if [the proposition] were employed even though it is already obtained through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*), there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); this is what he states:
"And there would be the consequence of employing that which is already understood," [referring to] the case of the application of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
There would also follow the undesirable consequence of [redundant] application;
yet this is not accepted. Furthermore, it is a repetition to state by its own word what has already been established through the force of the meaning (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.16).

15) Because of the mention of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). [Objection: In that case, even in the absence of a thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, there will be a fixed order regarding the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
To this, he says: "In the remaining cases," and so forth.
He states another defect regarding the position that the connection [between words] is not perceived:
"This does not differ from the 'meaningless' (*apārthaka*); therefore, it should not be mentioned separately. (4)

In a statement where any one of the members, beginning with the proposition and ending with the conclusion, is absent, that statement is deficient. He states the reason for its being a point of defeat: because in the absence of the means of proof, the probandum cannot be established.
This he refutes with the words "not [the validity] of the proposition and so forth.
The mention of the "proposition" (*pratijñā*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), and thus includes the "application" (*upanaya*) and the "conclusion" (*nigamana*) as well.
He sets forth the opinion of Uddyotakara:
"That is inferior;
it is deficient in its thesis."
"Because there is defeat even when that proposition is deficient.
He states the impropriety of this [position]:
"He who employs in his proof a word expressing the probandum—which is already understood through the power of the proof itself and is thus redundant—would deserve defeat."
For instance, when an inquiry into the impermanence of sound has been introduced, if one says,

"It is observed that produced things are impermanent, and sound is produced," then the object to be proven is understood from these two statements alone; thus, the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is useless.

It is an unconsidered statement by the author of the *Vārttika* that one should not state merely the connection of the property with the subject (*pakṣadharma-sambandha-mātra*) when it is connected with reason and associated with the goal [of the argument]. For this very reason— since one deserves defeat when a word is employed whose meaning is already implied— Abhidhakarṇa here objects by means of a counter-argument (*pratibandhaka-nyāya*).
If this is so, then even the statement "sound is produced" need not be made. Why?
Because by the very [statement] "what is the reason for impermanence?", both being produced and impermanence are understood in relation to sound as well.
This is because the opponent has already accepted that sound is produced; since it was previously established through its production, sound is already present in the mind.
By this positive statement (*anvaya-vākya*), only a mere recollection (*smṛti*) is produced;
however, for one who has not yet understood the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), even from the statement "and sound is produced," [the conclusion] does not arise at all.
Or rather, it should simply be stated that "sound is produced."

However, since the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) of "being produced" with "impermanence" is well-established for the opponent, he understands impermanence even in the case of sound; thus, he has acted quite appropriately. For instance, if the produced nature of sound is somehow ascertained by the proponent—such that it is accepted by him that sound is produced—then he need not even apply the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) because it would be fruitless;
rather, he should merely demonstrate the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Now, even if she has not reached a definitive conclusion, nevertheless, if this opponent, when I have formulated the application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*), should raise the objection that it is unestablished (*asiddhi*),

then I shall ward it off by means of such arguments as "because it varies according to the variation of the cognition" (*pratyayabhedabheditvāt*). Or else, having anticipated this even without being prompted, one should indeed formulate the application of the property to the subject, keeping this very thought in mind.
And "sound is produced.
Even when the proponent has ascertained that the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) of being produced with impermanence is well-known to the opponent, at that stage too, he need only say:
"Sound is produced," just as it has been stated.
For the state of being the cause of that cultivation is demonstrated by means of an example for those who do not know it; however, for the learned, only the reason itself needs to be stated. (44)

This is an additional point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) called "accepting a restriction" (niyamābhyupagama). One establishes a specific subject matter and then states that specific subject matter with the words beginning "where... and so forth.
But has this not already been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya himself, that "this is to be understood as occurring when a restriction is accepted"?
What, then, is the refutation stated here by the Ācārya? Nothing at all is said;
rather, the Ācārya merely restates what was said by Pakṣila for the sake of granting permission.
He states an exception to the rule that "repetition of word or meaning is *punarukta* (tautology)" with the words "except for restatement" (*anyatrānuvādāt*).
Restatement (*anuvāda*) refers to the conclusion (*nigamana*).
