For a restatement does not receive the designation of tautology.
The production of a specific meaning arises from two words; for it has been stated that the statement of the probandum is the proposition (*pratijñā*),
while the statement of what is already established is the conclusion (*nigamana*).
Furthermore, the word "again" (punar) is observed to signify multiplicity;
it has already been explained that this light of lightning flashes again.
If this is so, then [the objection on] page 110 does not hold.
Since there is no possibility of redundancy at all, for what purpose is this exception (apavāda) being undertaken?
This is true;
however, those very eminent logicians themselves must be questioned on this point.
"How is this so?
[The reply is: "But for us, what is the use of considering the household concerns of others? Enough of this digression.
And here there is also this second sūtra: "The restatement in one's own words of that which has already been established by implication" (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.16).
15) That was not set forth by the Teacher because it was intended as an illustration;
he will refute it after introducing its commentary.
By the words "the restatement of what is already understood," and so forth, [the author] indicates that it is redundant.
With the words "here," and so forth, he begins the refutation.
This is what is meant:

Where there is identity of word but no difference in meaning, that case is already covered by the fault of repetition of meaning (*arthapunarukta*). However, where there is a difference in meaning despite the identity of word—even in the case of what would otherwise be a repetition of word (*śabdapunaruktatā*)—nothing [of that fault] is established.
Is such a possibility even conceivable, that there could be a difference in meaning despite a repetition of word? To this he says:
"For example, *hasati hasati*," and so forth.
For here, the first word *hasati* ends in the locative case while the second is a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), and thus there is a difference in meaning.
This is likewise in the subsequent cases.
Anticipating the objection that such a possibility exists in poetry but not in formal discourse, he provides an example.
"And as [stated in] 'yathā ca' and so forth.

Now, one might object: "But here too, just as there is a difference in meaning, there is also a difference in the words themselves, by virtue of being nominal stems (*subanta*) or verbal endings (*tiṅanta*)."
It is true not only there, but here as well.
Even in the case of "sound is impermanent" and "sound is impermanent," there is indeed a difference in sound due to the difference in its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);
otherwise, there would be no sequential hearing.
If redundancy is established here on the basis of identical phonetic form and identical substratum, then it is exactly the same in this case as well;
for there is indeed a difference in meaning,
due to the difference in the expressed objects such as the distinction between actions and so forth.
For indeed, the distinction between words is constructed by that very [repetition].
Furthermore, the second sūtra defining *punarukta* (repetition) indicates that even the restatement of a meaning already understood constitutes repetition.
An example of this has been stated by Vātsyāyana in the *Nyāyabhāṣya*:
In an argument based on similarity (*sādharmya*), there is [an absence] of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

However, the Teacher (Ācārya), intending to demonstrate that this [objection] applies equally even to the thesis (*pratijñā*)—having anticipated it with the thought "this is the same"—and wishing to establish that the thesis is not to be presented within the proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*), employs a roundabout expression and presents the statement of the thesis itself as an example: "in a proof-statement where the employment of words is restricted, just like the statement of the thesis. The compound *niyatapadaprayoga* is to be analyzed as "that in which there is the employment of restricted words."

This [objection] is rejected by the very fact that it is already included under "repetition of meaning" (*arthapunarukta*), since its meaning has already been understood; thus, it need not be stated separately.

For just as employing another synonymous word to express a meaning already conveyed by a single word is useless, so too is it when the meaning is already accessible through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*). Therefore, this is subsumed under "repetition of meaning"—this is the collective sense.

To the question, "Where, moreover, does this statement of the proposition and so forth—being redundant as something already obtainable through implication (*arthāpatti*)—become a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)?", he explains this by way of an alternative: "In a syllogism where the application of words is fixed, this too is a fault caused by the restatement of an implied meaning. This continues [to mean]: "In a syllogism where the employment of specific terms is restricted. What is meant is this: [The opponent objects: "If the restriction on the use of words applies even to the *sādhana* (the means of proof), then there would be no point in stating the *hetu* (reason) and the *udāharaṇa* (example) in a syllogism, because they are already implied by the *pakṣa* (proposition). For instance, when one says, 'Sound is non-eternal,' its non-eternality is already understood from that very statement; therefore, the reason 'because it is produced' and the example 'like a pot' are superfluous. Furthermore, since the *pratyakṣa* (perception) and other means of knowledge are included within the *pramāṇas* (means of valid cognition), their separate mention would be redundant. Likewise, since the *anumeya* (the object to be inferred) is included within the *pakṣa*, its separate mention would be redundant. Similarly, since the *sādhya* (the probandum) is included within the *dharma* (property) and the *sādhyadharmin* (the subject possessing the property to be proved), their separate mention would be redundant. And since the *sādhyadharmaviśiṣṭadharmin* (the subject qualified by the property to be proved) is included within the *pakṣa*, its separate mention would be redundant. Thus, because these are already implied, there would be no purpose in stating them separately. [The author replies: This is not so. Even though the *hetu* and the *udāharaṇa* are implied by the *pakṣa*, they are stated separately for the sake of clarity (*spaṣṭīkaraṇārtha*). Just as, although the *prameya* (objects of knowledge) are included within the *pramāṇas*, they are stated separately for the sake of clarity, so too are the *hetu* and the *udāharaṇa*. Furthermore, the *pratyakṣa* and others are mentioned separately from the *pramāṇas* because they are the most important among the *pramāṇas*. Similarly, the *anumeya* is mentioned separately from the *pakṣa* because it is the most important among the things to be proven. Likewise, the *sādhya* and the *sādhyadharmin* are mentioned separately from the *dharma* and the *dharmin* respectively, because they are the most important among those things. And the *sādhyadharmaviśiṣṭadharmin* is mentioned separately from the *pakṣa* because it is the most important among the things to be proven. Therefore, there is no fault here. [The opponent asks: "But why is the *pratijñā* (proposition) stated separately? Is it not already implied by the *pakṣa*? [The author replies: It is stated separately for the sake of making known the specific nature of the *pakṣa*. That is to say, the *pakṣa* is defined as "that which is desired to be proven" (*sādhyitumiṣṭa*). However, the *pratijñā* is defined as "that which is intended to be proven" (*sādhyitavyatvenopadarśita*). Therefore, the *pakṣa* is the thing itself, while the *pratijñā* is the verbal expression of that thing. Consequently, the *pratijñā* is not implied by the *pakṣa*. Moreover, the *pratijñā* is stated separately because it is the first step in the process of proving the *pakṣa*. Just as, although the *prameya* is included within the *pramāṇas*, it is stated separately because it is the first among them, so too is the *pratijñā*. Furthermore, the *pratijñā* is stated separately because it serves to indicate the specific nature of the *pakṣa*. That is to say, the *pakṣa* is that which is desired to be proven, but it is not yet established. The *pratijñā* indicates its specific nature by showing that it is intended to be proven. Therefore, the *pratijñā* is not redundant. [The opponent asks: "But why is the *upasaṃhāra* (conclusion) stated separately? Is it not already implied by the *anumāna* (inference)? [The author replies: It is stated separately for the sake of indicating the completion of the proof. That is to say, the *anumāna* is the process of proving the *pakṣa* through the *hetu* and the *udāharaṇa*. However, the *upasaṃhāra* is the final statement that shows the *pakṣa* has been proven. Therefore, the *upasaṃhāra* is not implied by the *anumāna*. Furthermore, the *upasaṃhāra* is stated separately because it serves to indicate the certainty of the proof. That is to say, the *anumāna* is the process of proving, but it is not yet certain that the *pakṣa* has been proven. The *upasaṃhāra* indicates that certainty by showing that the *pakṣa* has indeed been proven. Therefore, the *upasaṃhāra* is not redundant. Thus, although the *hetu*, the *udāharaṇa*, and the *upasaṃhāra* are implied by the *pakṣa*, they are stated separately for the sake of clarity, for the sake of indicating the specific nature of the *pakṣa*, and for the sake of indicating the completion and certainty of the proof. Therefore, there is no fault in stating them separately. As for the *pratyakṣa* and others, they are mentioned separately from the *pramāṇas* because they are the most important among them, and so forth, as explained above. Thus, there is no fault in stating the *pratijñā* and the others separately. [The opponent asks: "But why is the *pratijñā* stated separately if it is already obtained through implication? [The author replies: It is stated separately because it is the first step in the process of proving the *pakṣa*. That is to say, the *pakṣa* is the thing to be proven, but it is not yet established. The *pratijñā* indicates its specific nature by showing that it is intended to be proven. Therefore, the *pratijñā* is not implied by the *pakṣa*. Furthermore, the *pratijñā* is stated separately because it serves to indicate the specific nature of the *pakṣa*. That is to say, the *pakṣa* is that which is desired to be proven, but it is not yet established. The *pratijñā* indicates its specific nature by showing that it is intended to be proven. Therefore, the *pratijñā* is not redundant. [The opponent asks: "But why is the *upasaṃhāra* stated separately? Is it not already implied by the *anumāna*? [The author replies: It is stated separately for the sake of indicating the completion of the proof. That is to say, the *anumāna* is the process of proving the *pakṣa* through the *hetu* and the *udāharaṇa*. However, the *upasaṃhāra* is the final statement that shows the *pakṣa* has been proven. Therefore, the *upasaṃhāra* is not implied by the *anumāna*. Furthermore, the *upasaṃhāra* is stated separately because it serves to indicate the certainty of the proof. That is to say, the *anumāna* is the process of proving, but it is not yet certain that the *pakṣa* has been proven. The *upasaṃhāra* indicates that certainty by showing that the *pakṣa* has indeed been proven. Therefore, the *upasaṃhāra* is not redundant. Thus, although the *hetu*, the *udā
When the judges are experts in the investigation of words, meanings, and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), being discerning and possessing extremely attentive minds;

and when they declare that the opponent is likewise of such a nature, [the proponent] should employ only that which is indispensable for the establishment of the thesis (*sādhya*) and nothing more. Otherwise, this fault does not apply, because those whose minds are dependent on compassion and who are unconditionally affectionate do not [seek to] overwhelm the opponent.
In order to lead a disciple—who is as if difficult to find—onto the path of logic, they strive; in that case, even repetition is not a fault.
This very point he states:

for a proponent explaining [the argument], out of the apprehension that witnesses and others might not hear or understand correctly—which apprehension serves as the cause—he may indeed speak again and again for the sake of correct hearing and understanding.

The opponent [argues] that it is not so because [the teacher] is not the subject matter [of the debate]. He explains this very point: "This proponent is neither the teacher of the respondent, nor is the respondent the student of the proponent."
"Because both [parties] are situated in a mutual desire for victory.
Therefore, the opponent need not be diligently instructed by the proponent.
To this, the Teacher replies: "No," and so forth.
Granted that the opponent need not be persuaded through effort;

however, the witnesses must certainly be persuaded with effort, for it is precisely through their being informed that the proponent achieves victory, and otherwise, defeat. Why, then, would one not persuade the witnesses themselves? Furthermore, the opponent must also necessarily be persuaded, just like the witnesses.

Why? Because a fault is stated in the case of its non-communication. By the word "that" (*tat*), the witnesses and others are referred to; for if the witnesses and others were not to communicate [the meaning], then that which has been thrice stated by you, the assembly, and the opponent, but remains uncomprehended, would constitute the ground of defeat called "unintelligible meaning" (*avijñātārtha*) according to the Nyāya Sūtra (5.2.16).
The meaning is that this contradicts that [position]. Furthermore, as for what is said— that "this person is not a disciple"— that is unproven,
because one who is being instructed is indeed a disciple.

Since the very definition of a disciple is one who is to be instructed for the sake of attaining knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and because no other such characteristic exists, how is it that a respondent (*prativādī*) is not likewise a disciple?
It might be argued: "He is certainly not a disciple, because he has risen up in opposition out of a desire to compete for the sake of knowledge of reality."
That is incorrect, because the position of one who desires victory was refuted previously.
Even so, it is not something that must be established through effort, since the Great Sage has prescribed the rule of stating [the thesis] three times; therefore, he says:
"Because of the statement regarding the threefold utterance," and so forth. By this, he shows what he will state later.

If, first of all, the activity is for the purpose of communicating to another, why is it stated three times? [The opponent should be made to grasp it] in such and such a way that understanding arises in him. Or, if it is for the purpose of tormenting the other, even so, why is it stated three times?

Having informed the witnesses in the ear, the proponent should harass the opponent with difficult, unintelligible, rapid, or abbreviated speech, so that he becomes bewildered in his response and falls silent.
This is neither a restatement of the word and its meaning as "this is not," nor is it a restatement of a meaning already understood; rather,
it establishes non-difference itself.
By the words "viniyata" and so forth:
"excess" (ādhikya) is a fault of both the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*udāharaṇa*).

Because it has already been established by one [member], the other is rendered purposeless; thus, even in the case of repetition, that subsequent word whose meaning has already been understood by the preceding word is described in this way.
It has been established that its very excess constitutes a fault.
If it is asked, "Why is this said to be a fault when there is the employment of fixed words? he replies:
"The connection is that this is not a fault in the case of elaborate discourse (*prapañcakathā*)."
Of what? Of the abundance of reasons and so forth, and of repetition. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of an abundance of examples is intended.

In what kind of locus is the object to be proven (sādhya) established? It is established in a locus where the status of being the substratum for the proof of a single, unascertained object [is present]. Since it is "sought" (arthyate), it is called the "means of proof" (sādhana);
the reason (hetu) is the means of proof, and the locus (adhikaraṇa) is the property-bearer (dharmin).
The means of proof (*sādhana*) accompanied by the object (*artha*) is "the means of proving the object" (*arthasādhana*),
due to the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopa*).
That which is both singular and such a means of proving the object is described as "that."

The meaning is this: in that discourse on elaboration (*prapañcakathā*) where the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)—the substratum not yet determined—is one that accomplishes a single objective, and wherein the opponent does not desire to prove a single property (such as selflessness) regarding the subject (*dharmin*), such as the living body, but rather multiple properties (such as momentariness, non-selfhood, and non-divine agency), and likewise not by means of a single reason but by multiple reasons; it is in such a case [that the following applies]. He states this very point in its proper order:

In the case of a listener who desires the proof of various objects or the proof by various means, the former term *sādhana* (proof) denotes "accomplishment" because it is derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*),
whereas the latter denotes the "reason" (*hetu*) because it is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*).
Therefore, a multiplicity of reasons and so forth, as well as a multiplicity of statements, constitutes a fault when the proof is restricted to a single word.
Why? Because there is no established tradition [to support it]. Since the fault would be equal to that of the opponent, inclusion alone is logical;
the meaning is that one must either state something additional or else it is merely a repetition.
Because the second is included within one of these two.

But how is the "redundant" (adhika) included within "verbal repetition" (śabda-punarukta)? To this he says: for the second reason, which is conceived as a synonymous term, operates upon a subject already established by a single reason.
What is the reason?

Because there is no distinction in the object to be communicated. Then, how is repetition included within the "additional" (*adhika*)? He says: "The meaning, however, does not differ from its restatement."

By the word *artha*, he indicates *arthapunarukta* (repetition of meaning). That which causes something to be explained again is "re-explanation" (*punaḥpratipādana*), which consists precisely in the addition of further reasons and examples.
This is what is meant:
It is quite clear that this is included within the section on "Exemplification" (*udāharaṇa*).

For instance, it has been stated that the non-employment of a dissimilar exemplification (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*) in a syllogism based on similarity (*sādharmyavat prayoga*) is an example of "redundancy of meaning" (*arthapunarukta*). Furthermore, the prohibition of what is merely redundant is easily understood as an exception to the aforementioned [definition of redundancy]. || 0 ||
"That whose sentence-meaning is understood when it has been stated three times" means that;

or, it may be analyzed as a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), meaning "that which is both a sentence-meaning and understood," [this being understood] to have been stated three times by the proponent.
The phrase "the opponent's reutterance of the words" is to be connected [to the definition].
The mention of "three times" is for the purpose of making known that there is no defeat even if one fails to restate what was stated once.
And this failure to restate may occur either by way of the word or by way of the meaning.

He states the reason for its being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*): "Without restating [the opponent's position], on what basis could one state a refutation regarding the other's thesis? This does not mean that he points out a flaw in the subject matter; rather, the meaning is that without restating it, there is no statement of a refutation because there is no subject matter [to refute].

"Having formed a judgment regarding what has been said by you, a refutation must be stated; likewise, the proponent of the proof (*sādhana*) must also state the refutation in response and then offer a rebuttal.
Therefore, this constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for both parties.
Here, Bhāradvāja first raises an objection: "If it is argued that this is not a point of defeat because the conclusion is reached through understanding the subsequent [rebuttal]," he says.

He explains this statement with the words beginning "It might be so" (*syādetat*), and he himself provides the rebuttal with the words "not because of a complete understanding of the subject matter of the response" (*nottaraviṣayaparijñānāt*).
The phrase "If this... and so forth is a division of that very [point].
"And because of non-assertion" refers to the same.

Furthermore, the opponent's text is as follows: "Since there is no basis for it, and since there is no presentation of the other side's position, it is improper; thus, failure to restate [the opponent's argument] is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). This much is the opponent's treatise.
Here the Teacher begins to state the refutation:
even if the proponent, under the guise of explaining his own thesis, were to proclaim various other points by way of a consequential argument (*prasaṅga*)—

just as was previously illustrated where, under the pretext of explaining the body of the proposition that "the instruments and worlds are preceded by an intelligent cause," he might proclaim the entire Vaiśeṣika system.

Likewise, if the proponent, having stated merely the matter sought to be known, should expand the discussion—this is what is meant by "if the proponent"—the author asks: having done what should he expand it?
He replies: having introduced a succession of qualifications for the meaning in the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, which are other matters not useful for establishing [the point].

As was previously illustrated, in the dispute concerning whether sound is eternal or non-eternal, the follower of Jaimini (the Jaiminīya) provides proof by means of the "twelve characteristics" (*dvādaśalakṣaṇa*) and so forth;
he also explains those twelve characteristics.
Or, for example, as the followers of Akṣapāda argue:
"In the dispute over whether all these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāras*) are momentary or not, [they claim] that because they are the substrata of universals such as 'form-ness' (*rūpatva*),
the cognitions— perception and the rest— which have those [universals] as their substrata and objects do not perish immediately after attaining their own existence."

Because it is denotable by the term "sound" (kārya-śabda), which is produced by conjunctions and disjunctions with substances of the same or different classes—just like prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth.
Now, in the phrase "in the proposition and so forth" (*pratijñādiṣu*), what is included by the word "and so forth"?
It cannot be the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*udāharaṇa*), because of the statement: "having stated only that much."
And since nothing else has been introduced here, this is not a fault; for it should be understood that [the phrase] "even having stated merely the reason and so forth" is intended.
Therefore, some maintain that by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the reasons and other factors are implied.
Others, however, say that this objection raised regarding the use of the suffix *ktvā* here is misplaced;

for this is the meaning intended: having stated that mere object of inquiry which the opponent desires to know—such as non-momentariness and so forth, devoid of any other qualification—the proponent, thinking "I shall establish this," subsequently formulates a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while introducing further unintended matters through a succession of qualifications to the subject of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so on.
"One should expand the discussion.

This means that when something entirely irrelevant—merely resembling the formal announcement of a drama or a narrative—is brought forward by the proponent through a succession of specific qualifications such as the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, then what is the basis for debate? Since it is merely a matter of words (*arthamātra*) such as "non-momentariness" and the like, there is no impairment whatsoever of the capacity for a response in the subsequent statement. This is the meaning.
Therefore, it is not the case that the respondent is incapable because he does not repeat the opponent's discourse;
rather, the connection [of the argument] is as follows: that statement without which the establishment of the sought-after object is impossible must necessarily be demonstrated.
Why? Because the function of a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) has as its object the members of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*).

The connection is that refutation proceeds only when a proof has been presented by another; therefore, he asks: "What is the necessary concomitant for the establishment of the object of inquiry? He replies:

"It is merely the establishment of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). That by which pervasion is established is "the means of establishing pervasion," namely, the presentation of a subverting valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). He says "no" to the objection that one must also raise the issue of a different matter, such as "What is this [pervasion]? even during the employment of a proof. No.
In that case as well, there would be the introduction of another consequence; thus, the thought is that it is purposeless.
Only this much is demonstrated here. Why [is it] not refuted later in sequence? He says: "No."

Even in that case, when repeating [the opponent's argument] for the purpose of demonstrating the object of refutation, one need not utter everything exactly as it was presented by the proponent prior to stating the refutation; for why? Because that would entail the necessity of reciting it three times.
He begins the initial course of action in order to demonstrate precisely the contingency of repeating [the argument] twice,
starting with the words "dūṣaṇa" and so forth.
He says this because, if one does not announce the sequence of the statements, the critique would now be rendered irrelevant.
Because it is invariably concomitant, the presentation of the object is indeed performed by one who points out a fault.
How so? With respect to every statement of a fault; that is to say, for whichever fault is stated, its object is explained.
He says this very thing:
"This is the fault of this argument stated by the proponent.
If one asks, "What is the reason that a refutation is not stated by repeating everything all at once? he replies:
"Not so," and so forth.
Why? Because the defects differ for each respective object; that is to say, the defect varies according to the object, just as the object itself does.
Thus, having formulated the initial position, he demonstrates the contingency of repeating [the opponent's argument] twice;
for it is impossible to state the fault in the subject matter once the entire restatement has been shown. He says that this is merely a ground for defeat based on a purposeless [repetition].

When a critic must state a refutation, if there is a recitation of everything in its entirety, it is employed for the purpose of agitating the opponent's position; its expression consists of this [recitation] and the pointing out of repeated words, and thus the arrangement of words should be done in such a manner. Therefore, the recitation of everything in its entirety should be declared a ground for defeat. At this point, Ākṣapāda [the follower of Akṣapāda/Gautama] states that all of this refutation is [invalidated] by our non-acceptance of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Thinking that it has been countered, he grants permission,
saying, "So be it.
He explains this very point with the words, "It might be so."

Since the statement "from whatever source" is merely a pretext for elaborating upon the means of proof (*sādhana*), and because it involves the introduction of a succession of qualifications to the meaning within the thesis (*pratijñā*) and other members, it does not constitute a relevant consequence (*aprasaṅga*). Rather, because it is like a commentary on names such as *Rūpasiddhi* that mentions what is not necessarily implied (*anantarīyaka*), it is simply a departure from the subject matter (*arthāntara*) for the proponent;
thus, he is liable to defeat by that [charge].
If it is asked, "Why is one who speaks incidentally (*prāsaṅgika*) defeated? he replies:
For there is no one anywhere who does not employ something when it follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*),
as was stated previously regarding the proponents of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*):
"In proving that [selflessness], it would follow as a consequence even for dancing, singing, and so forth."
Nor should that which was introduced by the proponent as a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) be repeated by the opponent,
as it is of no utility [to him].
The meaning is that it is not at all appropriate for you to repeat [the entire argument].
By this, what was previously stated—that "even if the proponent, under the pretext of explaining the meaning of his own proof," and so forth—is hereby admitted.
Now, regarding what was said there as well: not everything must be uttered in its entirety in sequential order.
He permits that the refutation should be stated afterwards because of the consequence of having to utter [the argument] twice, saying:
"And this too is not by us," and so forth.
The Teacher says: "If even by you..."
In that case, since it is merely a form of defeat (*pīḍana*), non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) should not be stated as a separate [ground for defeat].
Why? Because it is included within "inability to respond" (*pratibhā*).
He demonstrates precisely this inclusion:

For "non-rebuttal" (*apratibhā*) occurs because of the opponent's failure to understand the reply (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.18). To this he asks: "How is that so? He replies: Furthermore, without demonstrating the subject matter of the reply, the respondent is incapable of understanding, knowing, or expressing the reply.
He asks, "Why is he not capable?
and replies with the words beginning "For not," and so forth.
The phrase *uttara-pratipattiḥ* means a subsequent understanding; that is, a later comprehension.
That [objection] was not raised by him through that failure to repeat;
rather, because of the double negation, it is determined as an affirmation, and thus it is simply the non-comprehension of the response that was implied.
This is what is meant.

For indeed, one who understands the reply must necessarily understand its object as well; and since he recognizes, "this is the refutation of that," how could a conscious person not repeat it once its object is known? Therefore, wherever there is non-repetition, there non-reproduction (*apratibhā*) must be present; thus, non-reproduction is pervaded by non-reproduction. Since the status of being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) has been prescribed for the former (non-reproduction), it implies it for the latter (non-repetition) when it is the pervaded. He states this under the guise of a conclusion.
"Teneti," and so forth.

Here he states an illustration: "Just as [the property] is prescribed with respect to that which is not specifically grasped (*aparāmṛṣṭa*)—namely, the universal (*sāmānya*) consisting of its various particulars—it is likewise found in the *bāhuleya* (a type of ox) pervaded by that [universal], because it possesses a dewlap and so on.
Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is obtained even though it is not explicitly stated, by virtue of the capacity of the prescription of one thing.
Indeed, one who acts with foresight should not establish [a property] repeatedly.

For example, since the possession of dewlaps and so forth has already been established within the genus "cow" by the force of the injunction, it is therefore not to be established again in those very individuals.

[The opponent argues: "The state of possessing [the capacity for] rejoinder (*snādimattva*) is necessarily connected to the non-establishment of the ground of defeat known as 'lack of rejoinder' (*ananubhāṣaṇa-nigrahasthāna*), by virtue of the efficacy of the rule that establishes 'lack of rejoinder' as a ground of defeat. Thus, there is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Now, even if a respondent understands both the subject and the object through a detailed exposition of the answer, yet—his mind being distracted by excessive fear, trembling, and so forth—he does not repeat them; that subject is untouched by 'lack of rejoinder' because it is not seized by 'lack of confidence' (*apratibhā*). Therefore, how [can there be a contradiction]?"
That [fear] would have to pervade him, for only then would this reason be established; however, it is simply not possible.

For one who understands the object and the subsequent understanding of that object does not fear or tremble from any cause, since fear, trembling, perspiration, and so forth are produced by ignorance of that [object].
If, on the other hand, even such a person were agitated by fear and the like, then he would not even venture to engage in debate at the very outset, being already in such a state.
Moreover,
if only fools were of such a nature,
then treatises on logic (nyāyaśāstra) would not be composed with reference to the conventional dealings of fools.
Alternatively, even in this way, its inclusion within *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity) is not at all contradicted;
for a counter-argument (*vidhottara*) consists of either a failure to understand the opponent's argument or a failure to state a reply.
Therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
Now, even if [the statement] is for the purpose of tormenting the opponent, why is it stated three times?
Rather, what is the task? He says:

having whispered into the ear of the witnesses the approach of a bribe, saying, "This is the matter intended by me here," at a later time, the wretched defendant—being helpless—is [tormented] by means of difficult, unintelligible, rapid, and abbreviated [speech], and so forth.
The word "by means of sounds" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. [He] is to be harassed. Why? Because they are difficult to pronounce.
"Unfamiliar" means those that are unintelligible, like the Sinhalese language and so forth.
"Rapid" means pronounced quickly.
"Condensed" means having their meanings rolled together, like a thread of a sūtra.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), those meanings that are concealed are included.

For example: "O wind, blow from the direction of the being; O sun, shine from the direction of the east; O moon, move in your own quarter; O fire, be present for the sake of consciousness; O water, touch us for the sake of peace."
For example:
when the proponent is currently bewildered regarding the formulation of a reply, he remains silent;
this is "the unintelligible" (*avijñātārtha*), defined as that which is stated three times by the assembly and the opponent but not understood (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.19).

If it is argued that because the Sage did not prohibit the use of words that are punning (*śliṣṭa*) or difficult (*kaṣṭa*), etc., one cannot thus commit such an impropriety, he replies: "For this is not a method for afflicting others," and so forth. Furthermore, it has been stated in the section on the "Misconduct of the Wicked" (*durjanavipratipattyadhikaraṇa*)—specifically in the passage "the virtuous do not engage in [such things], nor are treatises composed by them for the purpose of afflicting others"—that the virtuous do not apply themselves to treatises for that reason.

Since the virtuous do not proceed to act for the sake of afflicting others, it must be stated [by the proponent] as many times as necessary until [the opponent] has grasped [the argument]; however, the rule that "it should be stated only three times" is the established limit. Alternatively, if it is determined that the respondent is unable to grasp [the argument] despite the proponent stating it repeatedly—even up to a hundred times—due to extreme dullness, and once this incapacity for comprehension is somehow ascertained, then even before the formal application of the proof (*sādhana*), the proponent should withdraw, deciding: "I shall not engage in debate with this person. This is the settled conclusion.
[The opponent's] capacity is severed.
Regarding "in the grasping," [it refers to] that which belongs to the opponent, whose other name is extreme dullness; by the proponent, he is thus [described].
To the question, "How can one who avoids [the objection] in such a manner be suspected of being incapable? he says:
Having awakened other witnesses, [one says]: "This person is not capable of understanding the meaning of the statement; rather, the matter is established as follows. || 4 ||

Since the rule for the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied in the sense of the action (*bhāve*) in the Nyāya Sūtra (5.2.17), "ignorance is that which is not cognized," the failure to comprehend the meaning of the statement establishing the proof (*sādhanavākyārtha*) constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
For this very reason, the authors of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) and the Sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) explain: "Ignorance is the non-arising of cognition regarding the object of the sentence-meaning."

Or, even if the rule for the suffix *niṣṭhā* were applied only to the verbal root *kṛ*, nevertheless, because no knowledge regarding the meaning of the sentence arises, it is precisely the sentence uttered by the proponent—which is thus qualified—that constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the opponent; thus, others, seeing that the word "meaning" (*artha*) is included in the commentary, mistakenly read the word "meaning" (*artha*) even in the original Sūtra.
Furthermore, the reading of others is that "non-understanding of the meaning" (*avijñātārtha*) is [the definition of] "ignorance" (*ajñāna*).

A proof-statement whose meaning has been understood by the assembly—that which is not understood or comprehended by that opponent is "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). Such is the arrangement of the words in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvapakṣa*). In the sense of an object (*karmapakṣa*), however, the word "of him" (*tasya*) need not be supplied; rather, it is explained as a single syntactical unit: "that which is understood by the assembly. Why is it specified "by the assembly"? It is for the purpose of making known that even when [the statement] is not understood by the assembly, the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) of "not understanding the meaning" belongs to the proponent alone.
He states the reason for its being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*): "Indeed, if the meaning is not understood, the opponent would not be able to state a refutation of it.
Others, however, connect this with the subsequent section on refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), but that is incorrect because this belongs to the body of the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika*.

It establishes that [the opponent] is indeed defeated (*gamyatvam eva sādhayati*). Just as in the case of non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), one is defeated precisely because of the failure to understand the reply; how then can there be a failure to understand the reply? To this he says: "Because the subject matter has not been displayed. This means that since the respondent is unable to understand the reply because the subject matter has not been displayed—this being understood either as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that by which the subject matter was not displayed," or as a *karmadhāraya* (descriptive) compound. For instance, one reproduces [the argument] for the purpose of making known the subject matter of the refutation; yet, having abandoned that, if one instead reproduces whatever web of words the proponent has not brought forward, [one is defeated].
In that case, since such a restatement would be useless without the context of demonstrating the subsequent point (*uttara-viṣaya*), the term "impossible" (*aśakya*) is understood [to apply].
Or, it may be that its status as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is due solely to the opponent's failure to grasp the favor [of the argument].
He concludes the application to the subject at hand (*dārṣṭāntika*).
Likewise, even in the case of knowledge, it constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) precisely because of the failure to provide a reply;
for how could one who does not know the opponent's refutation and its object state the subject matter of the reply? The subject matter of the reply is that which is to be refuted.

In some places, however, there is a different reading: "How is it that the answer, the subject matter of the answer, and the answer itself [are distinct]? In this regard, the point is that there is no connection [between them].

And how could one who does not know the subject matter of the rejoinder (*uttara*) state that rejoinder? Therefore, ignorance of the subject matter and ignorance of the rejoinder constitute "inability to respond" (*an-uttara*), since they are understood as being nothing other than "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*). The term "is not to be stated" (*avācyam*) continues [from the previous context]. What is the reason? Because otherwise, if this were not established as a distinct ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), lack of ingenuity would be rendered devoid of a specific object (*nirviṣaya*).
He explains how there is an absence of an object [of refutation] with the words "for one who has not ascertained the meaning," and so forth.
That opponent by whom the meaning of both the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the response (*uttara*) has not been ascertained would not be able to repeat them.
Furthermore, if this [objection] were not restated, and the subject matter were not shown, one would be unable to formulate a reply; thus, one would fail to provide a response.

One would neither know it nor be able to state it. Why does the failure to provide a reply follow from the ignorance of both the reply and its subject matter? To this he says: "Because it is impossible to fail to provide a reply when the knowledge of that subject matter and the reply itself is present."
One who knows the answer and its subject matter is thus defined. Therefore, both of these—
the ignorance of the answer and the ignorance of the subject matter— are the cause of *pratipatti* (failure to respond), which is synonymous with *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity).
But surely, it is the very ignorance of the answer that constitutes *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity); how then can that [ignorance] itself be taught as the cause of oneself?
No, for what is intended here is *apratibhā* characterized by the non-statement of an answer.

Thus, "in the absence of that" means that when there is an absence of those two—the ignorance regarding the answer and [the inability to respond]—the understanding, that is, the statement of the answer, indeed occurs.

Thus, since non-rejoinder (*apratibhā*) is already included within the ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) designated as "ignorance" (*ajñāna*)— which consists of ignorance regarding the subject matter and subsequent knowledge regarding it— if it were stated separately from that ground for defeat, one must state what its specific domain is; otherwise, if no domain is stated,
then non-rejoinder would be indefinable due to having no domain.

Others explain that there is a separate mention of these two—ignorance (*ajñāna*) and restatement (*anubhāṣaṇa*). Another says this in order to establish the distinction between the objects of ignorance and lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*):
"Ignorance is not said to be the non-knowing of the opponent's reply."
Since non-inspiration (*apratibhā*) would be inexpressible due to having no object, what then is it? He says: it is ignorance of the object (*viṣayājñāna*).
Even so, he explains how non-elocution (*aprati-bhā*) has an object:
because when the subject matter is known, one subsequently lacks the knowledge of a reply;
thus the opponent would neither comprehend nor state a response to it.
Therefore, there exists an object for non-apprehension (*apratibhā*):
one who is overcome by ignorance.
Even so, he says that you are not released because you remain inexpressible.
Regarding the word "eantarhi" (in this case):
it establishes that non-reproduction is indeed a consequence of ignorance.
For no conscious person, correctly understanding the subject matter, would fail to reproduce it; therefore, non-reproduction need not be mentioned separately from ignorance.

Furthermore, he states that non-reproduction (an-anubhāṣaṇa), like non-elucidation (a-pratibhā), need not be mentioned separately from ignorance (ajñāna), because the latter implies the former: "And because of the implication of ignorance regarding the reply.
He explains this with the passage beginning "viṣaya... and so forth.

The opponent says, "When the object is known," and so forth. What is meant is this: there are two kinds of ignorance regarding the answer—namely, that which accompanies ignorance of the object, and that which accompanies knowledge of the object. Among these, although the first does not imply ignorance of the answer, the answer itself is not implied by it; therefore, *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity) is mentioned separately with respect to the second kind.
He states that an infinite regress of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) would result:
"In that case, then," and so forth.
"Just as," and so forth, is the analysis of that very point.
Likewise, it applies to cognitions as well; that is, to the subsequent cognition and its object.
This refers to the ignorance regarding every subsequent cognition and its object.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of [ignorance regarding] two, three, four, or more parts, and so forth.
If it is argued that there is a fault in the summary statement regarding ignorance subsequent to [the realization of] the poison, he says:
"No. If it is argued that just as there is no fault, so too there is no excellence, he says:
It is logical that the quality known as lightness (*lāghava*) should be included;
however, because it falls within the scope of "inability to respond" (*apratibhā*), it is not mentioned separately.
The meaning is that these two are subsumed by the very mention of *apratibhā*.
It is not only logical that these two alone are mentioned without distinction;
rather, it is appropriate for others as well. Thus he says, "Moreover," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by the mention of both of those" alone:

by the mere mention of *hetvābhāsa* (fallacious reasons) and *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity), all [other points] such as *pratijñāhāni* (abandonment of the proposition) and *ananubhāṣaṇa* (failure to restate) are already included.

For it cannot be said that anyone other than the proponent of the proof (*sādhanavādī*) would ever concede the property of the opposing side or adopt the opponent's proposition for the sake of proving their own. Thus it should be stated.
In that case, there is no objection whatsoever, since it is evident that he neither repeats [the opponent's statement] nor diverts the discussion.

If it is argued that one should say "he also approves of the other's view," since both [positions] are implied, and therefore the elaboration (*prapañca*) is meritorious because the Sage does not state them— [the author] replies:
"In the various distinctions implied by those two, there is no excellence of quality (*guṇātiśaya*)."
Because a quality (*guṇa*) is not perceived [as a distinct entity], and because there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if one were to insist on speaking of such elaborations (*prapañca*),
and because it would entail the naming of things like "the back of the armpit" (*kakṣapiṭṭita*) and so forth;
therefore, this elaboration was rendered useless by the Great Sage.

When the opponent's position is to be refuted, if one does not find, does not know, or does not state a counter-objection (*uttara-dūṣaṇa*), then one should be understood as defeated (*nigṛhīta*); such is the extent of the other's text. This point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is correct;
for this very reason, we too have stated here that "this is the pointing out of a non-fault. Thinking thus, [the author] grants his assent.
"Regarding the passage beginning with *sādhana* and so forth:
immediately after the statement of the proof (*sādhana*), the opponent (*prativādin*) must state the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).

When he, instead of doing all of that, wastes time by restating the entire sequence, reciting verses, describing the assembly, or through other such means, then, by passing time fruitlessly and without purpose, he [commits a fault] regarding what ought to be done..."
One is defeated by the non-performance of the understanding of what has been stated as a refutation.
This [term] is a qualification of the time of this futile action.
Interruption due to preoccupation with business, the introduction of a side-issue, breaking off the conversation, and the cessation of the conversation—
for instance, by saying, "An ailment afflicts my limbs;
I am unable to speak now, but I shall tell you later"— in such ways, one cuts short the commencement of a discourse.

He states the reason for the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*): When one of the two parties—the proponent (*vādin*) or the opponent (*prativādin*)—is defeated by the failure to state a constituent of proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) or by the failure to point out a fault (*adoṣodbhāvana*), the debate concludes in defeat. Since such a debate has thus come to its conclusion, that person himself reaches the end of the discussion; therefore, this is a point of defeat.
Regarding this, the Teacher says:

"This too is a diversion to another task (*kāryavyāsañjanam*), provided that the proponent (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) should do so because he lacks the power to state a proof; the meaning is that it is merely a pretext, by some kind of trickery, and not that he would do so when there exists a real task of that sort which obstructs the debate."
That work which has the nature of interrupting such a discourse in the form of a formal recitation (*udgrāhaṇikā*), characterized by indigestion, colic, burning sensations in the stomach,
and so forth— [this applies] if, at that very time, there is indeed [an occurrence of] colic or a burning sensation in the throat/stomach for him.

The meaning is that if such things as burning [the opponent] were to occur, it would certainly not constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). However, when one resorts to such means merely as a pretext, then for that proponent of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), there occurs a diversion (*vikṣepa*) precisely because his own proof has been determined to be incompetent. To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"And thus, this point of defeat known as 'diversion' would be included within 'irrelevance' (*arthāntara*) itself."

Because the presentation of the *karaṇīya* (the thing to be accomplished) is identical to the explanation of the name and so forth in the *Rūpasiddhi*, it would necessarily be included among the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). Why? Because that proof is incapable and because it merely names [the object]. Furthermore, how does this differ from the "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*) and the "incoherent" (*apārthaka*)?

What is the reason? It means that this subject matter (*prakṛta*) and its proof (*sādhana*) are present, yet that comprehension (*pratipatti*) is unrelated to them; therefore, because no connection is perceived between it and the statement of the proof—just as in the case of the phrase "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*) or the sequence of phonemes *ja-ba-ḍa-ga-ḍa*—it is stated separately from [the actual argument] due to a mere slight difference in form and a trifling cause. To this, he says:
"Excessive prolixity (*atiprasaṅga*) and so forth":

those who possess a comprehension (*pratipatti*) [of the argument] through an unrelated proof-statement (*asambaddha-sādhana-vākya*) are "those who comprehend an unrelated proof-statement. These are both "those" and "the varieties" (*prabheda*); thus, the compound is formed. In this way, it has been stated that distraction (*vikṣepa*) is not mentioned separately because of its connection with the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādin*).

Now, he speaks also with reference to the opponent (the respondent). If the proponent of the subsequent position (uttarapakṣavādin) should divert the discussion by such means as "he thus wears away his throat, which consists of a mass of phlegm," and so forth, then—since a rejoinder must be formulated immediately after the proof (sādhana) has been presented—that proponent of the subsequent position, by failing to formulate it, incurs the recognition of diversion through the non-statement of that rejoinder; this [diversion] is included within either "lack of ingenuity" (aprati-bhā) or "irrelevancy" (arthāntara). But the opponent, unable to tolerate this aforementioned inclusion, objects:
Now, he confirms that very point by stating, "Indeed, it is not necessarily so":

for there exists debate—conducted even with an unstructured syllogism, or even within a disconnected discourse—for the purpose of robbing an opponent of their presence of mind, even down to the level of accusing one's own mother of adultery.
To this, the Teacher says:
It is not because such a dispute is impossible;

for a dispute would occur between two parties, a proponent and an opponent, who hold mutually contradictory admissions regarding a single locus, such as sound, concerning its permanence or impermanence.
Why is this so? He says:

Those two whose acceptances are not contradictory are such; those two persons for whom there exist no contradictory or non-contradictory acceptances—because there is an absence of dispute between them.
In that case, when this determination by means of logic (*nyāya*) has been established, the word "there" (*tatra*) refers to that.
Either the proponent or the opponent must necessarily initiate speech first;
why does he say they do not speak simultaneously?
The connection is that when there is simultaneous activity, those who are composed in mind do not act [in such a manner].
He asks, "Why is this so? and replies:
because activity would be futile due to the impossibility—serving as the instrumental cause—of hearing, comprehending, and responding to one another's speech.
For if one were to hear the other's speech without confusion, then one would comprehend its meaning and offer a response.
Furthermore, if they were to proceed simultaneously, none of this would be possible—just like the confused clamor of Digambara reciters. Therefore, one must necessarily proceed with speech first.

Thus, when that self-composed proponent of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣavādin) has presented his own accepted view by stating, "I shall prove that sound is impermanent," and so forth, he must necessarily state a proof (*sādhana*).
Otherwise, if the reason (*hetu*) is not stated, for others...
Because witnesses and the like do not provide [the required testimony],
and because it follows that the other— the proponent of the counter-position— must state a refutation related to the proof (*sādhana*) uttered by the first proponent;
therefore, for both the proponent and [the opponent]...

When the debate proceeds incorrectly, there is the inclusion of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*). Thus, every presentation of the prima facie and final positions conducted according to the rules of logic does not transcend these two: fallacious reasons and lack of ingenuity.
[Objection: But if the debate is proceeding according to the rules of logic, how can there be scope for these two?

And how could two contradictory propositions be presented regarding a single subject when a formal argument (*nyāya*) is being conducted? For in that case, there must necessarily be one proposition by which the argument proceeds; otherwise, it would consist of two distinct subjects.
This is not due to a failure to understand the intended meaning.
Your Honor has not fully understood that this was intended by the Teacher as being consistent with logical procedure (*nyāyapravṛtta*).

For, in accordance with logical procedure, it is intended that the presentation of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the conclusive (*uttarapakṣa*) positions does not occur simultaneously, and that there is an absence of [logical] fallacies such as deviation (*vyabhicāra*) or contradiction with the mother [the thesis].
By this—namely, the statement beginning with "for there would be a dispute between two who accept contradictory positions regarding a single locus"—the *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is refuted.
He asks: "How is it refuted? and replies: "Because in the absence of any acceptance [of a position], there is an absence of dispute."
This is what is meant: "A collection of statements consisting merely of the establishment of one's own position is called *vitaṇḍā* (cavil)" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.3).
If, however, the caviller has no position of his own, it must be explained how there can then be a dispute.

If it is argued that the caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) proceeds for the sake of refuting the opponent's position, then the very refutation of the opponent's position would constitute his own position; thus, the definition of the cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) collapses.
For indeed, whatever is accepted by someone is his own position.
And the refutation of the opponent's position accepted by him does not transcend the status of being his own position.

This means that when, having entered into a debate, he—due to timidity before the assembly and being distracted—offers nothing by way of a proof or even an effort toward one, merely through a thesis alone; [then he is defeated].
Or he may prattle something else entirely:
"A crow is cawing discordantly; surely this portends some calamity in my house, so enough with this dispute!
I shall go home for now to see whether my father has died or if something else has occurred," and so forth.
Likewise, how can there be inclusion within the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)? He considers that because of the absence of a proof (*sādhana*), the fallacies of the reason are impossible;
the intention is that even "non-comprehension of the reply" does not exist at all, since he is the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādin*).
With this, the opponent intends to connect [the two points] by showing that [the argument] does not fall outside of these two [alternatives].
The Teacher says:
"It is stated that it does not fall outside of these two only when an unestablished proof is being asserted; that is to say, this was stated regarding the aforementioned proof."
But as for how one should proceed when [the reason] is unproven, he says:
it has already been stated at the very introduction of the treatise that there is defeat even in the cases of non-statement and statement of something else;
he now recalls that very point.

Regarding the statement "because of stating that which is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) within the context of an admission (*abhyupagamyavāda*)," it is explained there as follows: it is the non-utterance of a member of the proof.
Whatever is the statement of something other than a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), all that is the "statement of what is not a member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacana*).

By this—namely, by the statement of defeat consisting in the mention of something else—the status of the superfluous (*adhika*), the redundant (*punarukta*), and the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth as points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is explained. He asks, "How so? and replies with the words beginning, "For that too... (*tad api hi...*) and so on.
By this he says the following:

if any point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) has been stated by us as being logically consistent and impartial, it is already subsumed under our very term "stating what is not a constituent of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacana*). If that is so, then for what purpose was the statement "and of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) etc. made? For the statement of the proposition, the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*) has not been declared a point of defeat by us in an impartial manner.

On the contrary, the very failure to state that [reason] constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). For it has been established [in Nyāya-sūtra 5.2.12] that "if [a statement] is deficient by even one of its members, it is *hīna*. If this is so, then this [example] is for the sake of illustration: just as that [deficient statement], because it lacks the capacity to make the [proposition] understood, is designated by the term "statement of a non-member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacana*).
The same applies to "redundancy" (*adhika*) and "repetition" (*punarvacana*). For this very reason, the second *ca* functions in the sense of *iva* (as if).
Otherwise, the meaning would have to be understood as "and [the fault of] repetition."
However, some do not recite the subsequent *ca* (and), because they consider it already included within the tautology (*punarukta*).
"Conceding the opponent's position" (*matānujñā*) is the attribution of a fault to another's position by accepting a fault in one's own position (Nyāya Sūtra 5.2.20).
Since one fails to recognize the fault when a refutation must be stated, one concedes the other's view and is thereby defeated.
As it is said: having failed to avoid the fault pointed out and questioned by the opposing disputant, one follows that line of reasoning and says, "This same fault applies to you as well."
For example, when a proponent says, "You are a thief because you are a human being, like a Śabara and others," the opponent might reply to that proponent:

"You too are a thief. By employing this very word, he accepts his own status as a thief and, while attributing that same fault to the opponent's position, he brings about what is considered by another proponent to be the opponent's status as a thief.
He permits that,
for indeed, as long as you have not been freed from the suspicion of being a thief yourself, you would not otherwise address him in such a manner.
But since one must consider whether that [reason] exists or does not exist in the disputant, "admission of the opponent's view" (*matānujñā*) is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
The Teacher refutes this as well:
even here, if the intention of the respondent is, "Because you are a human being, you too might be a thief, just like me," [then it is not a fault].

Furthermore, you yourself do not accept that the self is a thief; therefore, when "thievery" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the reason "because of being human" (*puruṣatvāt*) is present even in one who is not a thief—that is, in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Thus, it is vitiated by the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to its occurrence there.
Consequently, according to this intention of the opponent, there is no fault for the proponent—neither the fault characterized as "admission of the opponent's position" (*matānujñā*) nor any other.
Why? Because the proponent has refuted [the opponent] by demonstrating the existence of the reason in the form of the self, which is the counter-example where thievery is not admitted.
This means because it brings about the manifestation of a deviation that is difficult to discern.

He anticipates the objection of Uddyotakara: "Why has the reason not been shown to be deviant even by you, in a straightforward and simple manner, through the consequence that 'you too would be [a thief]'? For the property of being a human (puruṣatva) exists in you as well, who are not a thief; therefore, the reason is inconclusive."
"Therefore, he is refuted precisely because he practices deceit when he ought to act without deceit.
The Teacher says: "This statement by Uddyotakara is trivial, for there certainly exist in the world such transactions conducted through cleverness."

For instance, when it is argued that "your mothers are prostitutes because they are women, like other prostitutes," even cowherds and others— who follow the cleverness common to the likes of the *jaḍa* and *janaṅgama*—
oppose this and establish that their own mothers are not prostitutes; rather, they refute the opponent by means of a stylistic maneuver that points out the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason.

Therefore, by thus casting aside even the light of worldly convention—which is evident even to common folk such as plowmen—Uddyotakara has merely illuminated his own status as a "light-maker" (udyotakara).

Now, if it is argued that he does not demonstrate deviation through this turn of phrase, but rather, having admitted the validity of that proof, uses that very defect to defame the opponent, [the author] says:

Now, if he accepts that [accusation] by saying, "Because you are a human being, you are a thief," even then he is worthy of defeat solely due to his failure to provide a response (*uttarāpratipatti*) to that proof; it is not because of the opponent's introduction of his own fault—namely, the state of being a thief. The term "worthy of defeat" (*nigrahārha*) carries over from the previous context.
This very point is further substantiated. For the remainder of the sentence is: "provided that the faultlessness of its proof is admitted.

That very acceptance of the [opponent's] proposal is itself the "non-apprehension of a reply" (*uttarāpratipatti*); for by that alone—by the mere non-apprehension of a reply—one incurs the charge of a fault in the other case.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "of one who has incurred—that is, reached—the defeat (nigraha) of the opponent who was previously established in proof.

The sense is that since the raising of another's fault—characterized by *matānujñā* (admission of the opponent's position)—is not to be taken into account, there can be no defeat of one who is already defeated. || 0 ||
Not pointing out a defeat when it has been incurred is "overlooking the censurable" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*). One who is "censurable" (*paryanuyojya*) is one who has incurred a defeat;
overlooking him means not declaring, "You have incurred a defeat.
But who, then, points out this "overlooking of the censurable" as a ground for defeat?
It is not reasonable to say that he is not subject to censure,
because it is impossible;
for there is no possibility that he would admit his own possession of faults for the sake of demonstrating the faults of another.
Having reached a point of defeat, I was overlooked by him due to his failure to recognize that ground of defeat.
Therefore, it is not reasonable to say that he is at fault for having overlooked me,
because he simply did not know that I had reached a state of defeat.
For indeed, it is precisely because of a lack of full understanding that he does not pursue [the opponent] with the words, "You have incurred defeat.
If, on the other hand, he did possess full understanding, how could he remain indifferent?

And if he were indifferent, being equanimous, how could he manifest this [defeat] by saying, "This fault was overlooked by me; therefore, my overlooking constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for him"? Thus, the opponent should press him on this point.

And since there is no third party here who is a participant in this context, by what means could this objection be raised? Anticipating all such doubts, Pakṣilasvāmin says: "This neglect of one who should be questioned" (paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa) must be stated; that is to say, when the assembly—whether consisting of the proponent and the opponent themselves, or others more competent than them—is properly constituted and has been questioned, it is the duty of the judges (prāśnikas) to declare [the defeat]. This is the meaning.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
It is precisely this [that constitutes the fault],
while the other points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) belong to the proponent (*vādin*).
These [faults] are pointed out by the two disputants themselves, whereas this [specific point] is pointed out only by the judges. He asks:
what is the reason that it is not stated by those two [disputants] themselves? He says:
Indeed, one who has incurred defeat should not expose or reveal his own private parts—that is, his own faults.
Regarding this, the Teacher says "even here," and so forth.
However, if one considers the logic of the matter, then it is not logical for victory and defeat to belong to either one [of the two parties].
He explains how the proponent wins: because the object of inquiry has not been established by means of a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*).

For this very reason, there is no defeat for the opponent either, since the determination of the opponent's defeat is made in relation to the establishment of the meaning intended by the proponent. He then asks: "What then is the victory of the opponent? and replies:
And because faults [in the proof] have not been stated regarding the [opponent's] position,
for this very reason there is no defeat for the proponent, since that [defeat] is established in relation to the refutation of his proof.
Now, even though many faults exist in the proof of the proponent, the proponent of the counter-position may point out some fault [of it], while [failing to point out] another.
At that time, he does not deserve defeat.
Why? Because it means that he has stated his understanding of the response. The opponent says:
"One deserves censure precisely because of the failure to point out all the faults.
The Teacher said: "Indeed, sir, it is not the case that all faults must necessarily be stated by the opponent simply because they are real."
Or, if there is no statement [of the fault], there is the suppression of another fault; the word "not" carries over from the previous context.

Why? He says: because all faults need not be pointed out, since even by the pointing out of a single fault, such as "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and so forth, there is the subversion of that proof (*sādhana*) employed by the proponent.
The meaning is: because it demonstrates the incapacity [of the reason] with respect to the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*).
Alternatively, the word *sādhana* is used in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*).
He states an example for this very point:
"Like the statement of a single means of proof.
This is an analysis of the very first [point], beginning with "just as," and so forth.

Even though there exists a plurality of means of proof—such as existence, being an effect, or being produced by effort—for the purpose of establishing a single object such as momentariness, [the proof is established] by employing only one of those, such as existence.

Because that object, such as momentariness, is established—that is, ascertained—through even one [reason], there is no need to employ all the means of proof (*sādhana*). Likewise, because the proof of that [object] is thwarted by even a single fault (*doṣa*), there is no need to employ all [faults]. Thus, there is a similarity with the example of the finger.
Therefore, the proponent of the subsequent position (*uttarapakṣavādī*) is not subject to defeat merely by pointing out one prior fault, on the grounds of failing to point out another fault.

The phrase "as before" [is used] because the argument was not established by means of a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) and because no actual fault was pointed out. Now, one might ask: how can there be victory for the proponent when he did not employ a fallacious proof?

But since the opponent raises a non-existent fault, he says: for the proponent there is no victory when he fails to drive back—that is, to turn away—the respondent who is speaking a fallacious objection; that is to say, when he fails to demonstrate that what was stated by the other is a fallacious refutation. Why? Because the members of the proof are not properly coordinated.
The state of being that which possesses a means of proof lacking its constituent parts is "deficiency" (*asamanvitatva*).
Why is this so? He says:
because the constituent parts of the proof are established by demonstrating the absence of all defects.
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used [here] in the sense of a characteristic mark of a state (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*) or as an instrument (*karaṇa*), according to Pāṇini 2.3.21–29.
The concise meaning is that because it is not established, what has been employed by him is merely a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*).
It follows that there is likewise no victory for the proponent of the counter-position (*uttarapakṣavādin*).

"Therefore, even in this way" (*tasmādevamapi*): the word "even" (*api*) implies that if the proponent (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) does not point out that the opponent (*uttarapakṣavādī*) has reached a state of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), it is not only in connection with the latter's [specific] response. || 0 ||
The objection against one who is not to be objected to;
the declaration "you are defeated" when a ground for defeat has not been reached.
To the question "Why do you say this?", he replies:

3) The meaning is: because of the incorrect determination of the definition of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), that is, due to not correctly understanding the aforementioned definition of the points of defeat.
And thus, one is defeated through non-comprehension (*apratipatti*).
Regarding this, the Teacher says "here too," and so forth.

If one should charge [the opponent] thus: "This proof you have employed is flawed by defects such as *savyabhicāra* (inconclusiveness) and others—unreal and false defects against the proponent; therefore, you are defeated," then that [accusation] is an exposition in the wrong place. This is because this [defeat] belongs specifically to the classification of a faultless point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). The term "accuser" (*abhiyoktṛ*) is explained as "one who brings to light" (*udbhāvayitṛ*).

Thus, when one expresses a false fault, since the respondent fails to understand the rebuttal characterized by the pointing out of that fault and instead merely utters [something else], the respondent is defeated by *aprati-bhā* (lack of ingenuity) acting as the cause. Therefore, this [utterance of a false fault] is not a separate point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "accusing one who should not be accused" (*aniranuyojyānuyoga*), but rather is included within the point of defeat known as *aprati-bhā*. He states when this person is defeated by *aprati-bhā*:

The intention is that if the other debater demonstrates that what was stated [by the first] is a fallacious reply (*uttarābhāsa*), otherwise there would be neither victory nor defeat for either of the two as before. Having thus established that this is not mentioned separately in connection with the respondent (*prativādin*), he speaks also in connection with the proponent (*vādin*): "Now, [if the proponent points out] a real and true defect in the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*)—such as being inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*)—" to the respondent.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), addressing the opponent who is manifesting a direction [of argument], should attack him with a statement regarding a fallacious fault (*doṣābhāsa*):
"A futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*), such as an inconclusive [reason] (*anaikāntika*) or other fallacy, has been employed by you;
therefore, you are defeated."

The meaning is: if one should thus challenge [the opponent] by saying "it is a *toṣī*," then, once that fault—such as the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*)—which was pointed out, has been demonstrated by the respondent (*uttaravādin*) to be a real fault, the status of it being a *jāti* (futile rejoinder) is thereby refuted; such is the sense.
The proponent is defeated by the very statement of what constitutes a fallacious proof.
Therefore, even in this way, since this [fallacy] does not differ from the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) even when considered in relation to the opponent, it should be stated separately.

This very point is further reinforced by the fact that one who maintains twenty-two points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) must necessarily state the fallacies of the reason as a distinct category of defeat.
He asks: for what purpose? [And he replies:]

The intention is that [the list] includes even those cases where the collection [of arguments] has not been attacked by points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) such as "irrelevant rejoinder" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*) for the sake of reaching another subject; otherwise, the acceptance of twenty-two points of defeat would be contradicted. And thus, when they are stated—meaning, when those fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) have been stated as points of defeat—the opponent's statement follows.
The statement of another [type of defeat], namely the "objection against one who is not to be censured" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), is purposeless,
because it is already subsumed under the mention of "fallacious reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*).

The sūtra states: "Deviation from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*) is the introduction of an irrelevant topic (*kathāprasaṅga*) after having accepted a tenet (*siddhānta*), due to a lack of consistency. This means that after having accepted a tenet—that is, having undertaken the adoption of a thesis—due to a lack of consistency, one obstructs the previously established subject matter by disregarding the systematic rules of the treatise (*śāstra*). "Introduction of an irrelevant topic" refers to the description of a different subject matter.

"Of some object" refers to a further property of the subject (*dharmin*) having been asserted; contradiction (*virodha*) is the reversal of that which was asserted. He clarifies this by means of an example:
"Just as there is no destruction of an existing entity without any residue, but only its disappearance; nor does a non-existent thing, such as a donkey's horn, arise."
Rather, [it arises] from manifestation.
Having thus presented the established doctrine of the followers of Kapila—that what already exists is produced—the author formulates his position:
"The unmanifest is the single primordial nature (prakṛti) of the manifest."
"Of the manifest" refers to the mahat and so forth.
Here he states the reason: because one observes the persistence (anvaya) of modifications such as sound and the rest. The example is "of those things that persist as clay," and so on.
And thus, this is the application (*upanaya*):
