"endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion," which demonstrates its being composed of pleasure and the rest.
And the fact that the manifest (*vyakta*) is composed of pleasure and the rest has already been demonstrated previously, according to what is accepted by the Sāṃkhya.

Therefore, this differentiation of manifest entities—that they possess a single primordial nature by virtue of pleasure and so forth—is the conclusion. In the phrase "by pleasure and so forth" (*sukhādibhiḥ*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of a defining characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, [the world] is characterized by pleasure and so forth, having pleasure and so forth as its mode.
The meaning is that its primordial nature (prakṛti) is one.
Others read it thus:
"The primordial nature is one, because a continuity is observed among manifest transformations."
And they explain it as follows:
there is one primordial nature (*prakṛti*), undivided and having the essence of all selves, because of the observation of its persistence (*anvaya*) in manifest and unmanifest transformations.

This is because its persistence is observed even in those manifest transformations such as the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, as well as in those unmanifest ones that abide within the self of the Primal Substance (*pradhāna*).
Others, however, read it differently: "The unmanifest is a single primordial nature;
[it is the source] of manifest transformations," by which they mean the transformations that take manifest form.
In order to demonstrate how this [system] proceeded by way of a perversion of the original meaning, he says:
"That very follower of Kapila, having spoken thus, is being questioned."
"Now, how are both 'primordial nature' (prakṛti) and 'modification' (vikāra) to be characterized and understood? Being thus questioned, he replied:

That which remains constant while one property ceases and another property arises is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), whose form is stable; that other property which undergoes such arising and ceasing is to be characterized as a modification (*vikāra*). However, the Sāṅkhya has stated that this [position] is undermined by the fault of abandoning the intended meaning of the subject matter.
The proponent of the "I-am" doctrine (*so'yam-vādī*), by reversing the subject matter under discussion and due to a lack of consistency, leads the debate to an undesirable conclusion;
that is to say, he abandons what was previously introduced.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Indeed, he has made this very promise," thus he recalls what was stated previously.
To the question, "If this is so, what is the fault? he says:
"Of the existent and the non-existent," and so forth.
Without the absolute disappearance—that is, the destruction—of an existent thing, the cessation of the activity of any dharma cannot be established.
If it exists in some altered state, that hidden part must be either identical with or different from the persisting entity.

If it were identical, then because it would not be distinct from the hidden part, one would have to suspect that what persists is non-existent just like the hidden part; and conversely, because it is not distinct from the persisting part, one would suspect that even the hidden part is existent.
Even if [the effect] were something other [than the cause], how could there be continuity? There would be no destruction [of the cause], for when one thing persists, another does not persist.
Nor can one thing be the continuity of another; otherwise, it would follow that a jar could be the continuity of anything whatsoever.
Likewise, the activity of any property is not established without the manifestation or production of what was previously non-existent.
But surely it is only another existing property that is manifested;
it is brought into the state of being an object of apprehension.
For there is no action or acquisition of what already exists, because it is already present.

The Sāṅkhya, having been refuted by the opponent who argues that [the effect] is not produced by a cause, is in some cases met with the locative case. In that context, it should be explained as: "when the opponent has thus stood his ground."

If that proponent accepts the destruction of an existing entity (*sat*) and the origination of a non-existent entity (*asat*), then he falls into the fallacy of contradicting his own tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
The meaning is that because he asserts something contrary to what he has previously accepted, he incurs the point of defeat known as *apasiddhānta*.
Alternatively, if he does not accept the destruction of an existing entity nor the origination of a non-existent entity...

Even so, this position previously asserted— that there is a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*) for all transformations (*vikāra*)— is not established, because the definition of primordial nature and transformation is untenable.
For it was stated that their definition applies to "that which remains constant," and that [definition] is inapplicable here.
The portion of another's text ending with "of the existent and non-existent," etc., has been set forth;
here, the Master now offers a rebuttal. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "For this reason as well, we offer a rebuttal."
There is no undesirable consequence for the Sāṅkhya due to lack of restriction, because that would contradict the logic of his own established tenets.
Therefore, this was stated in order to support the position he has accepted: that what is non-existent does not arise, and what exists does not disappear.
He asks, "What was said? and replies:
"This manifest world has a single primordial nature (ekaprakṛtika), because of the observation of a commonality (anvaya).
He then analyzes this very term "single" [as follows].
This manifest world has its origin in that which is undivided;

those [qualities], pleasure and the rest, are the undivided—meaning non-distinct—origin, place, or substratum of this manifest world, and thus it is said to have an undivided origin. For what reason? Because of the observation of their persistence; because one observes their persistence and perceives their identity with those qualities of pleasure and the rest.

To the question, "What is established from this?", he says: "The manifest has that as its nature," meaning it has pleasure and so forth as its nature. To the question, "How is its very nature ascertained there?", he says:
"Because of the perception of non-difference."
This means that because one does not perceive a difference between sound and the like on the one hand and pleasure and the like on the other.
Even so, what is established? He says:
it is possible that there is neither arising nor destruction for the entire aggregate of transformations—sound and the rest—which consists of pleasure and the like.
He asks "Why? and replies:
because there is no arising or destruction of pleasure and the other [qualities].
Since sound and the others are non-different from pleasure and the rest, they too are established as eternal, just like the self.
And thus, that which was previously accepted— that there is no destruction without a cause and that what is non-existent does not arise—
is thereby established.

In this very context, when the follower of Kapila has thus established his own position, Akṣapāda— without pointing out any defects such as the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason (the demonstration of positive concomitance) stated by that Sāṅkhya— responds as follows. Then, asking for the definitions of both the modification and the primal nature (*prakṛti*) in the form, "How is it to be characterized that the primal nature is devoid of modification?", this Akṣapāda himself, by deviating from the subject at hand due to a lack of restriction, obstructs the relevant topic.

He initiates this discussion: since the definition of the relationship between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*) was not the very subject under consideration here, why is it being introduced and then subjected to inquiry? Therefore, because he is inquiring about something irrelevant, the meaning is that Akṣapāda alone is worthy of defeat.
However, he states that the following sentence is connected to this [point]:
"In that regard, concerning the reason for observing positive concomitance (*anvaya*), this should be stated:

'Indeed, the manifest (*vyakta*) possesses the properties of engagement and withdrawal; however, pleasure and so forth do not possess the properties of engagement and withdrawal like the manifest. Here, the connection is made by modifying the gender and number [of the terms]."

And thus, regarding the connection of the manifest with pleasure and so forth, the explanation—that if it were of the nature of pleasure and so forth, the characteristic of having the properties of activity and cessation would be lost for the manifest—is untenable;
because, being non-different from that [pleasure], they too would exist eternally.
Therefore, the manifest does not have a nature consisting of pleasure and so forth devoid of those [properties].
Those who are devoid of those two—activity and cessation—are described as such; and "those" refers to pleasure and the rest.
That which has these as its nature is [the self], and the state of being that is "the state of having a nature consisting of pleasure and the rest devoid of those.
He asks, "Why? and says:

"Because of the contradiction with the characteristics of the manifest (*vyakta*). The characteristic of the manifest is its nature of having the properties of activity and cessation; [the unmanifest] is the opposite of that. Furthermore, there is a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion between pleasure and the other [feeling-states].

Consequently, this manifest of yours would result in being non-existent, because it would possess a nature consisting of pleasure and the like that exist eternally, since it would have properties contrary to those [of the manifest].
Nor is the reason—namely, the non-perception of the association with pleasure and so forth—established as being like that of the *kṣetrajña*.
Why is this criticism relevant?

He says: for in this way, by pointing out the defect in the Sāṅkhya’s proof and by challenging the unestablished nature of the reason, the thesis "this manifest world has a single primordial material cause" becomes refuted.

Furthermore, that Naiyāyika, failing to point out the flaw called "unestablishedness" (*asiddhatā*) in the proof, prolongs the debate by means of an irrelevant inquiry into the characteristics of the primary cause (*prakṛti*) and its modifications (*vikāra*), while not relinquishing his own fault. He thus casts this extraneous issue upon the poor Sāṅkhya opponent. The opponent replies: "This very flaw called 'unestablishedness' is also asserted by us through this method, namely, by way of the inquiry into the characteristics of the primary cause and its modifications."
The Teacher said:
"This is the domain of those who interpret omens and those who know the science of astrology;
it does not mean what you have stated in your words."

Since the world is not capable of understanding a meaning that has not been communicated by words—provided there is no supplementation [of missing terms] through context, purpose, and so forth—it follows that this very "logic of the clown's painting" (*bhaṇḍālekhyanyāya*), which was previously pointed out in the discussion on the contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*), constitutes an "abandonment of a tenet" (*apasiddhānta*) here as well; it is not merely a term used in that [previous] context. For just as clowns, in order to amaze common folk, draw a very small line in the shape of a half-moon and quickly say, "Look! We have drawn an elephant the size of a palm tree!"
In this regard, some of dull intellect understand it exactly as it is; others, being perversely clever, raise an objection:
"Surely its ears, feet, tusks, and so forth are not perceived; how then can this be an elephant devoid of those parts?"
They replied:
"It is true that they are not recognized;
however, we have depicted this elephant with every detail fully completed."
Just as all its parts are not perceived because they are submerged in water, yet only this portion of the jar is perceived, so too is this [position] of another merely a manifestation of audacity;
for even if this object is not actually cognized as external to it, it is nevertheless stated in this manner.

Furthermore, although this very same point has been stated in this manner, since that which is unestablished (*asiddha*) is included among the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), it is expressed by that very [category]; thus, it would not be appropriate to adopt it as a separate "departure from a tenet" (*apasiddhānta*). With the guise of a conclusion, he says:
"By the logic already stated," and so forth.
"And the fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsas) are as previously stated" is the sūtra. Vātsyāyana explains this by means of a preliminary objection:
"But what [is meant]?"—that is to say, they incur the status of points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) because of their connection with a definition other than the definition of a fallacious reason.
To the question "In what way?", he says:

just as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) come to possess the status of objects of cognition (prameyatva) by virtue of another characteristic; for they [are so called] because they are the causes of the act of valid cognition (pramiti).
When, however, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇas*) are themselves cognized by another means of valid cognition, they are then objects of cognition (*prameyas*) because they function as objects.
Consequently, since they possess the status of being categories (*padārthas*), a doubt arises.
To this, [the author] says: "As stated by the Sage."
This is its explanation:
that the state of being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurs precisely through the aforementioned definition of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
This is what is meant:

Having introduced the classification of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) as "the erratic, the contradictory, the equal-to-the-question (*prakaraṇasama*), the equal-to-the-probandum (*sādhyasama*), and the mistimed" (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.4), the definition for each one was stated.

The inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is that which deviates [from the probandum] (*savyabhicāra*). (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.5) The contradictory (*viruddha*) is that which, having accepted a tenet (*siddhānta*), contradicts it.

(Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.6) That for which there is deliberation regarding the subject (*prakaraṇacintā*) and which is adduced for the sake of a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*) is the "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*). (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.7)
7) "That which is not distinct from the thesis, because it is itself yet to be proven, is 'equal to the thesis' (sādhyasama)" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.8);
"that which is stated when the time has passed is 'mistimed' (kālātīta)" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.9).
By these very definitions, their status as points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) is established; no further definition is required for them.
Regarding this point, the Teacher says: "In this case as well.
He asks how they are to be considered:
"Do those [categories] exist exactly as their divisions have been characterized by you, or rather otherwise?"
The analysis is as follows: "those for whom a distinction has been observed.
To the question, "What then is that which is being considered? he says: "But that which is being considered here would lead to an over-extension; therefore, it is not elaborated upon."
This very point has been restated:

some recognize that here certain fallacies of reason (*hetvābhāsa*) are simply not applicable, while others are not even included among the fallacies of reason; and if one were to introduce the entire *Hetvābhāsavārttika* into this investigation, it would become a separate treatise altogether.
However, those of pure intellect, because they are far removed from the opposite of the characteristics of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) as formulated by us, [perceive] that disparity;
therefore, indifference alone is appropriate for them.
Nevertheless, this treatise is also being composed for the sake of awakening those of dull intellect.
The way in which the status of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is untenable for both the *kālātīta* and the *prakaraṇasama* is now described.

Among these, the *kālātīta* is that which is "indicated by the lapse of time. Regarding this, having set aside the opinion of the ancient Naiyāyikas because it was spoken against by the venerable teacher Diṅnāga, contemporary scholars such as Vātsyāyana and others maintain this very position.
Regarding this, we say the following:

that whose portion of the meaning being taught is associated with the lapse of time is called "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), or "one whose time has passed" (*kālātīta*). An illustration [is as follows]:
Sound is eternal because it is manifested by conjunction, like color. Just as color, which exists prior to and after its manifestation, is manifested through the conjunction of a lamp and a jar,
so too sound, being eternally present, is manifested through the conjunction of a drum and the ear, or through the contact of wood and a leaf.

Therefore, because it is manifested by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), sound is eternal. This is not a valid reason, because it is a case of "pointing out a lapse in time" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*). The manifestation of the object to be manifested does not exceed the time of the manifesting conjunction; when there is conjunction with a lamp, the form is perceived, but once the conjunction has ceased, the form is no longer perceived.

But when the conjunction of wood and leaf has ceased, the sound is heard at a distance at the time of their disjunction; thus, this manifestation of the sound transcends the time of the conjunction, and so it is caused by the conjunction.
For it is a principle that in the absence of the cause, there is an absence of the effect.
[Objection: But is this not indeed inconclusive?
"Because it is manifested by conjunction.

[The opponent argues: "Even that which is impermanent is seen to be manifested by conjunction, as in the case of a jar. [The author replies: No; we do not say that sound is eternal because its persistence is established on the grounds of being manifested by conjunction. We do not claim that sound is eternal.

However, if the meaning of the thesis is "the sound persists," then the reason "because it is manifested by conjunction" becomes inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For nothing that is non-persistent is ever manifested by conjunction.
How so? By this very method, the fact that sound is manifested by conjunction is precisely what is being negated; thus, this [reason] does not avoid the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddha*).
Otherwise, if this manifestation of sound were not to persist beyond the time of the conjunction, it would not be caused by conjunction.

It must be stated what the meaning of this statement is. One might think that [a reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) if it does not exist at all in the subject (*dharmin*); however, this [reason] is not unestablished in every respect, since at the time of its production, it possesses the quality of being manifested by conjunction (*saṃyoga-vyaṅgyatva*).
But it is not at the time of apprehension.
As it has been said:
"Because even that which is unestablished in one respect is recognized as being unestablished."

For example: "Atoms are eternal because they possess odor," and "Trees are sentient because they sleep. Furthermore, one who asserts that sound is impermanent must necessarily accept that sound arises from the conjunction of an axe and wood, and so forth.
Furthermore, since it is not the case that what is already present is manifested, this reason is unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddhatva*).
If it is argued in defense that this reason is not unestablished because the meaning of the reason is accepted as "because [the object] is perceived when there is conjunction," even so,
lamps, pots, and the like are perceived when there is a conjunction of oil, wick, and flame, as well as when there is a conjunction of a potter, a lump of clay, and a staff.
Furthermore, because their state of non-attainment of conjunction does not persist there, the reason becomes inconclusive; thus, it is not a case of "missing the time" (kālātīta).

Moreover, if one intends to prove that they persist even at a later time, the argument is contradictory for one who maintains the doctrine of the dissolution of the composite whole (*samudāyāntaravyayavādin*).

Precisely because there is no similar instance (sapakṣa), there is an absence of presence therein; yet, it exists in a subject (dharmin) such as form (rūpa) and so forth, which possesses the property of momentary duration.

However, for one who maintains that existence is permanent, there is a failure of the probans due to the absence of an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) and a lack of efficacy in the proof (*sādhanavaiphalya*).

Furthermore, when the opponent is a proponent of logic (*nyāyavādin*) who does not accept the established doctrine (*asiddhānta*), the defect previously set forth in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) applies.
In this manner, the refutation should be formulated by considering similar cases in other examples as well. || 0 ||

Because it is that for which there is an investigation of the matter (*prakaraṇa*), it is designated as "the equal-to-the-matter" (*prakaraṇasama*) for the purpose of reaching a decision. (Nyāya Sūtra 1.2.7) The "matter" (*prakaraṇa*) consists of the thesis and the counter-thesis, which are based on doubt and remain unsettled; the "investigation" (*cintā*) of that matter is the examination starting from the doubt until before the decision. That [fallacy] occurs where such an investigation has been made for the sake of a decision.

Because it remains within the scope of the inquiry by being equally applicable to both sides, the *prakaraṇasama* (the "equivalent-to-the-inquiry" fallacy) is not fit for reaching a definitive conclusion.

Why, then, is there an inquiry into the matter? Because the inquiry ceases once the reality of the object has been apprehended; therefore, when that which has been understood in a general way is not apprehended in its specific details, that lack of specific apprehension instigates the inquiry.
The example is: "Sound is impermanent because its permanent properties are not perceived.
That which is observed to have impermanent properties when its permanent properties are not perceived is seen, for instance, in the case of a pot and so forth.
When a common property is adduced as a cause for doubt, that is the "equal-to-doubt" (saṃśayasama) fallacy, which is indeed a form of the "inconclusive" (savyabhicāra).
However, when an inquiry requires further investigation and no specific property is perceived for either of the two sides, that initiates a *prakaraṇa* (a formal debate).
For instance, just as a permanent property is not perceived in sound, so too is an impermanent property.
This non-perception of specific properties on both sides necessitates an inquiry into the *prakaraṇa*; for how could the debate be resolved if the opposite were the case?
If a permanent property were perceived in the word, the context would not be applicable;
if a non-permanent property were perceived, the context would likewise be set aside.
Thus, this reason, by operating upon both sides, is not fit for the determination of either one.
But this [reason] is not identical with the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*).
It is not non-distinct,
because that very property which is the cause for the commencement of the discussion is employed as the reason (*hetu*).

Where a property identical to that of the probandum (*sādhya*) is adduced as the reason (*hetu*), that is "indistinguishable from the probandum" (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*). On the other hand, where the reason is precisely that which causes the debate to proceed, that is "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*).
Here too, the deliberation regarding the point at issue arises solely from the non-perception of both the properties of permanence and impermanence.

But not from a single [reason], because of the statement: "In the case of the opposite, there is the cessation of the context. Therefore, if this were the reason—"because of the non-perception of permanent and impermanent properties"—[it would be insufficient].

It might be argued that this is a *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized reason). However, if one takes the non-perception of a property belonging to only one of the two sides as the basis, one must explain how it can be called *prakaraṇasama*.

Furthermore, even if one takes the non-perception of properties belonging to both sides as the basis, since there is no certainty regarding the presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) or the exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), it becomes an uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason; so how could this be a [valid] reason?
As for the state of having an internal interval:
let it be granted that the non-perception of a single property (*ekadharmānupalabdhi*) alone is the reason;
even so, since the proponent of the eternality of sound must necessarily perceive eternal properties due to delusion, this remains unestablished for the opponent (*prativādyasiddha*).

Now, if it is argued that the non-perception of eternal properties (*nityadharma*) is established by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the refutation of eternal properties, even then, because it functions as a determiner, this [reason] is indeed a cause of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); how then could it be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) of the "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) type?
For in that case, the meaning of the reason is established precisely as the perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣopalabdhi*).
Furthermore, specific properties such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth do not belong to that which is eternal.
Nor is there an investigation of the subject (*prakaraṇacintā*) based on those [properties], because of the statement: "For in the case of the opposite, the subject ceases to exist.

Moreover, regarding the phrase "because the properties of an eternal thing are not perceived," is this a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), or is it an affirmation of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogividhāna*)?

If it is an absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), then this perception of the property of permanence is a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason, like "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth; for a mere negation is possible even in non-existent things that lack impermanence.
If, on the other hand, it is an affirmation of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi-vidhāna*), then by the reasoning just stated, it is unfit to be a semblance of a reason (*hetu-pratirūpaka*).
However, another [author] explains these two sūtras differently.

That reason which, having been stated at the time of the reason, passes away or departs—why does it depart? Because it is contradicted by perception, by scripture, or by both; being thus sublated, it has passed its proper time and is therefore called "kālātīta" (a reason that has passed its time).
If it is asked, "How, then, can a contradiction with perception or scripture be found?
[the answer is: because of the statement that "the logical reason has four characteristics.
For instance, [these are] the *pūrvavat*, the *śeṣavat*, and the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.5).
5) Here, in this context, the reason is held to be fourfold:
"pūrvavat" means that which pervades the probandum;
"śeṣavat" means that which exists in what is similar to it.
It is that which is generally observed and not contradicted by verbal testimony.
Likewise, there is also a statement in the Bhāṣya:
"Furthermore, that inference which is contradicted by perception or scripture is a fallacy of reasoning (nyāyābhāsa)."
Thus, when the three conditions [of a valid reason] are present, that which is sublated by perception or scripture is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
It is divided into three types: contradicted by perception, contradicted by scripture, and contradicted by both.
An example of what is contradicted by perception is: "Fire is not hot, because it is a substance, like water."
An example of contradiction with scripture (*āgamaviruddha*) is: "Wine should be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa, because it is liquid, like milk.
An example of contradiction with both [scripture and perception] is: "The visual faculty is like a ray of light, because it is a sense organ, like the olfactory faculty and so forth.
Now, this is certainly not a contradiction of the thesis (*pakṣavirodha*), because contradiction of the thesis has already been rejected.
This is the lack of clarity regarding the understanding of the definition of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*).

For when the three characteristics—namely the triad beginning with "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*)—are thoroughly ascertained by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and there exists a sublation (*bādhā*) regarding that [subject], then there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
This is because sublation and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) are mutually contradictory.

For inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is the presence of the reason (*hetu*) only when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is present; how then could that which possesses such a definition be a reason in a subject (*dharmin*) where the property to be proven is not [present]? This and other points should be stated here in accordance with the refutation regarding the "unsublated object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*). Furthermore, in those cases where this sublation (*bādhā*) has been cited, there is not even a slight degree of the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*), due to a deficiency in the necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
Furthermore, for one who employs a formal argument (*prayoga*) based on an accepted thesis (*pakṣa*), it is appropriate that this be considered a fault of the thesis itself.
As for the extensive and irrelevant arguments raised in order to avoid the charge of a faulty thesis, they are utterly worthless and are not examined here.
Since it is said that "an investigation [arises] from a topical context" (*prakaraṇa*), the *prakaraṇa* has been defined in the Bhāṣya. An example of this is as follows:
regarding the inquiry as to whether or not an atom (*aṇu*) is established as being produced by another atom, someone might state:
[The argument is: "An atom is the effect of another atom because it possesses color and other qualities, like a dyad (dvyaṇuka) and so forth.

Regarding that atom which is taken as the cause, since it too possesses color and other qualities, there arises the inquiry: "Is this [atom] the effect of another atom because it possesses color and other qualities, or not? And if, in this inquiry, one says that even that [atom] is the effect of another atom because it possesses color and other qualities, then since that [atom] also possesses color and other qualities, the inquiry recurs. Thus, it sets in motion a discussion in the form of an infinite regress; therefore, it is called *prakaraṇasama* (the equal-to-the-issue).

Now, if it is argued that the atom does not admit of being an effect of another atom because it possesses color and other qualities, then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, the "equal-to-the-issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacy is distinguished from the inconclusive.
Nor is this [reason] contradictory (*viruddha*), because it does not establish the opposite;
nor is it unestablished (*asiddha*), because its presence as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is observed.
It is not "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), because it is not sublated by perception or scripture;
therefore, it is a different matter (arthāntara).
Alternatively, the meaning is that the establishment of the cause consists in its occurrence in a specific location and its relevance to the context (prakaraṇa).

This [fallacy] called *pradeśasama* (the "equal to the part") is that for which the reason is stated because of a specific instance (*pradeśa*). It is "equal" (*sama*) because it is equal in its capacity to prove the subject (*prakaraṇa*), since it is non-probative with respect to one part and likewise with respect to the other; thus, it is "equal" due to the commonality of its lack of probative power. Therefore, a property (*dharma*) residing in only one part is *prakaraṇasama*.
For example: "Earth, water, fire, air, and space are impermanent because they possess existence (*sattāvat*), like [the other elements].
In this case as well, if one who follows the doctrine of Akṣapāda (Gautama) were to formulate the following proof:

"An atom (*paramāṇu*) is preceded by another atom because it possesses color and so forth (*rūpādimat*), like a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth," then that would constitute a contradiction with what he himself accepts; thus, this [fallacy] does not differ from the "past time" (*atītakāla*) fallacy.

Now, suppose a Buddhist were to offer this argument; even then, the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished (*asiddhi*), because atoms are not admitted to exist apart from form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities].
Furthermore, since dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth are impossible and do not exist, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of both [the subject and the predicate].

Even when a proponent of logic (*nyāyavādī*) speaks without regard for established tenets (*siddhānta*), the defects pointed out regarding the second alternative (*pakṣa*) do not cease; thus, this [fallacy] does not differ from the "unestablished" (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, that property which resides in only one part of the subject (*anumeyaikadeśavartin*), such as "earth and so forth are non-eternal because they possess odor," is also included within the "contrary to tenet" (*apasiddhānta*) and need not be mentioned separately. It is not "unestablished," because it is a property residing in one part of the subject.

If it is argued that [the definition] is like "subsisting in one part of the similar instances" (*sapakṣaikadeśavartin*), this is an unequal comparison. For in the phrase "existence only in the similar instances" (*sapakṣa eva sattvam*), the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is indeed conjoined [with "only"], but it does not establish that the probans possesses the property of all similar instances. On the other hand, the statement of existence in the object of inference (*anumeya*)—acting as a regulator by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*)—establishes that [the probans] is a property of every individual subject (*sādhyadharmin*). It is by this very [definition] that the various types of "unestablished in one part of the subject" (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*) are excluded.
To say that [the word] "done" (kṛta) is a redundant effort is merely a trifle. || 0 ||
Bhāvivikta also falls right here into the "braying donkey" [of incoherence].
He attempts to justify *prakaraṇasama* otherwise:

"Because the investigation of the matter (*prakaraṇacintā*)—that is, the consideration of the counter-position—occurs subsequently, a reason characterized in this way, when being taught for the sake of a definitive conclusion, becomes *prakaraṇasama*."

When the subject (*prakaraṇa*) is to be proven, [the reason] is equal (*sama*) whether it concerns existence or non-existence. For example: "The omniscient one exists, because he is free from that which is other than him and its opposite, just like form (*rūpa*), etc.
Since this reason is the same in both cases, it is equally applicable even to one who seeks to prove non-existence:
"Omniscience does not exist, because it is free from that which is other than it and its opposite, just like a donkey’s horn."
Nor is this [reason] inconclusive despite possessing both properties, because of the absence of its occurrence in the counter-example (vipakṣa).
This very point has been refuted by the Master himself in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*: "But how, in this case, do you conceive of the counter-example as the absence of the probandum?"

How, then, [can one say] that "the presence of the reason in the counter-example (vipakṣa) possesses both properties," and so forth? Furthermore, whatever was stated in the explanation of the term "object" (artha) must also be said here. Moreover, its specific refutation has already been set forth in detail.
Thus, the [fallacies of] *prakaraṇasama* (the counter-balanced) and *atītakāla* (the mistimed) are untenable.

However, it is appropriate that the deviation from the probandum (*sādhyavyabhicāra*) constitutes a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), though not in the manner you accept. For you do not admit that a reason whose exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Because it is accepted that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established by mere non-perception alone; for this very reason, you yourselves, free from doubt, employ the following argument: "The eyes and ears reach their objects, because they are external sense organs, like the nose and so forth."
"Perceptual cognition accompanied by conceptual construction (*savikalpa-pratyakṣa*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it possesses the nature of inference (*anumāna*), and so forth.

Furthermore, it has been elaborated elsewhere that the establishment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot occur through mere non-perception alone in the absence of an invariable relation (*pratibandha*).
"That which does not establish the existence of the self, clay, consciousness, and so forth..."
By the passage beginning with "Is that very non-perception the prover of the absence of the reason? [it is shown that non-perception is not a valid reason].

Likewise, you yourselves maintain that even when the presence or absence [of the reason] in the similar and dissimilar instances (*sapakṣa* and *vipakṣa*) is doubtful, it can still be a cause for correct knowledge and not an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason—as in the case of the argument: "The living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth. And its validity in that regard has been established in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya* and other works. As for the variety of the contradictory (*viruddha*) reason formulated by Bhāradvāja, it has already been refuted in the section concerning contradiction with the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*).

Regarding that which is described as "established otherwise" (anyathāsiddha) even in the case of the "equal-to-the-probandum" (sādhyasama)— for example, "atoms are non-eternal because they possess activity, like a jar"— this too is indeed said to be equal to the probandum, because the atoms' possession of activity is due to their having form, action, color, and so forth, and not due to their non-eternality. That [objection] is not tenable.
Since it must be established in the subject (*dharmin*), a reason that exists in the subject cannot be considered unestablished;
for if it were, it would follow that all reasons would be unestablished.
This is not so, because the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) does not consist merely in the fact that [the reason] will exist in the subject.
For the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is intended by virtue of the probandum (*sādhya*).
Since it is the [probandum] alone that is to be proven,

if the property to be proven cannot exist in the subject without that means of proof (*sādhana*), and if that means of proof cannot exist in the subject in the absence of the property to be proven, then from that reason follows the property of being a feature of the subject.

Furthermore, when a property is established even otherwise in the subject (dharmin) that has been taken up for proof, then it possesses the very nature of being a reason (*hetu*). In this way, existence (*sattva*) is intended as a specific [property] by virtue of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Otherwise, [if it were merely existence], its being "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhatva*) would indeed be equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*). This is the rebuttal here: if, indeed, existence is intended as a property of the subject precisely in such a way that the reason is impossible in the subject when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is absent—and not as mere existence—[then it is a valid reason].

In that case, is this "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) which reveals the object of inference something that remains unascertained, or is it something already fully determined? Regarding these two alternatives, if it were a revealer while remaining unascertained, it would overstep the logic of a probative reason (*jñāpaka-hetu*).
For a probative reason reveals the object to be known only when it depends upon its own cognition.
Moreover, if reasons were capable of dispelling disagreement by their mere existence alone, then the diversity of mutually contradictory doctrines among opponents would not exist.

Even if that which has been cognized is communicative, its definitive ascertainment must arise either from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or from something other than a means of valid cognition. It cannot arise from what is not a means of valid cognition, because that which is not a means of valid cognition lacks the capacity to cause the ascertainment of a real object; otherwise, its status as a means of valid cognition would be undermined.
For this alone constitutes the validity of a means of valid cognition: namely, its quality of illuminating an object exactly as it exists.

If this [property of being a property of the subject] belongs even to that which is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then how can the existence of a reason—which cannot subsist in the subject to be proven (*sādhya-dharmin*) without the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*)—be apprehended as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) on the basis of such an invalid means? For in that case as well, since the establishment of the reason arises from the very same means of knowledge from which the establishment of the property to be proven arises, for what purpose is this useless form of the reason (*hetu-rūpa*) adopted?

Nor is it reasonable to say that the establishment of the probans alone occurs from that [evidence], while the establishment of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) does not; for this would entail the consequence that the probans itself is unestablished by that [evidence]. For indeed, this probans is established in that subject (dharmin) only if it is established that it is not possible here without this property to be proven, but is possible only together with it. And if that is so, one must reflect upon why the establishment of the property to be proven does not likewise arise from that very same means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

And thus, by that very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be a relationship of the signified and the signifier between this property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and that [cognition], but not with this reason (*hetu*); consequently, a great undesirable consequence (*mahadaniṣṭa*) ensues.

Furthermore, if one relies upon such a form of "property-of-the-subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*), then as long as the probandum is unestablished, the reason is likewise unestablished, and as long as the reason is unestablished, the probandum is likewise unestablished; thus, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

Furthermore, since the establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is accomplished at the very moment of ascertaining the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), it is useless to subsequently pursue the nature of the subsequent marks [of concomitance]. Thus, the reason should not be described as having two characteristics, four characteristics, or five characteristics. In our view, however, once the mere existence [of the reason] in the subject is known, the knowledge of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) follows thereafter; or rather, the positive and negative concomitances themselves are known through a universal generalization (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) at a subsequent time.

Since only the existence [of the reason] in the subject (*dharmin*) has been cognized, the cognition of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in that [subject] is established by its very force through immediate succession.
Therefore, this entire web of faults finds no footing here, like [a reflection] in the sky or in pure water; enough with these unstable, false prattlings—so we desist.
If this is so, what then is intended here as the desired [conclusion]? He says:

Regarding the phrase "fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), however, according to the rules," and so forth: the statement of those fallacious reasons which are defined by the rules of logic constitutes a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna); and these have been stated by us.
"When there is doubt regarding the non-establishment of one [reason], it partakes in the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddha*) and the inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*);
when both are unestablished, it partakes in the fallacies of the contradictory (*viruddha*), the unestablished, and the inconclusive.
Now, this path of the science of debate was indeed made into a great royal highway by the noble Vasubandhu in his *Vādavidhāna* and other works, he who is the kinsman of all the world’s compositions.

Furthermore, this was already threshed out in the great *Nyāyaparīkṣā* by the venerable teacher Dignāga, who was skilled at splitting the frontal globes of the intoxicated elephant of false doctrines; so why do you now resort to chewing what has already been chewed?
To resolve this objection, he presents this verse beginning with "The world... and so forth.
"Timira" means cataract; "timirapaṭala" is thus the cataract of ignorance (*avidyā*). It is called the "cataract of the darkness of ignorance" because it obstructs the vision of reality.
Its connection [to the title] is: "the *Vādanyāya* is the scraper (*ullekhana*) of that. The word "scraper" (*ullekhana*) is derived as an agent-noun (*kartṛ-sādhana*).
Whose, then, is this cataract of the darkness of ignorance? He says: of the vision of reality—that is, of the seeing of reality;
the meaning is, of the eye of wisdom.

This very method of debate (*vādanyāya*) which has just been explained was composed by the virtuous former teachers, who were devoted to the welfare of others and dependent upon compassion, in order to establish people on the correct path; it has been brought to supreme renown and well-clarified in the world—
this is the meaning.
But it is not out of mutual rivalry, nor from a desire for fame and the like. If that is so, then the objection remains as it was; therefore, he says:
"The light of reality—that is, illumination—has been taught by the teachers through the logic of debate (*vādanyāya*)."

It "darkens" means it makes [the path] shrouded in darkness; that is to say, it obscures it with the gloom of fallacious objections. Who, then, is this most audacious person who seeks to block the path already trodden by the Great Nāgas? He says: "This person"—namely, Udyotakara, Prīticandra, Bhāvivikta, and others—is "wickedly clever," meaning he is devoid of correct discernment.

Since this is so, I have made an effort here in this treatise on the logic of debate (*vādanyāya*) for the purpose of rekindling that [system] which was cast aside by those of middling and inferior intellect after it had been expounded by the great ones.
The concise meaning is: because I am occupied with avoiding fallacious refutations and illuminating its principles, I have not ground what has already been ground.

Though I possess no small power of intellect and have applied myself with great effort, I have not perceived the ultimate essence of this priceless immersion in women; yet, having clearly and correctly analyzed this view, whatever abundant merit I have thereby attained, may it bring peace to all beings. (47)

And may I, having attained the glory of Mañjuśrī— whose vast power is capable of bearing the burden of the Fully Awakened One upon the mountain of faults leveled by the realization of selflessness— become skilled in effecting the destruction of all obscurations for all sentient beings.
By means of great speed itself, nothing here has been abandoned, nor is there anything secluded that needs to be analyzed;
nevertheless, this lamp of light has been ignited for the sake of awakening those of dull intellect.
In the world, it scrapes away the film of the darkness of ignorance for the vision of reality. (48)
This *Vādanyāya* has been correctly composed by him who seeks the welfare of others;
it dispels the darkness that obscures the light of reality. Therefore, I have made this effort here in order to rekindle that very light for those people who are poorly trained. (49)
The commentary on the *Vādanyāya*, titled *Vipañcitārthā*, is completed.
This is the work of the venerable Śāntarakṣita.
It was written by me on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa in the Saṃvat year [blank],
on an auspicious day during the victorious reign of the illustrious Ānandadeva, the supreme lord, the great emperor, the most venerable sovereign.
And the extent of this work has been accurately calculated as two thousand nine hundred [verses] by the learned scholars of old. ||0||
May there be well-being for all the world;
let it be protected with effort by everyone.
Homage to the Omniscient One.
